# Majmu' al-Fatawa - Tome 11

## Page 5350

Volume Eleven
The Book of Sufism

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Praise be to Allah alone, and blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked about the various categories of “Sufis” and “fuqarā’” (the poor): What characterizes each category? What is obligatory for its members, and what path is recommended for them to follow?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The term “Sufis” was not widely known during the first three generations; its use became widespread only afterward. Its use has been reported from several imams and shaykhs, including Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, and others. It has also been related that Sufyān al-Thawrī used it, and some attribute its use to al-Hasan al-Basrī. They disagreed about the “meaning” to which

---

## Page 5351

the designation “Sufi” is related—for it is a relational adjective, like Qurashī (of Quraysh), Madanī (of Medina), and the like.

It has been said that it derives from “Ahl al-Suffa” (the people of the sheltered platform). This is incorrect, for in that case the form would have been Suffī. It has also been said that it derives from the foremost rank before Allah. This too is incorrect, for in that case the form would have been Saffī. Another suggestion is that it derives from the chosen among Allah’s creation. This is incorrect, for in that case the form would have been Safawī.

It has also been said that it derives from Sūfa ibn Murr ibn Udd ibn Tānja, an Arab tribe whose members had resided in Mecca since ancient times, and to whom devout worshippers were said to be affiliated. Although this derivation is sound in form, it too is weak. These people are neither widely known nor familiar to most devout worshippers. Moreover, had devout worshippers been affiliated with them, this designation would more fittingly have existed in the time of the Companions, their successors, and the generation after them. Furthermore, most of those who have used the designation “Sufi” do not know this tribe and would not accept affiliation with a tribe from the pre-Islamic age of ignorance that has no existence in Islam.

It has also been said—and this is the well-known explanation—that it derives from wearing wool. The Sufis first emerged in Basra, and the first small Sufi lodge was built by some of the companions of ʿAbd al-Wāhid ibn Zayd. ʿAbd al-Wāhid was one of the companions of al-Hasan. In Basra there was an intensity of asceticism, worship, fear of Allah, and the like

---

## Page 5352

that was not found among the people of other cities. Hence the saying:

“Jurisprudence is Kufan, and worship is Basran.”

Abū al-Shaykh al-Asbahānī narrated through his chain of transmission that Muhammad ibn Sīrīn heard that some people preferred wearing wool. He said:

“Some people choose wool, saying that they are emulating the Messiah, son of Mary. Yet our Prophet’s way is dearer to us, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wore cotton and other fabrics”—or words to that effect.

Thus, most accounts of extremes in this regard concern devout worshippers from Basra, such as reports of people dying or fainting upon hearing the Quran and the like. One example is the account of Zurāra ibn Awfā, the judge of Basra, who recited during the dawn prayer:

“When the Trumpet is sounded,”

and fell down dead. Another is the account of the blind man Abū Juhayr, to whom Sālih al-Murrī recited, whereupon he died. Others, too, are reported to have died upon hearing his recitation. Among them were groups who would swoon upon hearing the Quran, whereas none of the Companions experienced such a state.

When this phenomenon appeared, a number of the Companions and their successors objected to it, including Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, and others like them.

Those who objected did so on two grounds. Some believed it to be affected and contrived. Muhammad ibn Sīrīn is reported to have said:

“The only way to settle the matter between us and those who swoon upon hearing the Quran is to have it recited to

---

## Page 5353

one of them while he is atop a wall. If he falls, he is sincere.” Others objected because they considered it an innovation contrary to the known way of the Companions, as was reported from Asmā’ and her son ‘Abd Allāh.

The majority of scholars hold that if such a person is involuntarily overcome, he is not to be censured, although the state of someone who remains composed is more perfect. Thus, when Imam Ahmad was asked about this, he said:

“The Quran was recited to Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, and he fainted. If anyone could have prevented this from happening to him, Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd would have done so, for I have never seen anyone more level-headed than him”—or words to that effect.

It has also been reported that al-Shāfi‘ī experienced this, and the account of ‘Alī ibn al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād is well known. In short, this has happened to many whose sincerity is beyond doubt.

However, the states experienced by the Companions are those mentioned in the Quran: trembling hearts, tearful eyes, and shivering skin. As Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Allah has sent down the best of speech: a Book consistent and oft-repeated, which causes the skin of those who fear their Lord to shiver; then their skin and hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah.”

And Allah Most High says:

“When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down in prostration, weeping.”

And He says:

“And when they hear what has been revealed to

---

## Page 5354

the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized.” And He says:

“They fall upon their faces, weeping, and it increases them in humility.”

The state of these people may be condemned by those who themselves have a blameworthy degree of hardness and rust upon their hearts and estrangement from religion—and indeed, some have done so. Others suppose that this state of theirs is the most perfect, complete, and exalted of all states. Both extremes are blameworthy.

Rather, there are three levels:

The first is the state of one who wrongs himself: his heart is hard and does not soften through listening and remembrance. Such people bear a resemblance to the Jews. Allah Most High says:

“Then your hearts hardened after that, becoming like stones or even harder. For there are stones from which rivers gush, others that split and water flows out, and others that fall down out of fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled at the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed, and that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture before, for whom a long time passed, so their hearts hardened? And many of them are defiantly disobedient.”

The second is the state of the pious believer who lacks the strength to bear what comes upon his heart. It is such a person who is struck down, either dead or unconscious, for this

---

## Page 5355

occurs only because of the intensity of what comes upon the heart and the heart’s inability to bear it. Something similar may happen to someone who experiences joy, fear, grief, or love concerning worldly matters: it may kill him, make him ill, or deprive him of his reason. Among those who worship physical forms are people whom passionate love has made ill, killed, or driven mad. The same applies in other cases. This happens only when something comes upon a person that he is too weak to resist, much like the causes of illness or death that affect the body, or when a person is overcome by it.

If he has committed neither negligence nor transgression, he bears no sin for what has befallen him, and there are no grounds for suspicion. An example is someone who listens to the Quran in the prescribed manner and has not been negligent by abandoning what makes this possible for him. The same applies to what comes upon the heart of what they call intoxication, loss of self-awareness, and similar states that deprive a person of reason against his will.

If the cause is not prohibited, the intoxicated person is not blameworthy but excused, for an intoxicated person lacks discernment. Such a state may also arise through intoxication from wine or hashish. This is forbidden without any disagreement among Muslims, and whoever regards intoxication from these things as lawful is a disbeliever. It may also arise through loving physical forms and becoming passionately infatuated with them, as has been said:

Two intoxications:
The intoxication of passion and the intoxication of wine—
When will one afflicted by both regain his senses?

---

## Page 5356

And this is blameworthy because its cause is forbidden. Intoxication may also result from listening to stirring sounds that induce such a state. This too is blameworthy, for a person may not listen to sounds he has not been commanded to hear if they deprive him of reason. Causing the loss of reason is forbidden, and whenever a means not sanctioned by the religion leads to it, that means is forbidden. Any accompanying pleasure of the heart or spirit—even through things containing an element of faith—is outweighed by the loss of reason that accompanies it. Allah has not permitted us to delight our hearts or spirits with the pleasures of faith, or any other pleasures, through anything that causes us to lose our reason. This differs from the case of someone who loses his reason through a prescribed means, or through something that befalls him which he has no way of warding off.

Intoxication may occur without any action on the person’s part, as when he unintentionally hears something that rouses what lies within him and stirs what is dormant, or something similar. He is not blameworthy for this, and he is excused for whatever proceeds from him while deprived of reason. The pen of accountability is lifted from anyone who loses his reason through a cause that is not forbidden, such as someone who falls unconscious, someone who is insane, and others like them.

As for someone who loses his reason through wine, does he remain religiously accountable while deprived of reason? There are two well-known views on this. There is also a well-known disagreement over the validity of a divorce pronounced by someone in this state. Someone who loses his reason through banj (a stupefying plant) is placed in the same category, according to those followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad who hold this view. Another view distinguishes between it and wine, since one is craved and the other is not. For this reason,

---

## Page 5357

the prescribed punishment is required in the one case but not the other. This is Ahmad’s explicitly stated position and the view of Abū Hanīfa.

Among these people are those whose spiritual experience becomes so overpowering that they become insane, whether because a bodily humour gains ascendancy over them or for some other reason. They include the “wise among the insane,” who are counted among the ascetics and are sometimes called “the bewildered.”

One scholar said of them:
“Allah granted these people intellects and spiritual states; then He took away their intellects and, through what He took away, relieved them of the obligations He had imposed.”

These states may be accompanied by fainting, death, insanity, intoxication, or self-effacement to the point of losing awareness of oneself, and similar experiences. If their causes are prescribed by the religion, and the person experiencing them is sincere and unable to ward them off, then he is praiseworthy for the good he has done and the faith he has attained, and excused for what he could not prevent and what befell him involuntarily. Such people are more complete than those who have not reached their station because of deficient faith, hardness of heart, or similar causes involving neglect of what Allah loves or commission of what He dislikes.

However, someone who retains his reason while attaining what they have attained of faith, or its like, or something more complete, is superior to them. This was the state of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and it was the state of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He was taken by night to heaven, and Allah showed him what He showed him; yet in the morning he was like someone who had passed an ordinary night, his state unchanged. His state was therefore superior to

---

## Page 5358

the state of Moses, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who fell unconscious when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain. Moses’ state was noble, exalted and virtuous, but Muhammad’s state, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was more complete, higher and better.

The point is that these heightened forms of worship and spiritual experience arose in Basra because of intense fear. Indeed, the accounts of the fear experienced by ‘Utba al-Ghulām, ‘Atā’ al-Sulaymī and others like them describe something tremendous. Undoubtedly, their state was more complete and better than that of anyone whose fear of Allah neither equalled nor surpassed theirs.

Yet someone whose measured fear of Allah moves him to do what Allah loves and abandon what Allah dislikes, without these additional manifestations, is in a more complete and better state than theirs. This was the state of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

It is reported that ‘Atā’ al-Sulaymī—may Allah be pleased with him—was seen after his death and asked, “How did Allah deal with you?” He replied, “He said to me, ‘O ‘Atā’, were you not ashamed before Me to fear Me so greatly? Had you not heard that I am All-Forgiving, Most Merciful?’”

Likewise, accounts of the asceticism, scrupulousness, worship and similar spiritual states of such people may describe practices exceeding those of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and what the Messenger prescribed. Such accounts lead people to fall into two extremes. One group censures and disparages these people, sometimes going too far in doing so.

---

## Page 5359

Others go to excess in venerating them and regard this path as one of the most perfect and exalted. The sound assessment is that they exercised independent judgment in these acts of worship and spiritual states, just as their neighbours in Kufa exercised independent judgment in matters of adjudication, governance and the like. Among the latter there arose forms of reasoned opinion involving departures from the Sunnah that most people condemned. The best among the “scholars of jurisprudence and reasoned opinion” fall into two extremes regarding those Kufans. Some censure them excessively, while others go to excess in exalting them, considering them more knowledgeable in jurisprudence than anyone else, and sometimes even preferring them to the Companions. Likewise, those who go to excess regarding those devout worshippers may prefer them to the Companions. This is an issue over which people become divided.

The correct approach is for the Muslim to know that the best speech is Allah’s speech, the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the best generation is the generation among whom he was sent. The best paths and ways leading to Allah are those followed by him and his Companions. It should also be understood that believers must fear Allah according to their best efforts and capacity, as Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

---

## Page 5360

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Allah also says:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

Many believers—Allah’s pious allies—may not attain the perfection of knowledge and faith attained by the Companions. They fear Allah as much as they can and obey Him to the best of their efforts, yet inevitably make mistakes, whether in their knowledge and statements or in their deeds and spiritual states. They are rewarded for their obedience, and He forgives their errors. For Allah Most High says:

“The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and so have the believers. Each believes in Allah, His angels, His Books and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ They say, ‘We hear and we obey. Grant us Your forgiveness, our Lord; to You is the final return.’”

And later in the passage:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

Allah Most High said: “I have granted this.”

Whoever considers the path of any scholar or jurist, or that of any devout worshipper or ascetic, superior to the path of the Companions is mistaken, misguided and an innovator. Likewise, whoever regards everyone who strives to obey Allah but errs in some matters as blameworthy, flawed and deserving of hatred is mistaken, misguided and an innovator.

In their love and hatred, allegiance and enmity, people also exercise their judgment, sometimes getting it right and sometimes getting it wrong. [Many people, when they learn something they love about a man, love him unreservedly and overlook his evil deeds; when they learn something they hate about him, they hate him unreservedly and overlook his good deeds. Muhāt? And the case of one who

---

## Page 5361

advocates tahāfuz? This is among the views of the people of innovation—the Khārijites, the Muʿtazilites and the Murjiʾites] (*).

Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah affirm what the Quran, the Sunnah and scholarly consensus establish: a believer deserves reward for his good deeds through Allah’s promise and grace, and deserves punishment for his evil deeds. A single person may possess things for which he is rewarded and others for which he is punished; things for which he is praised and others for which he is blamed; things that are loved in him and others that are hated. Such is the matter.

Now, once it is understood that “Sufism” originated in Basra, where some people pursued paths of worship and asceticism according to their own considered judgment, just as some in Kufa pursued paths of jurisprudence and learning according to their own considered judgment, these people’s designation relates to their outward garb: woollen clothing. Hence an individual among them was called a “Sufi.” Their path was not restricted to wearing wool, nor did they make it obligatory or make their undertaking depend upon it. Rather, they were associated with it because it was an outwardly visible feature of their way of life.

Furthermore, “Sufism,” in their usage, comprises recognized spiritual realities and states. They have discussed its definitions, its way of life and its moral qualities. For example, some of them say: A “Sufi” is one who is free of all taint, filled with reflection, and to whom gold and stone are alike. Sufism is to conceal inward meanings and relinquish claims. They offer other descriptions of this kind.

Their conception of the Sufi approaches

## Page 5362

that of the eminently truthful. The best of creation after the prophets are the eminently truthful, as Allah Most High says:

“They will be with those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the eminently truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!”

For this reason, they hold that no one after the prophets is superior to the Sufi. In reality, however, the Sufi belongs to one category of the eminently truthful: he is someone of eminent truthfulness who specializes in asceticism and worship according to the approach they have pursued through their considered judgment. He is thus one of the eminently truthful who follows this particular path, just as one speaks of the eminently truthful among scholars or among rulers. This is a narrower category than that of the eminently truthful in general, and falls below those Companions, Successors and their followers whose truthfulness was complete.

Thus, describing those ascetics and devoted worshippers of Basra as eminently truthful is like describing the leading jurists of Kufa as eminently truthful as well. Each is so according to the path he has followed in obedience to Allah and His Messenger, in keeping with his considered judgment. They may be among the most distinguished of the eminently truthful in their own age, and thus among the most accomplished of their contemporaries in this rank. Yet those of eminent truthfulness in the earliest age were more accomplished than they. The eminently truthful comprise different ranks and types. Accordingly, each has a particular kind of spiritual state or worship that he has fully realized and mastered, and that predominates in him, even though someone else may be more accomplished and superior in another kind.

Because of the exercise of considered judgment among many of them, and the disputes surrounding it, people disagreed about their path. One group condemned “the Sufis and Sufism” and said that they are

---

## Page 5363

innovators who have departed from the Sunnah. Well-known statements to this effect have been transmitted from a number of leading scholars, and groups of jurists and speculative theologians followed them in this. Another group went to excess concerning them, claiming that they are the best and most accomplished of creation after the prophets. Both extremes are blameworthy.

The “correct view” is that they strive to obey Allah according to their considered judgment, just as others devoted to obeying Allah have done. Among them are those who are foremost in good deeds and brought near to Allah, according to their efforts, and those who follow a moderate course and belong to the companions of the right. In both categories are people who may exercise their judgment and err. Among them, too, are those who sin and then repent—or do not repent. Some who affiliate themselves with them wrong themselves and disobey their Lord.

Groups of people given to religious innovation and heresy have also affiliated themselves with them, but the discerning authorities among the Sufis do not regard such people as belonging to them. Al-Hallāj, for example, was rejected by most masters of the path, who excluded him from it. These included al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, the leader of the Sufi community, and others, as Shaykh Abū 'Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī related in Tabaqāt al-Sūfiyya (Generations of the Sufis), and as the hadith master Abū Bakr al-Khatīb related in Tārīkh Baghdād (History of Baghdad).

This, then, is Sufism in its original form. Later, it branched out and took various forms, and there came to be

---

## Page 5364

“three categories” of Sufis: Sufis of genuine spiritual attainment, Sufis of stipends, and Sufis of outward form.

As for the “Sufis of genuine spiritual attainment,” they are those whom we have described. The “Sufis of stipends” are those for whom endowments have been established, such as Sufi lodges. They are not required to be people of genuine spiritual attainment, for such attainment is rare, and most who possess it do not reside permanently in Sufi lodges. They must, however, fulfil three conditions:

The first is uprightness according to Islamic law: they must perform their religious obligations and avoid what is forbidden.

The second is to observe the manners of those who follow the path. These are, for the most part, manners prescribed by Islamic law. As for invented rules of conduct that constitute religious innovations, no regard is to be paid to them.

The third is that none of them should be attached to superfluous worldly possessions. Anyone who hoards wealth, lacks praiseworthy character and fails to observe the manners prescribed by Islamic law, or is sinful, is not entitled to such support.

As for the “Sufis of outward form,” they content themselves with affiliation alone; their concern is with clothing

---

## Page 5365

and conventional rules of conduct and the like. Among Sufis, these people are like someone who merely adopts the dress of scholars or those who engage in jihad, together with some of their sayings and practices, so that someone unaware of his true condition thinks he belongs to their ranks, although he does not.

As for the term “faqīr” (poor person), it occurs in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In the Book and Sunnah, however, it means someone who is poor, as opposed to wealthy—as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: (1)

“The poor and poverty” fall into several categories. One kind of poverty entitles a person to receive zakat; its opposite is the wealth that disqualifies a person from receiving it. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person or for a strong person able to earn a living.”

According to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, the wealth that makes zakat obligatory is different from this: it consists in possessing the minimum taxable amount. In their view, a person may be obliged to pay zakat while also being permitted to receive it, contrary to the view of Abū Hanīfah.

Allah, glorified is He, mentions the poor in several places. He mentions the poor entitled to zakat in one passage and those entitled to fayʾ revenues in another. In the first, He says:

“If you disclose your charitable gifts, that is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you.”

Then, further on, He says:

“For the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah

## Page 5366

and are unable to travel through the land. Those unaware of their circumstances think them wealthy because they refrain from asking. You will recognize them by their appearance; they do not beg people persistently.”

In the second passage, He says:

“Whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns…”

—and so on, down to His words:

“For the poor emigrants who were driven from their homes and their wealth, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure and supporting Allah and His Messenger. They are the truthful.”

Among these “poor people,” some may be better than many wealthy people, while among the wealthy, some may be better than many of the poor.

People have disputed which is better: a poor person who is patient or a wealthy person who is grateful. The correct view is that the better of the two is the one who has greater fear of Allah. If they are equal in their fear of Allah, they are equal in rank, as we have explained elsewhere. The poor enter Paradise before the wealthy because they are not called to account. The wealthy are then called to account, and anyone whose good deeds outweigh those of a poor person will have a higher rank in Paradise, even though he enters it later. Anyone whose good deeds fall short of that poor person’s will have a lower rank.

However, because renunciation of worldly things is more prevalent among the poor, “poverty,” in the terminology of many people, came to denote the path of renunciation, which is a form of Sufism. Thus, when it is said, “This man possesses ‘poverty,’” or “He has no ‘poverty,’” what is meant is not a lack of wealth

---

## Page 5367

but rather the knowledge, spiritual states, moral qualities, proper conduct, and similar things denoted by the term “Sufi.”

Using these terms in this sense, people have disputed which is better: the faqīr (the practitioner of “poverty”) or the Sufi. One group preferred the Sufi, including Abū Ja'far al-Suhrawardī and others like him, while another preferred the faqīr—as many groups have done. Sometimes one group is associated specifically with zāwiyas and the other with khānqāhs (types of Sufi lodge), and so forth. Most people have preferred the faqīr.

The correct conclusion is that the better of the two is the one who has greater fear of Allah. If the Sufi has greater fear of Allah—meaning that he more diligently does what Allah loves and more thoroughly avoids what He does not love—then he is better than the faqīr. If the faqīr more diligently does what Allah loves and more thoroughly avoids what He does not love, then he is better than the Sufi. If they are equal in doing what Allah loves and avoiding what He does not love, they are equal in rank.

The “allies of Allah” are the believers who fear Him, whether one of them is called a faqīr, a Sufi, a jurist, a scholar, a merchant, a soldier, a craftsman, a ruler, a judge, or anything else. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the allies of Allah will have no fear, nor will they grieve—those who believe and fear Allah.”

---

## Page 5368

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards an ally of Mine has openly challenged Me to war. Nothing by which My servant draws near to Me equals his fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I have never hesitated over anything I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet he must undergo it.’”

This hadith identifies two groups of Allah’s allies: those who follow a middle course—the companions of the right—and those brought near to Him—the foremost.

The first group consists of those who draw near to Allah by fulfilling their obligations. The second consists of those who draw near to Him through voluntary acts of worship after fulfilling their obligations. They are the ones who continued to draw near to Him through voluntary acts until He loved them, as He, Most High, has said.

Allah has mentioned these two groups in several places in His Book, as when He says:

“Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who are foremost in good deeds.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss,
On adorned couches, looking on.
You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
They will be given sealed, pure wine to drink,
Its seal being musk. So for this let those who strive compete.
Its mixture will be of Tasnīm,
A spring from which those brought near to Allah drink.”

Ibn 'Abbās said: “It is drunk

unmixed by those brought near to Allah, while it is mixed for the companions of the right.”

## Page 5370

He was also asked: (*)

What do the jurists—may Allah be pleased with them—say concerning a man who says:

“Poverty is not something we have been required to practise as worship, nor have we been commanded to pursue it. It has neither substance nor meaning, and it is not a path leading to the pleasure of Allah Most High or His Messenger. Rather, Allah has required us to worship Him by obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, as set out in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The foundation of everything is knowledge, worship based upon it, acting upon it, mindfulness of Allah, and scrupulous avoidance of forbidden things.

“What the Sufis and their leading masters call ‘poverty’ is detachment from this world. Such detachment is acquired through knowledge of the revealed law. Detachment from this world thus consists in acting upon knowledge, and this is poverty. Accordingly, poverty is a branch of knowledge; that is how the matter stands. There is no more effective path than knowledge and acting upon it in accordance with what has been authentically established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

He also says:

“What is called poverty, as understood by most of those who wear the prescribed garb in these times—with its customary dress, expressions, and terminology—is pleasing neither to Allah nor to His Messenger.”

Is the matter as he says, or otherwise? Give us a legal opinion; may you be rewarded.

---

## Page 5371

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—replied:

Praise be to Allah. The fundamental principle underlying this “question” is that we must follow what the terms found in the Quran and Sunnah signify. These include faith, righteousness, mindfulness of Allah, truthfulness, justice, excellence in doing good, patience, gratitude, reliance upon Allah, fear, hope, love for Allah, obedience to Allah and His Messenger, kindness to parents, fulfilment of covenants, and similar terms describing the inward states and outward deeds that Allah and His Messenger love.

These things that Allah and His Messenger love constitute the path leading to Allah, together with abstaining from what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden: disbelief, hypocrisy, lying, sin, aggression, injustice, impatience, panic, associating partners with Allah, miserliness, cowardice, hardness of heart, treachery, severing family ties, and the like.

Every Muslim must therefore consider what Allah and His Messenger have commanded and do it, and what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden and abstain from it. This is Allah’s path, His way and His religion: the straight path, the path of those whom Allah has blessed—the prophets, the utterly truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.

This “straight path” encompasses both knowledge and action: knowledge of the revealed law and action in accordance with it. Whoever has knowledge but does not act upon it is wicked, while whoever acts without knowledge is astray. Allah, glorified be He, has commanded us to say:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your wrath, nor those who have gone astray.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “The Jews have incurred wrath, and the Christians

---

## Page 5372

have gone astray. This is because the Jews knew the truth but did not act upon it, while the Christians worshipped Allah without knowledge.”

For this reason, the early generations used to say:

“Beware the trial posed by the wicked scholar and the ignorant worshipper, for theirs is a trial for everyone who is led astray.”

They also used to say:

“Those scholars who become corrupt bear a resemblance to the Jews, while those worshippers who become corrupt bear a resemblance to the Christians.”

Whoever calls to knowledge without the action that is commanded leads others astray, and whoever calls to action without knowledge likewise leads others astray. More astray than either is someone who pursues knowledge by following the path of the people of religious innovation: he follows things contrary to the Quran and Sunnah, imagining them to be knowledge when they are forms of ignorance. The same applies to someone who follows the path of the people of religious innovation in worship: he performs deeds contrary to the prescribed deeds, imagining them to be acts of worship when they are forms of misguidance.

Both failings are common among those who deviate while claiming affiliation with jurisprudence or the path of poverty. Such a person combines calling to knowledge without action and calling to action without knowledge, while what he advocates contains innovations contrary to the revealed law. The path to Allah can only be fully followed through knowledge and action, both conforming to the revealed law.

Anyone following the path of “poverty, Sufism, asceticism and worship” who does not proceed with knowledge conforming to the revealed law will stray from the path and cause more harm than good. Likewise, anyone pursuing “jurisprudence, knowledge, rational inquiry and speculative theology” who does not follow the revealed law and act upon his knowledge will be wicked and astray from the path. This, then, is

---

## Page 5373

the principle that every Muslim must adopt. As for partisan attachment to any matter without guidance from Allah, this belongs to the practices of pre-Islamic ignorance.

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desires without guidance from Allah?”

There is no doubt that the term “poverty,” as used in the Quran and Sunnah and in the words of the Companions, the Successors and their followers, did not mean the path to Allah itself, doing what He commanded, refraining from what He forbade, praiseworthy character, or anything of that kind. Rather, poverty meant the opposite of wealth. The “poor” are those whom Allah mentions in His words:

“Alms are only for the poor and the needy”;

“For the poor who have been restricted in Allah’s cause”;

and:

“For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and deprived of their wealth.”

The “wealthy” person is one who may not lawfully receive zakat, or one who is obliged to pay it, or someone defined in similar terms. However, because poverty was likely to entail asceticism, whether voluntary or involuntary—for lack of means can itself be a safeguard—later generations frequently came to associate poverty with asceticism. Yet asceticism may coexist with either wealth or poverty. Among the prophets and the earliest forerunners were many who practised asceticism despite their wealth.

The asceticism prescribed by the revealed law consists in giving up whatever brings no benefit in the Hereafter. As for anything a servant uses to help him obey Allah, abandoning it is not part of prescribed asceticism.

---

## Page 5374

rather, what is prescribed is to give up superfluous things that distract one from obeying Allah and His Messenger. Likewise, during the second century AH, people began to express this through the term “Sufi,” because wearing wool was common among ascetics. Those who say that “Sufi” derives from al-suffa (the sheltered platform), safā (purity), al-saff al-awwal (the first row), Sūfa ibn Bishr ibn Udd ibn Tānja, or sūfat al-qafā (the fine hair on the nape) (*)—these are greater disbelievers than the Jews and Christians.

Some people, however, have perceived the distinction in certain matters but not others: they distinguish between the believer and the disbeliever, but not between the righteous and the wicked. Or they distinguish between some righteous people and some wicked people, but not between others, following their own assumptions and desires. Their faith is deficient to the extent that they treat the righteous and the wicked alike. Their faith in the religion of Allah Most High, which makes these distinctions, corresponds to the extent that they distinguish between His allies and His enemies.

Whoever acknowledges religious commands and prohibitions but not divine decree and predestination belongs to the Qadariyya, such as the Muʿtazila and others like them, who are the Magians of this community. These resemble the Magians, whereas the others resemble the polytheists, who are worse than the Magians. Whoever acknowledges both but represents the Lord as self-contradictory is among the followers of Iblīs, who objected to the Lord—glory be to Him—and disputed with Him, as has been related about him.

This is their classification with regard to speech and belief. The same applies to their “states and actions.” The correct state is that of the believer who fears Allah, does what is commanded, refrains from what is forbidden, and patiently bears whatever befalls him

## Page 5375

by divine decree. He thus adheres to Allah’s commands, religion, and revealed law, seeking Allah’s help in doing so, as the Most High says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

When he sins, he seeks forgiveness and repents. He does not invoke divine decree to excuse the evil deeds he commits, nor does he consider any creature to have a valid argument against the Lord of all creation. Rather, he believes in divine decree without using it as an excuse, as in the authentic hadith containing the foremost supplication for forgiveness, in which the servant says:

“O Allah, You are my Lord; none has the right to be worshipped but You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I remain faithful to Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your favour upon me, and I acknowledge my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.”

He thus acknowledges Allah’s favour upon him in his good deeds and knows that Allah is the One who guided him and eased his way to goodness. He also acknowledges his sins and repents of them. As one of them said:

“I obeyed You by Your grace, and all credit is Yours. I disobeyed You with Your knowledge, and the case against me is Yours. I therefore beseech You, by Your established case against me and my lack of any defence, to forgive me.”

In an authentic divine hadith, Allah says:

“O My servants, these are but your deeds, which I record for you and then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.”

This matter has been examined in detail elsewhere. Others may be mindful only of “the command,” so you find them striving to obey to the best of their ability, but they lack the awareness of divine decree that would bring about

---

## Page 5376

genuine seeking of Allah’s help, reliance upon Him, and patience. Others are mindful only of “divine decree,” and so possess a degree of seeking Allah’s help, reliance upon Him, and patience that the former lack. Yet they do not adhere to the commands of Allah and His Messenger, follow His revealed law, or hold fast to the religion taught by the Quran and Sunnah. These people seek Allah’s help but do not worship Him, while those mentioned before them wish to worship Him but do not seek His help. The believer both worships Him and seeks His help.

The fourth category is the worst: those who neither worship Him nor seek His help. They are aligned neither with His revealed commands nor with His universal decree. This division into categories concerns what precedes a decreed event—such as reliance upon Allah and seeking His help—and what follows it—such as patience and contentment.

With regard to piety, which is obedience to the religious command, and patience in bearing what is decreed for a person by the universal decree, people fall into four categories:

The first comprises those who possess both piety and patience. These are the people whom Allah has blessed, those who enjoy felicity in this world and the Hereafter.

The second comprises those who possess a measure of piety but lack patience, such as those who fulfil their obligations of prayer and the like and refrain from forbidden things, but when one of them is afflicted

---

## Page 5377

with bodily illness or the like, or in his wealth or honour, or is tested by an enemy who frightens him, he becomes deeply distressed and visibly panicked.

(The third category comprises people who possess a measure of patience but lack piety:

These include the wicked who patiently endure whatever befalls them in pursuing their desires, such as thieves and highway robbers who endure pain in their pursuit of forcibly seized property and unlawful gains. Likewise, scribes and administrative officials endure such hardships in pursuit of the money they acquire through breaches of trust and other means. Those seeking leadership and ascendancy over others similarly endure kinds of suffering that many people cannot bear.

Likewise, those enamoured of forbidden objects of desire, whether passionately infatuated or otherwise, endure various kinds of suffering and pain in pursuing the forbidden things they crave. These are the people who seek supremacy in the land or corruption: those seeking leadership and ascendancy over others, those seeking wealth through oppression and aggression, and those seeking pleasure from forbidden objects of desire, whether by looking, physical contact, or other means. They endure various hardships, but lack piety in neglecting what they have been commanded to do and committing what they have been forbidden to do.

Similarly, a man may patiently endure the calamities that befall him, such as illness, poverty, and other afflictions, yet show no piety when he has the power to act.

---

## Page 5378

As for the fourth category, it is the worst of all: they neither show piety when they have power nor exercise patience when they are tested. Rather, they are as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious:
impatient when evil touches him,
and withholding when good touches him.”

You will find such people among the most unjust and tyrannical when they have power, and among the most abject and panic-stricken when they are overpowered. If you overpower them, they abase themselves before you, behave hypocritically towards you, offer you gifts, and beg for your mercy. To protect themselves, they resort to all manner of lies, self-abasement, and exaltation of the person they petition. But if they overpower you, they are among the most unjust and hard-hearted of people, and the least merciful, kind, or forgiving.

Muslims have experienced this with all those furthest removed from the realities of faith, such as the Tatars whom the Muslims fought, and those who resemble them in many of their ways—even if they outwardly wear the attire of Muslim soldiers, scholars, ascetics, merchants, or craftsmen. What counts is the underlying reality. For Allah does not look at your appearance or your wealth; rather, He looks at your hearts and deeds. Whoever has a heart and deeds like those of the Tatars resembles them in this respect. Whatever Islam he possesses, or outwardly professes, is comparable to the Islam they possess and outwardly profess. Indeed, among those who outwardly profess Islam, other than the warring Tatars, are people whose apostasy is greater, who are more given to the character of pre-Islamic ignorance, and who are further removed from Islamic character than the Tatars.

An authentic hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his sermons:

“The best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best

---

## Page 5379

guidance is the guidance of Muhammad. The worst matters are newly introduced ones; every newly introduced matter is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance.”

Since the best speech is the speech of Allah and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, whoever is closer to these and resembles them more closely is nearer to perfection and more deserving of it. Whoever is further removed from them and resembles them less is further from perfection and more deserving of falsehood. The person who attains perfection is the one who is most obedient to Allah and most patient with whatever befalls him. The more closely a person follows what Allah and His Messenger command, the more fully he conforms to what Allah loves and is pleased with, and the more patiently he bears what Allah has decreed and ordained, the more complete and excellent he is. Whoever falls short in these two qualities is deficient to the extent that he falls short.

Allah Most High has mentioned patience and piety together in several places in His Book. He has explained that He grants His servant victory over his enemies among the disbelievers—those at war with the Muslims, those bound by treaty, and the hypocrites—as well as over Muslims who wrong him, and that the ultimate outcome belongs to the person endowed with patience and piety. Allah Most High says:

“Yes, if you remain patient and fear Allah, and they come upon you at once, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels bearing marks of distinction.”

Allah Most High also says:

“You will surely be tested in your possessions and yourselves, and you will surely hear much abuse from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with Allah. But if you remain patient and fear Allah, that is indeed among the matters requiring firm resolve.”

And He Most High says:

“O you who believe, do not take as intimates those outside your community. They spare no effort to ruin you and wish to see you suffer. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their hearts conceal

---

## Page 5380

is greater still. We have made the signs clear to you, if you will understand.”

“Here you are, loving them, while they do not love you, and you believe in all the Scripture. When they meet you, they say, ‘We believe,’ but when they are alone, they bite their fingertips in rage at you. Say, ‘Die in your rage.’ Indeed, Allah knows what lies within the hearts.”

“If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if harm befalls you, they rejoice at it. Yet if you remain patient and fear Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all. Indeed, Allah encompasses all that they do.”

Joseph’s brothers said to him:

“‘Are you indeed Joseph?’ He said, ‘I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly bestowed His favor upon us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and remains patient—Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.’”

Patience has also been coupled with righteous deeds, both generally and specifically. Allah Most High says:

“Follow what is revealed to you, and remain patient until Allah judges, for He is the best of judges.”

Following what was revealed to him encompasses all piety: believing what Allah has conveyed and obeying His commands. Allah Most High says:

“Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who take heed.”

“And remain patient, for Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

Allah Most High says:

“So remain patient; indeed, Allah’s promise is true. Seek forgiveness for your sin, and glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.”

Allah Most High says:

“So bear patiently what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before sunrise and before sunset, and during parts of the night.”

Allah Most High says:

“Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humbly submissive.”

Allah Most High says:

“Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with those who are patient.”

These are passages in which He has coupled prayer with patience.

---

## Page 5381

He has also coupled mercy with patience, as in His words, Most High:

“And urge one another to patience and urge one another to compassion.”

Mercy includes kindness to creation through zakat and other means. Here, too, there is a fourfold division. Some people are patient but show no mercy, such as those marked by strength and hardness. Others show mercy but lack patience, such as those marked by weakness and gentleness, including many women and those who resemble them. Others have neither patience nor mercy, such as those marked by hardness and panic. The praiseworthy person is the one who is both patient and merciful.

As the jurists have said concerning the qualities of a person entrusted with authority: he should be strong without harshness and gentle without weakness. Through patience he is strong, and through gentleness he shows mercy. Through patience the servant is granted victory, for victory comes with patience; and through mercy Allah Most High shows him mercy. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah shows mercy only to those of His servants who are merciful.”

He also said:

“Whoever shows no mercy will be shown no mercy.”

And he said:

“Mercy is stripped away only from a wretched person. The Most Merciful shows mercy to those who are merciful. Show mercy to those on earth, and the One in heaven will show mercy to you.”

Allah knows best. End.

## Page 5382

Shaykh al-Islām, exemplar of mankind, mufti to the various groups, and champion of the Sunnah, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-Abbās Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halīm ibn Abd al-Salām ibn Taymiyya—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

Concerning “Ahl al-Suffa” (the people of the shaded platform): How many were they? Were they in Mecca or Medina? Where was the place in which they stayed? Did all of them remain there, leaving only when necessary? Or did some remain at the platform while others sought their livelihood? How did they obtain their livelihood: did they perform manual labour, or did they beg with a basket?

What of someone who believes that “Ahl al-Suffa” fought alongside the polytheists against the believers? And what of someone who believes that “Ahl al-Suffa” were superior to Abū Bakr, Umar, Uthmān, and Alī—may Allah be pleased with them—and to the remaining six of the Ten, and to all the Companions? Were any of the Ten among them?

Did anyone at that time make vows for Ahl al-Suffa? Did they seek ecstatic states to the sound of a frame drum or flute? Or did they have a chanter who recited poetry, to which they moved, clapping their hands and seeking ecstatic states?

He was also asked about this verse, the words of Allah Most High:

“And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening.”

Does it apply specifically to Ahl al-Suffa, or is it

---

## Page 5383

general in scope?

Is the hadith narrated by many ordinary people authentic, in which they say that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No group gathers without there being among them a close friend of Allah: neither do the people recognize him, nor does he himself know that he is a close friend of Allah”?

Can the condition or way of Allah’s close friends be hidden from scholars or others? Why is a close friend of Allah called a walī, and what is meant by walī? Who are the poor who will enter Paradise before the rich? And who are the poor whom Allah commended to our care in His words, and whom the foremost of His creation and the last of His prophets and messengers, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned in his Sunnah? Are they those who lack sufficient means to meet their needs—the destitute and needy—or not?

Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyya—may Allah be pleased with him—gave the following response in his own hand:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The suffa, the shaded platform after which Ahl al-Suffa among the Prophet’s Companions were named, was at the rear of the Prophet’s Mosque, on its northern side, in Medina, the city of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Poor Muslims who had neither a family nor a place to stay would take shelter there. This was because Allah, glorified and exalted be He, commanded His Prophet

---

## Page 5384

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers to migrate to Medina, the city of the Prophet. When some of the leading men of Medina from the Aws and Khazraj embraced faith, he concluded the pledge of al-Aqaba with them near Minā, and the believers gained a home where they enjoyed strength and protection. Believers from Mecca and elsewhere then began migrating to Medina. The early believers there fell into two groups:

The Muhājirūn, who migrated there from their homelands, and the Ansār, who were the people of Medina. Muslims among the Bedouins and others who did not migrate were subject to a different ruling. Others were prevented from migrating by their leaders, who shackled and imprisoned them. Still others remained living among disbelievers who held power over them. All these “categories” are mentioned in the Quran, and the rulings concerning them continue to apply to those in comparable circumstances until the Day of Resurrection.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believed, emigrated, and strove with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah, and those who gave them shelter and support—they are allies of one another. But those who believed and did not emigrate—you have no obligation to protect them until they emigrate. Yet if they seek your help in matters of religion, you must help them, except against a people with whom you have a treaty. Allah sees all that you do. Those who disbelieve are allies of one another. Unless you do likewise, there will be persecution in the land and great corruption. Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the cause of Allah, and those who gave them shelter and support—it is they who are truly believers. For them there is forgiveness and a generous provision.”

This concerns the earliest believers. He then mentioned those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection, saying:

“And those who believed afterwards

---

## Page 5385

and emigrated and strove alongside you—they are of you. Blood relatives have a stronger claim upon one another in Allah’s Book. Indeed, Allah knows all things.” Allah Most High also says:

“And the first forerunners among the Muhājirūn and the Ansār, and those who followed them in righteousness—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him”—to the end of the verse.

In this surah, He mentions the believers among the Bedouins, as well as the hypocrites among the people of Medina and those around it. He, glorified and exalted, also says:

“Indeed, those whose souls the angels take while they are wronging themselves will be asked, ‘What circumstances were you in?’ They will reply, ‘We were oppressed in the land.’ The angels will say, ‘Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?’ Their refuge will be Hell—what an evil destination! Except for the helpless among men, women, and children who can neither find a means nor find their way. These are the ones whom Allah may pardon, for Allah is ever Pardoning, Forgiving.”

When the believers were migrating to Medina, the Prophet’s city, some stayed with the Ansār, with or without their families, for the pledge stipulated that the Ansār would shelter them and share their resources with them. At times, when an emigrant arrived, the Ansār would draw lots to determine which of them would host him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had formed an alliance between the Muhājirūn and the Ansār and established bonds of brotherhood between them.

Thereafter, the Muhājirūn gradually grew in number, as Islam spread and people embraced it. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would campaign against the disbelievers, sometimes in person and sometimes by sending military detachments

---

## Page 5386

and many people would thus embrace Islam, sometimes both outwardly and inwardly, and sometimes outwardly alone. Increasing numbers emigrated to Medina: poor and wealthy, those with families and those who were unmarried. Anyone unable to find somewhere to stay would take shelter in the Suffa, the portico within the mosque. Not all the people of the Suffa were there at the same time: some would marry or move elsewhere when accommodation became available, while others would arrive in succession. Their numbers therefore fluctuated: sometimes there were ten or fewer, sometimes twenty, thirty, or more, and sometimes sixty or seventy.

As for the total number who took shelter in the Suffa at different times, it has been said that they numbered around four hundred Companions; others have said that they were more numerous. Not every one of them was individually known. “Shaykh Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī” compiled their names in his “Kitāb Tārīkh Ahl al-Suffa” (History of the People of the Suffa), recording everyone whom he had heard described as belonging to the “people of the Suffa.” He devoted particular attention to accounts of ascetics and Sufis, the transmitted reports on which they relied, and their recorded sayings. He compiled accounts of the ascetics among the early generations, accounts of everyone whom he had heard belonged to the people of the Suffa and how many they numbered, and accounts of the later Sufis who came after the first three generations.

He also compiled material arranged by subject, as in Haqā’iq al-Tafsīr (The Realities of Quranic Interpretation), and on topics of Sufism arranged according to the chapters of jurisprudence. He likewise collected their statements on Allah’s oneness, knowledge of Him, and love; the question of listening; other spiritual states; and various other subjects. His compilations contain many valuable insights and substantial benefits.

---

## Page 5387

He himself was a man of goodness, religious devotion, righteousness, and virtue. Many of the reports he transmits are authentic. At times, however, he transmits weak reports, and even fabricated ones that scholars know to be false. Some hadith masters have questioned his direct reception of hadith. When al-Bayhaqī narrated from him, he would say:

“Abū 'Abd al-Rahmān narrated to us from his original record of the hadiths he had heard.”

Allah willing, neither he nor others like him should be suspected of deliberately lying. Rather, shortcomings in retention and precision allow errors to enter their narrations. Among ascetics and devout worshippers, some are meticulous in hadith transmission, such as Thābit al-Bunānī, al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyād, and others like them. Others have errors and weaknesses in some of their narrations, such as Mālik ibn Dīnār, Farqad al-Sabakhī, and others like them.

Likewise, the sayings, deeds, and spiritual states that Abū 'Abd al-Rahmān transmits from some who discourse on the spiritual path, or that he defends, contain much guidance and knowledge. At times, however, they also contain errors. Some of these arise from a legitimate exercise of independent judgment, while others are unquestionably false. An example is the substantial body of fabricated reports attributed to Ja'far al-Sādiq and others in Haqā'iq al-Tafsīr (The Realities of Quranic Interpretation). Some members of a group also transmitted from him various allusive interpretations: some are sound analogies and appropriate inferences, while others are falsehood and idle talk.

---

## Page 5388

Thus, what Shaykh Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān and others like him compiled in Tārīkh Ahl al-Suffa (History of the People of the Portico), accounts of the early ascetics, and biographical collections of Sufis offers substantial benefits. The false reports it contains should be avoided, and judgment should be suspended concerning its weak reports.

The same applies to many transmitters of reports and proponents of opinions and spiritual experiences among jurists, ascetics, speculative theologians, and others. What they transmit from their predecessors and what they themselves affirm and believe contain an abundance of the guidance and religion of truth with which Allah sent His Messenger. Yet at times their works also contain many false or weak reports, as well as opinions and spiritual experiences that are unsound or open to question.

Those who enjoy widespread good repute within the Muslim community, receiving praise and commendation across its various groups, are the leaders of guidance and lamps in the darkness. Their errors are few compared with what they get right, and most concern matters open to independent scholarly judgment in which they are excused. They are those who follow knowledge and justice, and are therefore far removed from ignorance and injustice, and from following conjecture and the desires of the soul.

## Page 5389

The circumstances of the People of the Portico, together with other poor Muslims who did not stay at the portico or stayed there only at times, were as Allah Most High describes them in His Book, where He identifies those among them entitled to charity and those entitled to fayʾ revenues. He says:

“If you give charity openly, that is good; but if you conceal it and give it to the poor, that is better for you, and He will expiate some of your sins. Allah is fully aware of what you do.”

Then, further on, He says:

“Charity is for the poor who are restricted in Allah’s cause and cannot travel through the land. Those unaware of their circumstances think them wealthy because they refrain from begging. You can recognize them by their appearance; they do not beg people persistently.”

Concerning those entitled to fayʾ revenues, He says:

“For the poor emigrants who were driven from their homes and property, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. It is they who are truly sincere.”

Poor Muslims, whether among the People of the Portico or others, would earn a living whenever they could do so without being diverted from something more obligatory or more beloved to Allah and His Messenger than earning a living. But when they were kept from earning a living in Allah’s cause, they gave precedence to what brought them nearer to Allah and His Messenger. The People of the Portico were the guests of

---

## Page 5390

Islam. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would send them whatever he had available, for they were generally in need: whatever they could earn was insufficient to provide the sustenance they required.

As for “asking,” they followed the Prophet’s instruction, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He prohibited it for anyone who had no need of it, but permitted a person to ask for what was rightfully his—for example, to ask someone in authority to give him his due from Allah’s wealth—or, if he had no choice but to ask, to approach righteous people of means when he needed to do so. He forbade his closest Companions from asking for anything at all, to the point that if one of them dropped his whip, he would not say to anyone, “Hand it to me.”

There are hadiths, detailed distinctions, and scholarly discussions on this subject that cannot be accommodated here. Among them is his saying to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Take whatever comes to you of this wealth without your asking for it or eagerly seeking it. Whatever does not come to you, do not set your heart on it.”

And his saying:

“Whoever seeks to be free of need, Allah will make him free of need. Whoever seeks to refrain from begging, Allah will enable him to do so. Whoever strives to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. No one has been given a gift better or more ample than patience.”

And his saying:

“Whoever asks people while having enough to suffice him will have his asking appear as scratches, scratch marks, or scrapes on his face.”

And his saying:

“For one of you to take his rope and go out to gather firewood is better for him than asking people, whether they give to him or refuse him.”

There are other hadiths besides these.

---

## Page 5391

As for permissible asking, examples include what Allah Most High relates about Moses and al-Khidr: they came to the people of a village and asked its inhabitants for food. Another example is the Prophet’s saying:

“Asking is not lawful except for someone burdened with a blood-money payment, an overwhelming debt, or grinding poverty.”

Likewise, he said to Qabīsa ibn Mukhāriq al-Hilālī:

“O Qabīsa, asking is lawful only for three kinds of people: a man whose wealth has been swept away by a calamity, who may ask until he obtains enough to meet his needs, or enough to sustain him, and must then refrain;

a man afflicted by poverty, whose condition is attested by three men of sound judgment from his people, who stand and say, ‘So-and-so has indeed been afflicted by poverty.’ He may ask until he obtains enough to meet his needs, or enough to sustain him, and must then refrain;

and a man who has undertaken a financial liability on behalf of others, who may ask until he obtains enough to discharge that liability, and must then refrain. Anything obtained by asking beyond these circumstances is unlawful gain, which its recipient consumes unlawfully.”

None of the Companions—whether the people of the Suffa or anyone else—made asking people, or importunate begging and soliciting alms, whether with a basket or otherwise, into a trade and occupation from which alone they sought their livelihood. Nor were there among the Companions people with surplus wealth who neglected to pay zakah, spend their wealth in Allah’s cause, or contribute in times of calamity. Rather, both these unjust groups, persisting in manifest wrongdoing—those who withhold zakah and other obligatory dues, and those who transgress the limits set by Allah Most High in taking people’s wealth—were absent from the Companions who have been praised.

toward the believers, firm against the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah and fearing no one’s blame. That is Allah’s bounty, which He grants to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, undertook numerous military expeditions, in nine of which fighting took place, including Badr, Uhud, the Trench, Khaybar, and Hunayn.

The Muslims were defeated at Uhud; at Hunayn they fled and then rallied. Allah granted them victory at Badr when they were weak, and they were besieged at the Trench until Allah repelled those enemies from them. Throughout these engagements, the believers—the people of the Suffa and others—were with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. They never fought alongside the disbelievers. These people equate those who believe and do righteous deeds with those who spread corruption on earth, and the God-fearing with the wicked. They treat Muslims like criminals, and place faith, piety, and righteous deeds on the same footing as disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. They equate the people of Paradise with the people of Hell, and Allah’s close servants with His enemies.

Sometimes they regard this as a matter of (contentment with the divine decree), and sometimes they call it “monotheism and reality,” on the grounds that it is the affirmation of Allah’s sole lordship, which the polytheists acknowledge, and that it is “cosmic reality.”

They say, “Nothing exists other than Him,” meaning that the creature is the Creator and the thing made is its Maker. They may also say:

These resemble the claims of Pharaoh, the Dajjāl, and others like them who deny the Maker, the Creator, the Originator, the Lord of all worlds, or claim that they themselves are He, or that He has indwelt them.

These people disbelieve in the two foundations of Islam: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

The obligatory affirmation of Allah’s oneness is that we worship Allah alone, associate nothing with Him, and set up no rival to Him in His divinity, whether as a partner or an intercessor. As for “the affirmation of Allah’s sole lordship,” meaning the acknowledgment that He is the Creator of everything, this was acknowledged even by the polytheists of whom Allah said:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating partners with Him.”

Nevertheless, they associate partners with Him in His divinity by worshipping other gods alongside Him, taking them as intercessors or partners; or in His lordship by making someone other than Him the lord of certain created beings in His stead, while acknowledging that He is the Lord of that lord and the Creator of those beings.

Paradise half a day before the rich,” they recited poetry and displayed ecstasy in response—all this and similar accounts are fabricated falsehoods and invented lies, as agreed by those people of knowledge and faith who are united on this matter. As for His words:

“And keep yourself patiently in the company of those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

This applies generally to everyone who fits this description, such as those who perform the dawn and afternoon prayers in congregation. They call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face, whether they belong to “Ahl al-Suffa” or not. Allah commanded His Prophet to remain patiently with His righteous servants who seek His Face, and not to let his eyes turn away from them in pursuit of the adornment of worldly life. This verse is in al-Kahf, a Meccan surah.

The same applies to the verse in Sūrat al-Anʿām:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face. You bear no responsibility for their reckoning, nor do they bear any responsibility for yours. Were you to drive them away, you would be among the wrongdoers.”

---

## Page 5405

It has been reported that these two verses were revealed concerning believers who were oppressed, when the arrogant demanded that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, send them away from his company. Allah forbade him to drive away anyone seeking Allah’s Face, even if he was oppressed, and then commanded him to remain patiently with them. This was before the migration to Medina and before the Suffa (shaded platform) existed. Nevertheless, the verse applies to everyone fitting this description, whether among Ahl al-Suffa or others.

The purpose is that he should remain with the pious believers, who are Allah’s friends, even if they are poor and weak. No one gains higher standing with Allah through his authority and wealth, nor through his lowly status and poverty. Rather, one gains higher standing with Him through faith and righteous deeds. Allah therefore forbade His Prophet to obey those possessing authority and wealth who wanted the weak or poor to be sent away. He commanded him not to drive away those among them who sought His Face, but to remain patiently with them in the congregational gatherings in which he was commanded to join them, such as the dawn and afternoon prayers. He was not to obey the dictates of those who were heedless of Allah’s remembrance and followed their own desires.

Section

As for the purported hadith:

“No group ever gathers without a friend of Allah among them.”

It is a fabrication, found in none of the compendia of Islam. How could it be true, when a group may consist of disbelievers or sinful people who die in that state?
