## Page 5467

And Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section

People have frequently disputed which is better: the patient poor person or the grateful wealthy person. Much of their discussion of this question is tainted by some degree of personal bias or lack of knowledge. The dispute involves jurists, Sufis, ordinary people, leaders, and others.

In his al-Tamām (Supplement) to his father’s Book of the Two Reports and the Two Views, al-Qādī Abū al-Husayn ibn al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā mentioned two positions reported from Ahmad on this question. According to the first, the patient poor person is better. This position is said to have been adopted by Abū Ishāq ibn Shāqlā and by Abū al-Husayn’s father, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā; Abū al-Husayn himself argued in its favour.

According to the second, the grateful wealthy person is better. A number of scholars adopted this position, including Ibn Qutaybah. The first view is favoured by many people of spiritual knowledge and jurisprudence

---

## Page 5468

and righteousness among the Sufis and the poor. This view is attributed to al-Junayd and others. The second view is favoured by a group among them, including Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAtāʾ and others. Some people have even claimed consensus on this matter, but that is mistaken.

There is a third view on this question, which is the correct one: neither is unconditionally better than the other; rather, the better of the two is the more pious. As Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb said: “Wealth and poverty are two mounts; I do not mind which of them I ride.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Whether one is rich or poor, Allah can best protect both.”

This view was chosen by a group of scholars, including Shaykh Ibn Hafs al-Suhrawardī. One condition may be better for certain people and in certain circumstances, while the other may be better for other people and in other circumstances. If the two are equal in what earns them honour, they are equal in rank; if one surpasses the other in that respect, he takes precedence. This is the general rule.

Poverty and wealth are two conditions that befall a servant, sometimes by his own choice and sometimes without it, like staying in one place and travelling, health and illness, holding authority and obeying authority, or leading and following in prayer. Neither condition in any of these pairs may be declared unconditionally superior to the other. Rather, one may be better in one situation and the other in another, while in some situations they may be equal. This is illustrated by the hadith traced back to the Prophet in al-Baghawī’s Explanation of the Sunnah, narrated by Anas from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who relates from his Lord Most High:

“And indeed, among My servants is one who

---

## Page 5469

can remain upright only through wealth; were I to impoverish him, that would corrupt him. Among My servants is one who can remain upright only through poverty; were I to enrich him, that would corrupt him. Among My servants is one who can remain upright only through health; were I to make him ill, that would corrupt him. Among My servants is one who can remain upright only through illness; were I to restore his health, that would corrupt him. I direct the affairs of My servants; I am fully aware of them and see them well.”

A report conveying this meaning states:

“Allah shields His believing servant from worldly things, just as one of you shields his sick patient from food and drink.”

Something similar is also reported concerning Moses’ intimate communion with Allah. Ahmad mentioned it in al-Zuhd (Asceticism). This concerns someone whom wealth harms and poverty sets right. Another hadith states:

“How excellent is good wealth for a righteous man!”

Just as there are “three views” on this question, people fall into “three categories”: the wealthy person, who possesses more than he needs; the poor person, who cannot fully meet his needs; and a third category, those who possess just enough to meet their needs.

Thus, among the greatest prophets and messengers and the earliest forerunners in faith were some who were wealthy, such as Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah; Job; David; Solomon; ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān; ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf; Talhah; al-Zubayr; Sa‘d ibn Mu‘ādh; Usayd ibn al-Hudayr; As‘ad ibn Zurārah; Abū Ayyūb al-Ansārī; ‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit; and others like them, who are among the finest of creation—the prophets and the utterly truthful.

---

## Page 5470

And among them were those who were poor, such as the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary; John son of Zechariah; ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib; Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī; Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr; Salmān al-Fārisī; and others like them, who are among the finest of creation—the prophets and the utterly truthful.

Among them were also those who experienced both conditions—wealth at one time and poverty at another—and combined the generosity of the wealthy with the patience of the poor, such as our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr, and ‘Umar.

The texts of the Quran and Sunnah judge with justice. In the Quran, Allah has not preferred anyone on account of poverty or wealth, just as He has not preferred anyone on account of health or illness, residence or travel, commanding or obeying, or leading or following. Rather, He says:

“Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”

He has distinguished people by righteous deeds: faith, its pillars and its branches, such as certainty, knowledge, love for Allah, turning to Him, reliance upon Him, hope in Him, fear of Him, gratitude to Him, and patience for His sake.

In the verse concerning justice, He says:

“O you who believe, stand firmly for justice as witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives. Whether a person is rich or poor, Allah is best able to care for both. So do not follow your desires, lest you deviate from justice.”

Accordingly, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs treated Muslims, rich and poor alike, justly in their affairs. When some wealthy people asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to send the poor away, Allah forbade him to do so and praised them for seeking His Face. He said:

“And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord”—to the end of the verse.

---

## Page 5471

He also said:

“Keep yourself patiently with those who call upon their Lord.”

When one of the poor asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for something he was unsuited to undertake, he forbade him to do so. He said:

“O Abū Dharr, I consider you weak, and I love for you what I love for myself. Do not take command over even two people, nor assume responsibility for an orphan’s property.”

Rich and poor were on an equal footing in their seating in his presence, in the rows behind him, and in other matters. Whenever any of them possessed particular merit, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, acknowledged that merit, as when he supplicated for the seventy Quran reciters. He would sit with the people of the Suffa—the shaded platform. Yet ‘Uthmān, Talha, al-Zubayr, Sa‘d ibn Mu‘ādh, Usayd ibn al-Hudayr, ‘Abbād ibn Bishr, and other wealthy leaders among the Muhājirūn and Ansār also enjoyed a standing that others among the poor did not have.

This is how the balanced imams treated the rich and the poor. This is the justice and equity brought by the Quran and Sunnah. It was the way of ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Ibn al-Mubārak, Mālik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others in their dealings with the strong and the weak, the rich and the poor.

Among the imams, however, were those such as al-Thawrī who favored the poor and were biased against the wealthy, exercising their judgment and seeking Allah’s pleasure thereby. Near the end of his life, he was reproached for this and abandoned that approach.

---

## Page 5472

Others among them favored the wealthy and those in authority, such as al-Zuhrī, Rajā’ ibn Haywa, Abū al-Zinād, Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad, and others. Some criticized them for this, though their position rested on interpretation and scholarly judgment. The first approach, however, represents the justice and equity indicated by the Quran and Sunnah.

The reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are balanced. For it is reported:

“The poor said to him, ‘O Messenger of Allah, the wealthy have taken all the rewards. They pray as we pray and fast as we fast, but they have surplus wealth from which they give charity, whereas we cannot.’ He said, ‘Shall I teach you something which, if you do it, will enable you to catch up with those who have surpassed you, while those who come after you will not catch up with you unless they do as you do?’ He then taught them the hundredfold glorification to recite after each prayer. They came to him and said, ‘Our wealthy brothers heard about this and have done the same.’ He replied, ‘That is Allah’s bounty, which He grants to whom He wills.’”

This addition in Sahīh Muslim is among the reports transmitted by Abū Sālih with an interrupted chain. This indicates the superiority of those wealthy people who perform the same acts of worship with their hearts and bodies as the poor, while surpassing them by spending in Allah’s cause and performing similar acts of financial worship.

It is also established in the Sahīh that he said:

“The poor of my community will enter Paradise half a day—five hundred years—before the wealthy.” Another version states, “Forty years.”

This indicates an advantage enjoyed by poor believers: they will enter Paradise before wealthy believers. Both statements are true, for the poor person does not possess much wealth that would require him to account for

---

## Page 5473

receiving and spending it. His entry into Paradise is therefore not delayed by the reckoning, and he enters first. He also has greater need for a swift reward because of the good things he missed in this world. The wealthy person, meanwhile, is called to account. If he has used his wealth well rather than badly and is superior to the poor person, his rank will be raised above the latter’s after entering Paradise. If he is his equal, their ranks will be equal; if he is inferior, his rank will be lower. His need for a swift reward is not like that of the poor person.

A parallel is the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning his “Pool,” whose length and breadth are each a month’s journey:

“Its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. The first people to reach me there will be the poor among the Emigrants: those with dirty clothes and dishevelled hair, who do not marry women accustomed to luxury and for whom the doors of kings are not opened. One of them dies with a need still stirring in his heart, finding no way to fulfil it.”

Thus, they arrive first at what relieves the hardship and distress they experienced in this world. This is an occasion of hospitality extended to all: those who are hungriest are fed first, even though some who come later may receive a kind of food not given to some who came earlier, having earned it through their generosity toward the host or for some other reason.

No reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this question are more authentic than these two hadiths. They contain the decisive judgment: the poor have precedence, while the wealthy have superiority in merit. At times one consideration may outweigh the other. This is like the seventy thousand who enter Paradise without being called to account, with another seventy thousand accompanying every thousand. Others may be called to account after them, yet, upon entering Paradise, be raised above them in rank.

As for the report:

“Ibn Awf will enter Paradise crawling,”

it is a fabrication with no basis;

## Page 5474

for the evidence of the Quran and Sunnah establishes that the best of this community are those who fought at Badr, followed by those who gave the Pledge of Divine Pleasure; that the Ten are superior to the others; and that the four caliphs are the best of the community.

It is established in the authentic hadith collections that he said:

“I looked into Paradise and saw that most of its inhabitants were poor, and I looked into the Fire and saw that most of its inhabitants were women.”

It is also established in the authentic collections that he said:

“Paradise and the Fire disputed. Paradise said, ‘Why is it that only the weak and lowly among people enter me?’ The Fire said, ‘Why is it that only the domineering and arrogant enter me?’”

He also said:

“I stood at the gate of Paradise and saw that most of those entering it were poor, while the wealthy were held back—except those destined for the Fire, who had already been ordered into it.”

Alongside this is his statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the authentic hadith:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both.”

These hadiths convey two meanings. The first is that Paradise is the abode of the humble and reverent, not of the arrogant and domineering, whether rich or poor. For it is established in an authentic hadith:

“No one with an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise, and no one with an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will enter the Fire.

“He was asked, ‘Messenger of Allah, a man likes his clothes and shoes to look fine. Is that arrogance?’ He replied, ‘No. Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Rather, arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.’”

Thus he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that Allah loves dressing well

---

## Page 5475

which is only possible with wealth, and that this is not arrogance.

An authentic hadith states:

“There are three to whom Allah will neither speak nor look on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and theirs will be a painful punishment: an arrogant poor man, an elderly adulterer, and a lying king.”

Likewise, another reported hadith states:

“A man keeps exalting himself, then exalting himself, then exalting himself, until he is recorded with Allah as a tyrant, though he has authority over no one but his own household.”

These two hadiths show that some poor people are arrogant and will not enter Paradise, while some wealthy people dress well without arrogance, and Allah loves their fine appearance. Alongside this is his statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in an authentic hadith:

“Allah does not look at your appearance or your wealth; rather, He looks at your hearts and your deeds.”

Related to this is what Heraclius said to Abū Sufyān: “Was it the weak among the people who followed him, or their nobles?”

He replied, “Rather, their weak.”

Heraclius said, “Such are the followers of the prophets.”

They also said to Noah:

“Shall we believe you when the lowliest follow you?”

This shows that people in positions of leadership and high social standing are less disposed to submit to worshipping and obeying Allah, because their love of leadership prevents them from doing so, unlike those who are weak and powerless. The following reported hadith—if it has been reliably preserved—conveys this meaning:

“O Allah, let me live as one of the lowly, let me die as one of the lowly, and gather me among the lowly.”

The lowly are the opposite of the arrogant. They are those who are reverently submissive to Allah, who humble themselves before His greatness, and who seek no exalted status on earth, whether they are rich or poor.

## Page 5476

Another example of this is that Allah gave him the choice between being a servant-messenger and being a prophet-king. He chose to be a servant-messenger, because a servant-messenger acts at his Master’s command, not for his own benefit, whereas a king acts for his own benefit, even when doing so is permissible. As Solomon was told:

“This is Our gift, so give or withhold without being called to account.”

These hadiths show that he chose servitude and humility, even though he and his followers held the highest standing. As Allah said:

“Do not lose heart or grieve, for you will have the upper hand.”

And He said:

“Honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.”

He did not seek ascendancy, even though he attained it. Moreover, he received gifts such as no one else received. Wealth is preferable only because it enables one to benefit others, spend in Allah’s cause, and draw upon it to obey and worship Him. Otherwise, merely possessing wealth brings no benefit and may even cause harm.

Alongside this, he patiently endured hardship and adversity such as no one else endured. Thus he attained the highest ranks of the grateful and the most excellent stations of the patient. He excelled in both poverty and wealth; unlike some of his Companions and members of his community, he was not someone whose spiritual well-being depended on only one of these conditions.

(The second meaning is that righteousness is more prevalent among the poor than among the wealthy, just as, when it is found among the wealthy, it is more complete than among the poor. Thus it is more prevalent among the former and greater among the latter, because the trial of wealth is greater than the trial of poverty, and fewer people emerge from it unscathed. Whoever emerges from it unscathed is superior to someone who has emerged unscathed only from the trial of poverty; and for this reason

---

## Page 5477

people came to look for righteousness among the poor, since it is more likely to be found among them. Such is the explanation, and Allah knows best. For this reason, humble submission came to be his distinguishing attribute. Likewise, when people saw that humble submission and humility were more prevalent among the poor, they assumed that humility and humble submission were poverty itself. But that is not so.

Rather, poverty here means lacking wealth, whereas humble submission is the submissiveness of the heart. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to seek refuge from the trial of poverty and the evil of the trial of wealth. One of the Companions said, “We were tested with adversity and remained patient; we were tested with prosperity and failed to remain patient.” The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“By Allah, it is not poverty that I fear for you. Rather, I fear that worldly prosperity will be lavished upon you as it was lavished upon those before you, and that you will compete for it.”

For this reason, poverty predominated among the Emigrants, while wealth predominated among the Helpers; and the Emigrants were superior to the Helpers. Yet some of the wealthy Emigrants were among the best of the Emigrants, even though, through emigrating, they had left behind so much of their wealth that they became poor compared with their former circumstances.

## Page 5478

He was also asked:

“What are the essential meanings of praise and gratitude? Do they have the same meaning or two distinct meanings? For what is praise offered, and for what is gratitude expressed?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. Praise entails commending and extolling the one praised by mentioning his excellent qualities, whether or not he has shown kindness to the person praising him. Gratitude, however, is expressed only for kindness shown by the one thanked to the one thanking him. In this respect, praise is broader than gratitude, since it concerns both excellent qualities and acts of kindness. Allah Most High is praised for His most beautiful names and loftiest attributes, and for what He has created in the Hereafter and in this world.

Thus, the Most High says:

“Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light.”

He also says:

“Praise be to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. To Him belongs all praise in the Hereafter.”

And He says:

“Praise be to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers with two, three, or four wings. He adds to creation whatever He wills.”

---

## Page 5479

As for gratitude, it is expressed only for favors bestowed, so in this respect it is narrower in scope than praise. Yet it is expressed through the heart, the hand, and the tongue, as the poet said:

Your favors have won you three things from me:
My hand, my tongue, and my hidden heart.

Hence the Most High says:

“Work, O family of David, in gratitude.”

Praise, however, is expressed only through the heart and the tongue. Thus, gratitude is broader in the forms it takes, while praise is broader in the reasons for which it is offered. This is reflected in the hadith:

“Praising Allah is the foremost part of gratitude; whoever does not praise Allah has not thanked Him.”

It is reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah is pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

And Allah knows best.

## Page 5480

Summary of a Debate on
“Praise and Gratitude”

A discussion between Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and Ibn al-Murahhal

The discussion concerned praise and gratitude: gratitude is expressed through the heart, the tongue, and the limbs, whereas praise is expressed only through the tongue.

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

One author—whom he named—has reported that the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah is that gratitude consists only in belief, whereas the position of the Khawārij is that it consists in belief, speech, and deeds. On this basis, they concluded that whoever abandons deeds is a disbeliever, because disbelief is the opposite of gratitude: whoever is not grateful is therefore a disbeliever.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

This position attributed to Ahl al-Sunnah is wrong, and its attribution to Ahl al-Sunnah is wrong. The position of Ahl al-Sunnah is that gratitude is expressed through belief, speech, and deeds. Allah Most High says:

“Work, O family of David,

---

## Page 5481

in gratitude.”

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stood in prayer until his feet swelled. He was asked, ‘Do you do this when Allah has forgiven your past and future sins?’ He replied, ‘Should I not be a grateful servant?’”

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

I am not discussing the evidence, and I concede the weakness of this position. I am merely reporting that it is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

Attributing this to Ahl al-Sunnah is wrong. Once a position has been shown to be weak, how can it be attributed to the people of truth? Moreover, scholars known for adhering to the Sunnah—as many as Allah has willed—have explicitly stated that gratitude is expressed through belief, speech, and deeds. The Quran and Sunnah also establish this.

I said:

The chapter on the prostration of gratitude in jurisprudence is too well known to need mentioning. Indeed, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning the prostration in Surah Sād, ‘David performed it in repentance, whereas we perform it in gratitude.’”

Then which of the leading scholars of the Sunnah said that gratitude consists only in belief?

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

This has been reported. The report cannot be rejected, but it may be considered problematic. One may say, “This is a problematic position.”

---

## Page 5482

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah said:

Reports are of two kinds. The first conveys what someone has heard or seen. The second is based on independent reasoning and inference. When someone says, “So-and-so’s position is such-and-such,” or “The position of Ahl al-Sunnah is such-and-such,” he may attribute it to them because he believes that their principles entail it, even though the person concerned never said it. Errors frequently occur in such attributions.

Do you not see that many authors say, “The position of al-Shāfiʿī, or someone else, is such-and-such,” when his explicit statement says otherwise? Their excuse is that they considered his principles to entail that position, so they attributed it to his school by inference rather than on the basis of an explicit statement.

The same applies here. Ahl al-Sunnah do not declare people disbelievers on account of sins, whereas the Khawārij do. The author then regarded kufr (disbelief or ingratitude) as the opposite of gratitude: “I believe that if we count deeds as gratitude, it necessarily follows that gratitude is absent when deeds are absent; and whenever gratitude is absent, kufr takes its place.” This is why he said that they based their practice of declaring people disbelievers on account of sins upon this. Hence, the exclusion of deeds from gratitude was attributed to Ahl al-Sunnah.

I said:

Likewise, many speculative theologians excluded deeds from faith for this very reason.

He said:

This is mistaken, for declaring kufr is of two kinds: the first concerns ingratitude for blessings, and the second concerns disbelief in Allah. The kufr that is the opposite of gratitude is only ingratitude for blessings, not disbelief in Allah. Thus, when gratitude disappears, it is replaced by ingratitude for

---

## Page 5483

blessings, not disbelief in Allah.

I said:

Moreover, even if gratitude were the opposite of disbelief in Allah, someone who abandons deeds while remaining grateful in his heart and with his tongue has fulfilled part of gratitude, including its foundation. Disbelief is established only when gratitude is entirely absent.

As Ahl al-Sunnah have said:

Someone who abandons the branches of faith does not become a disbeliever unless he abandons its foundation, which is belief. When something consists of branches and parts, the loss of its branches does not necessarily mean that its designation no longer applies—as with a person whose hand is cut off, or a tree some of whose branches are cut off.

Al-Sadr Ibn al-Murahhal said:

Your associates have disagreed with al-Hasan al-Basrī about calling a sinner ungrateful for blessings, just as they disagreed with the Khawārij about considering him a disbeliever in Allah.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

My associates have not disagreed with al-Hasan on this. From whom among my associates are you reporting this? Rather, they permit calling a sinner ungrateful for blessings where revealed law applies that designation.

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

I merely thought that your associates had said this. My associates, however, have disagreed with al-Hasan on this.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

Nor have your associates disagreed with him. For your associates

---

## Page 5484

have interpreted the Prophet’s hadiths—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in which he described certain sinful acts, such as abandoning prayer and fighting Muslims, as disbelief, as referring to ingratitude for blessings. It is therefore clear that they do describe sins, broadly speaking, as ingratitude for blessings. Thus, they agree with al-Hasan rather than disagree with him.

Ibn al-Murahhal then said again:

I am quoting this from the work. A report may be questioned, but its transmission cannot be disallowed.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

If the choice is between attributing a false doctrine to Ahl al-Sunnah and attributing an alteration in the report to the person reporting their views, it is more appropriate to attribute the alteration to the reporter than to attribute falsehood to the people of truth. Moreover, they have explicitly stated in several places that gratitude is expressed through speech, deeds, and belief. This is too evident to require attribution to any particular individual.

Furthermore, we know beyond doubt that excluding deeds from gratitude to Allah is not among the principles of the people of truth. Indeed, the jurists have explicitly stated that zakat is gratitude for the blessing of wealth. The evidence for this is too abundant to require citation. The explanation of gratitude as being expressed through speech and deeds, as given in books discussing the terms “praise” and “gratitude”—such as works of Quranic commentary and lexicography

---

## Page 5485

and hadith commentaries—is familiar even to ordinary people. Both the Quran and the Sunnah establish this.

Ibn al-Murahhal then turned to another point, saying:

“Al-Hasan al-Basrī calls the sinful person a hypocrite, whereas your associates do not.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn replied:

“On the contrary, he is called a hypocrite in the sense of minor hypocrisy, not major hypocrisy. Hypocrisy can refer both to major hypocrisy, which is concealing disbelief, and to minor hypocrisy, which is a discrepancy between one’s inward and outward states regarding religious obligations.”

Ibn al-Murahhal asked him:

“On what basis do you say that the term applies to both?”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn replied:

“This is well known among the scholars. They understood in this sense the words of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

‘The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks his promise; and when entrusted with something, he betrays that trust.’

“Al-Tirmidhī and others mentioned this and related it from the scholars. More than one of the early generations said:

‘There is disbelief of a lesser degree, hypocrisy of a lesser degree, and polytheism of a lesser degree.’

“If hypocrisy is a general category comprising two types, then the sinful person falls within one of those types.”

---

## Page 5486

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“How can you make ‘hypocrisy’ a generic term when you have made it an equivocal term? If it is a generic term, it is univocal, and univocal terms are distinct from equivocal ones. How, then, can you make it both equivocal and univocal?”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn replied:

“I did not say that it was equivocal. I merely said that it applies to both this and that; application is a broader notion.

“Moreover, even if I had said that it was equivocal, the statement would have been correct. A single term may be applied to two things either univocally or equivocally. Thus, I applied the term ‘hypocrisy’ to concealing disbelief and concealing disobedience, sometimes equivocally and sometimes univocally. Likewise, the term ‘existence’ is applied to necessary being and contingent being equivocally according to some, and univocally according to others. This is why it is called an analogical term.”

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“How can this be?” He then launched into remarks that would be unbecoming to repeat.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said to him:

“Subtle meanings require attentive listening and reflection. When two essences have something in common and something that distinguishes them, and a term applies to each, it may be applied to both with reference to that by which

---

## Page 5487

each essence is distinguished from the other. It is then equivocal, as in lexical homonymy. Alternatively, it may be applied with reference to what the two essences have in common, in which case it is a univocal term.”

I say:

A term may originally be assigned in the language to denote the common element; customary usage then comes predominantly to apply it now to one, now to the other. Thus, by customary usage, it comes to signify both what they share and what distinguishes them.

The distinguishing feature may instead be indicated by a contextual marker, such as the definite article or a possessive construction. An example is a generic term whose customary usage has come to refer predominantly to certain species within its scope. Thus, when the word “animal” is used predominantly for a horse, we may apply it to a horse with reference to what it shares with all other animals. In that case, it is univocal.

We may also apply it with reference to what is specific to a horse. In that case, it is equivocal between horses in particular and animals in general. Its application to a horse is therefore sometimes univocal and sometimes equivocal.

The same applies when a generic term comes to refer predominantly to particular individuals and becomes a proper name through predominant usage, as with “the son of ‘Amr” and “the star.” We may apply the term to the individual with reference to what he or it shares with the other sons of ‘Amr or the other stars. Its application is then univocal. We may also apply it with reference to what distinguishes that individual from the other sons of ‘Amr or the other stars. It is then equivocal between this individual sense and the generic sense. Likewise, every general term whose use has come to predominate for certain individual instances

---

## Page 5488

may validly be applied to such an instance according to its original, general designation, in which case its application is univocal, or according to its second designation, in which case its application becomes equivocal.

The term “hypocrisy” belongs to this category. In religious usage, it means outwardly professing religion while inwardly concealing its opposite. This religious meaning is narrower than the linguistic meaning of hypocrisy, which is not confined to outwardly professing religion. What is inwardly concealed in opposition to religion may be either disbelief or sinful disobedience.

If someone outwardly presents himself as a believer while inwardly denying the truth, this is major hypocrisy, whose perpetrator is threatened with being in the lowest depths of the Fire. If, however, he outwardly presents himself as truthful, faithful to his commitments, or trustworthy, while inwardly concealing lies, treachery, betrayal, and the like, this is minor hypocrisy, whose perpetrator is sinful. The term “hypocrisy” therefore originally applies to both univocally. Accordingly, hypocrisy is a generic term encompassing two kinds.

The term may then be used to mean hypocrisy concerning the very foundation of religion, as in His words:

“Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths,”

and:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars.”

Here, “hypocrite” means a disbeliever. The term may also mean hypocrisy concerning the subsidiary matters of religion, as in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

---

## Page 5489

“The signs of a hypocrite are three,”

and his words:

“There are four traits which, if found in a person, make him a complete hypocrite,”

and the statement of Ibn ‘Umar concerning someone who says one thing in the presence of rulers, then leaves and says the opposite:

“In the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, we used to consider this hypocrisy.”

When you intend either of these two kinds, its restriction to that kind may arise from a verbal indication, such as the definite article referring to something already known, or a genitive construction. This does not prevent the term from remaining univocal. For example, someone may say, “The judge has arrived,” meaning the judge of his town, because the definite article refers to someone already known. Likewise, the Exalted says:

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

Here, it is the definite article that restricts “the messenger” to Moses, not the word “messenger” itself. Alternatively, the restriction may arise because the term is predominantly used for that particular kind; it then becomes equivocal between the general expression and the specific meaning.

The same applies to His words:

“When the hypocrites come to you.”

The restriction of this term to the disbeliever may result either from the definite article, which indicates a known referent—the hypocrite in question being the disbeliever—or from the predominant use of this designation in religious usage for hypocrisy involving disbelief.

As for the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“There are three traits which, if found in a person, make him a hypocrite,”

he means a hypocrite in the general sense: someone whose outward profession of religion differs from what he inwardly conceals. Thus, when applying the term “hypocrisy” to both the disbeliever and the sinner, if you apply it to the disbeliever with regard to what distinguishes him from the sinner, its application to the two is equivocal. It may likewise refer specifically to the disbeliever while remaining univocal, if what indicates this restriction is not the word “hypocrite” itself, but rather the definite article.

---

## Page 5490

This valuable discussion applies to every general term used for a particular kind within its scope, whether because of predominant usage or because of a verbal indication restricting it to that kind, such as definiteness conferred by a genitive construction or the definite article.

If this results from predominant usage, it is valid to say that the term is equivocal. If it results from a verbal indication, the term remains univocal. Thus, it is valid to say that “hypocrisy” is a generic term encompassing two kinds, since the term is originally general and univocal.

It is also valid to say that it is equivocal between hypocrisy concerning the very foundation of religion and hypocrisy in religion in general, since, in established religious usage, it has come to refer predominantly to hypocrisy involving disbelief.

## Page 5491

Second Discussion

Praise and gratitude each have a broader scope than the other in a different respect.

Praise is broader with respect to the grounds for which it is offered: it may be offered for all attributes, whereas gratitude is offered only for kindness shown. Gratitude is broader with respect to its means of expression: it is expressed through belief, speech, and action. Praise is expressed through action, speech, or belief.

Shaykh and Imam Zayn al-Dīn Ibn al-Munajjā al-Hanbalī raised the following objection:

This distinction concerns only that to which praise and gratitude relate. The fact that either is offered for such-and-such or expressed through such-and-such is external to its essence, so this does not constitute a distinction in their essential nature. Definitions address only intrinsic attributes, not what lies outside them.

Shaykh al-Islam Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah replied:

Concepts are of two kinds: independent and relational.

The definitions of independent concepts do not include their relations. As for relational concepts, there must be included in

---

## Page 5492

their definitions the relations in question, for these form part of their essential nature. Such concepts cannot be conceived without conceiving the things to which they relate. These objects of relation therefore form part of their essential nature and must be mentioned in their definitions. Praise and gratitude relate to that for which praise and gratitude are offered. Their essential nature cannot be fully stated without mentioning their respective objects, which therefore form part of that nature.

Al-Sadr Ibn al-Murahhal objected:

A thing has no positively existing attribute by virtue of the object to which it relates. Thus, neither praise nor gratitude has any positively existing attribute by virtue of its object. For the attribute connected with that object is relational, and relations have no positive existence. If an attribute has no positive existence, it cannot form part of a thing’s essential nature, because nonexistence cannot be part of existence.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn replied:

Your statement that a thing has no positively existing attribute by virtue of the object to which it relates is not universally true. It may have such an attribute, or it may not.

What most speculative theologians actually say is:

The object of speech has no positively existing attribute by virtue of that speech.

Attributes involving a relation are of two kinds:

The first is a pure relation, such as fatherhood, sonship, being above, being below, and the like. It is this kind of attribute of which it is said:

It is merely a relation, and relations have no positive existence.

The second is a positively existing attribute that is related

---

## Page 5493

to something else, such as love, hatred, will, aversion, power, and other attributes. Love is a positively existing attribute connected with the beloved. Love is thus the subject of a relation, meaning that the relation is an attribute attaching to it—not that love itself is the relation. There is therefore a distinction between a relation and an attribute involving a relation.

It is the relation itself that is said to have no positive existence.

He continued:

“As for an attribute involving a relation, it may have positive existence, as love does.”

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“Love has no positive existence, because love is a relation, and relations have no positive existence.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“The claim that love, hatred, will, and aversion have no positive existence is self-evidently false. It contradicts the consensus of rational people. Moreover, this is the position held by some of the Muʿtazilah regarding Allah’s will: they claimed that it is a negative attribute, meaning that He is neither overpowered nor coerced. People have unanimously rejected this position as false.

“As for a created being’s will, love, and hatred, we know of no rational person who has said that they have no positive existence.”

Nevertheless, Ibn al-Murahhal persisted in maintaining that love (hubb)—the heart’s inclination toward the beloved—has no positive existence.

He also said:

“Love (mahabbah) has positive existence.”

---

## Page 5494

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“Mahabbah is the same as hubb: love. One may say either ahabbahu or habbahu (‘he loved him’), using either hubb or mahabbah as the verbal noun. There is no difference; both are verbal nouns.”

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“And I say that if they are verbal nouns, neither has positive existence.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said to him:

“Once a discussion reaches self-evident premises, it has reached its conclusion and is complete. That love and hatred have positive existence is self-evident. Everyone knows that when a living being is devoid of love, this absence is a negative attribute. When he becomes loving, the subject has changed and acquired a positive attribute beyond what he possessed before love came to subsist in him. Anyone who experiences this within himself perceives it just as he perceives his desire and aversion, his contentment and anger, his pleasure and pain.

“The proof is that you say: ‘He loved; he loves; love.’ The contradictory of ‘he loved’ is ‘he did not love.’ ‘He did not love’ expresses a negative attribute, and the contradictory of nonexistence is positive existence.”

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“This is refuted by the expressions ‘it was impossible’ and ‘it is impossible.’ The contradictory of impossibility is ‘no impossibility,’ yet impossibility is a negative attribute.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“Impossibility is a matter of mental conception. What is impossible has no external existence in which an attribute could subsist. It is known only to the intellect.

---

## Page 5495

and insofar as it is known, it has existence in knowledge. Negating this existence in knowledge means the absence of that existence. Thus, this does not refute our statement that the contradictory of nonexistence is positive existence. Love, however, is an attribute subsisting in the one who loves. You point to an externally existing individual and say: ‘This living being has become loving after not having been loving.’ You are thus speaking about external existence. If the contradictory of this attribute is external nonexistence, then the attribute itself must have external existence.

“In short, that love and hatred are positive, existent attributes is self-evident. No dispute over this can be entertained, and anyone who disputes it can only be debated as one debates the Sophists.”

I say: Since love, hatred, and similar attributes that relate to something else have positive existence, the distinction becomes clear between attributes that are themselves relations or connections and attributes that bear a relation or connection to something else. Praise and gratitude belong to the second category. Praise is something positively existent that relates to that for which praise is given. Likewise, gratitude is something positively existent that relates to that for which gratitude is expressed. Their true nature cannot therefore be fully understood without understanding their positive attribute that relates to something else. That attribute is part of their true nature. If, then, the object of one is more extensive than the object of the other, while that relation merely attaches to a positive attribute they possess, that positive attribute must be mentioned when explaining their true nature.

The proof of this is that someone who does not understand beneficence cannot understand gratitude.

---

## Page 5496

and thus it is clear that conceiving the object of gratitude is part of conceiving gratitude.

I say:

Even if it were said that this is merely something privative, if a thing’s true nature comprises both existence and nonexistence, both must be mentioned when defining it. Likewise, when defining a father precisely as a father, conceiving him depends on conceiving fatherhood, which is a relation, even though the father is something positively existent.

Praise and gratitude relate to that for which praise and gratitude are offered. Even if this relatedness does not attach to a positive attribute, praise and gratitude cannot be understood without understanding their object, just as the meaning of a father cannot be understood without understanding fatherhood, which is the relation involved.

Likewise, praise and gratitude are two things related to that for which praise and gratitude are offered, and this relation forms part of what these terms denote. The proof is that someone who does not understand admirable attributes cannot understand praise, and someone who does not understand beneficence cannot understand gratitude. If understanding them depends on understanding their respective objects, then it depends all the more on understanding the relation itself. For the relation is derivative of its object and dependent upon it. If understanding praise and gratitude depends on understanding their objects, which are further removed from them than the relation itself, then it depends all the more on understanding that relation—even if the relation is something privative. And Allah knows best.

## Page 5497

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah said to him:

His words, “Allah has permitted trade,” are immediately followed by His words, “and forbidden usury.” Most forms of usury are also called sales. If “usury” is an indeterminate term, then its meaning is unknown. Excluding something unknown from something known entails uncertainty about what is excluded. Thus, what is intended remains the permissibility of sales that are not usury. Unless a particular transaction is established not to be usury, it cannot validly be included among lawful sales. This precludes claiming general applicability. If, on the other hand, “usury” is a general term, it is still excepted from sales. The term “sale” therefore remains restricted in scope, and one cannot validly claim that it applies generally without qualification.

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“This is a case of restriction. Here, two general statements conflict; it is not a case of exception, for the forms used to express exceptions are well known. If this is a restriction, it does not preclude claiming general applicability for the expression.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“This is a connected statement whose parts are linked together, and it is a case of restriction by an attached qualification. Jurists call this an exception, as when someone says, ‘This house belongs to him, and this room within it belongs to me.’ This is equivalent to saying, ‘except this room.’ Likewise, if someone says, ‘Honor these people, and do not honor so-and-so,’ when that person is one of them, this is equivalent to saying, ‘except so-and-so.’ That being so, it amounts to saying, ‘Allah has permitted trade except that which constitutes usury.’”

---

## Page 5498

Thus, anyone who still claims that it applies generally to everything called a sale is mistaken.

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“I concede that it applies generally only to every sale that is not called usury.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn replied:

“That was precisely the point. But this invalidates the claim that its general applicability is unrestricted, for claiming unrestricted general applicability is incompatible with claiming that it applies generally to some categories but not others. This is perfectly clear.”

Someone claimed that there were two views on the matter: first, that it is a general statement whose scope has been restricted; and second, that its full generality is intended.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“The claim that its full generality is intended is certainly false, for we know that many individual forms of sale are forbidden.”

Ibn al-Murahhal objected that those forms had been forbidden after having been permitted, making this a case of abrogation.

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“That would entail that we could not prohibit any sale on the basis of a solitary report or analogical reasoning, for the Quran cannot be abrogated by either of these. Its general scope, however, may be restricted by them. The jurists have agreed on prohibiting sales on these grounds.”

---

## Page 5499

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“I withdraw that objection. However, I maintain that its general scope is intended to cover everything called a sale in Islamic law. For ‘sale’ is among the terms assigned new meanings, denoting every sale valid under Islamic law.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“‘Sale’ is not among the terms assigned new meanings. What it denotes in Islamic law and customary usage is what it denotes linguistically. The Lawgiver has, however, stipulated conditions for its permissibility and validity, just as the people of the pre-Islamic era also had conditions according to their own conventions. The same applies to all other names of contracts, such as lease, pledge, gift, loan, and marriage—when the contract is meant—and others: they retain their original meanings.

“Assigning new meanings to terms is needed only when the Lawgiver introduces concepts previously unknown to the Arabs, such as prayer, zakah, and dry purification. It is then that such a reassignment is needed. The meanings of these contracts, however, have always been known.”

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“The scholars of my school have said that these terms have been assigned new meanings.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“If the word ‘sale’ in the verse meant a sale valid under Islamic law, the meaning would be: ‘Allah has permitted sales valid under Islamic law,’ or ‘Allah has permitted sales that are lawful in His sight.’ Besides being repetitive, this would preclude using the verse as evidence. For we cannot know that any particular sale falls within the verse’s scope until we know that it is valid under Islamic law. Once we know that, we no longer need to cite the verse as evidence.”

---

## Page 5500

Ibn al-Murahhal said:

“Once it is established that a particular transaction is called a sale in the linguistic sense, I say: It is a sale in Islamic law, since the presumption is that the term has not been assigned a new meaning. Since it is a sale in Islamic law, it falls within the verse’s scope.”

Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn said:

“This would hold only if it had not been established that the term has been assigned a new meaning. But once that has been established, no particular instance can be included under it until it is established that the term, in its new meaning, applies to that instance.

“Otherwise, this would entail that anything referred to linguistically by the terms ‘prayer,’ ‘zakah,’ ‘dry purification,’ ‘fasting,’ ‘sale,’ ‘lease,’ or ‘pledge’ could, on this basis, be included within what those terms denote in Islamic law. On that assumption, no distinction would remain between terms assigned new meanings and those that have not been.

“The presumption that a term has not been assigned a new meaning applies only when such a reassignment has not been established. Once it has been established, however, the presumption is that a particular instance does not fall under the term in its new meaning until its inclusion under that meaning is established.”

Once it is understood that among people are “allies of the Most Merciful and allies of Satan,” the two must be distinguished, just as Allah and His Messenger have distinguished between them. The allies of Allah are the believers who fear Him, as He, exalted is He, says:

“Indeed, the allies of Allah will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

“Those who believe and are mindful of Him.”

In the authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī and others from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘Whoever shows enmity to an ally of Mine has openly waged war against Me—or: I have declared war on him. And there is no drawing near to Me

## Page 5505

by My servant comparable to his fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he strikes, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely grant him refuge. I have never hesitated over anything I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet he must inevitably face it.’”

This is the most authentic hadith narrated concerning the allies of Allah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that whoever shows enmity to an ally of Allah has openly waged war against Allah. Another hadith states:

“Indeed, I avenge My allies as an enraged lion takes revenge.”

That is, I exact vengeance on their behalf against those who show them enmity, just as an enraged lion takes revenge. This is because the allies of Allah are those who believe in Him and ally themselves with Him. They love what He loves, hate what He hates, are pleased with what pleases Him, and are displeased with what displeases Him. They enjoin what He enjoins, forbid what He forbids, give to those He wishes them to give to, and withhold from those He wishes them to withhold from. As narrated in al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The firmest bond of faith is to love for Allah’s sake and to hate for Allah’s sake.”

In another hadith, narrated by Abū Dāwūd, he said:

“Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

“Alliance” is the opposite of enmity. The basis of alliance is love and nearness, and the basis of

enmity is hatred and distance.

It has also been said that an ally is called a walī because he performs acts of obedience in succession. The first explanation, however, is more correct. A walī is someone near; thus one says, “This yalī that,” meaning that it is near it. This is also the sense of the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Give the prescribed shares of inheritance to those entitled to them, and whatever remains is for the nearest male relative.”

That is, the man most closely related to the deceased. He emphasized this by specifying “male,” to make clear that this ruling applies exclusively to males, rather than equally to males and females. Similarly, he said concerning zakat:

Since an ally of Allah is someone who concurs with Him and follows Him concerning what He loves and is pleased with, what He hates and is displeased with, and what He commands and forbids, whoever shows enmity to His ally shows enmity to Him. As Allah Most High says:

Whoever shows enmity to Allah’s allies has thus shown enmity to Him, and whoever shows enmity to Him has waged war against Him. For this reason, He said:

Nor do they know that the portico existed only in Medina. It was a portico on the northern side of his mosque, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, where newcomers stayed if they had no family or friends with whom to lodge; for the believers used to emigrate to the Prophet

---

## Page 5511

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to Medina. Whoever could find somewhere to stay lodged there, while anyone unable to do so stayed in the mosque until accommodation became available to which he could move.

“Ahl al-Suffa” were not a fixed group of people who remained permanently at the portico. Rather, their numbers sometimes decreased and sometimes increased; a man might stay there for a time and then move elsewhere. Those who lodged there were like other Muslims, with no special distinction in knowledge or piety. Indeed, among them were some who apostatized from Islam and whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, put to death, such as the men of ʿUrayna. They found Medina disagreeable—that is, unhealthy—so the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, arranged for them to have milch camels—that is, camels giving milk—and instructed them to drink their urine and milk. When they recovered, they killed the herdsman and drove off the camels. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent men in pursuit of them, and they were brought back. He ordered their hands and feet to be cut off, their eyes were seared, and he left them on the lava field, where they asked for water but were given none. Their account is related in both Sahīh collections through Anas, and it mentions that they stayed at the portico.

Thus, people like these lodged there, but so did some of the finest Muslims, including Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, who was the best of those who stayed at the portico and later moved away. Abū Hurayra and others also stayed there. Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī compiled a history of those who stayed at the portico.

As for the “Helpers,” they were not among Ahl al-Suffa. Nor were the leading Emigrants, such as Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Talha, al-Zubayr, and ʿAbd al-Rahmān

## Page 5512

ibn ʿAwf, Abū ʿUbayda, and others.

It has been reported that a servant of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba was staying there, and that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “This is one of the seven.” This hadith is a fabrication by the agreement of the scholars, even though Abū Nuʿaym related it in al-Hilya. Likewise, none of the hadiths attributed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, specifying the numbers of the “friends of Allah,” “abdāl,” “nuqabā’,” “nujabā’,” “awtād,” and “aqtāb”—such as four, seven, twelve, forty, seventy, three hundred and thirteen, or a single “qutb”—is authentically reported from him. The early generations did not use any of these designations except “abdāl.” A hadith concerning them states that they are forty men and that they are in Syria. It appears in al-Musnad among the hadiths narrated by ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, but its chain of transmission is broken, and it is not established as authentic.

It is well known that ʿAlī and the Companions with him were superior to Muʿāwiya and those with him in Syria. Thus, the best people could not have been in Muʿāwiya’s army rather than ʿAlī’s. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both related in their Sahīh collections, on the authority of Abū Saʿīd, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A faction will break away from the religion at a time of division among the Muslims. They will be killed by whichever of the two parties is closer to the truth.”

Those who broke away were the Harūrī Khārijites, who broke away when division arose among the Muslims during ʿAlī’s caliphate. ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib and his companions killed them. This authentic hadith thus shows that ʿAlī

Those with knowledge of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recognize this and similar reports as among the most blatant lies attributed to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The point here is that among those who outwardly acknowledge that his message is universal are some who inwardly believe things that contradict this. Such a person is therefore a hypocrite, yet he claims of himself and others like him

“who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them.”

Faith necessarily entails believing that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the Seal of the Prophets, that there is no prophet after him, and that Allah sent him to all jinn and humankind. ## Page 5516

Likewise, the sages of “Greece,” such as Aristotle and others like him, were polytheists who worshipped idols and heavenly bodies. Aristotle lived three hundred years before the Messiah, peace be upon him, and was a minister to Alexander of Macedon, son of Philip. This is the Alexander from whom Roman and Greek chronologies reckon their dates, as do the Jews and Christians. He is not Dhū al-Qarnayn, whom Allah mentioned in His Book, although some people suppose that Aristotle was a minister to Dhū al-Qarnayn. Seeing that one was named Alexander and that the other is also sometimes called Alexander, they assumed that the two were the same, as Ibn Sīnā and a group who share his view suppose.

Among the various polytheists—the Arabs, Indians, Turks, Greeks, and others—there are those who devote themselves earnestly to learning, asceticism, and worship. This is why devils descend upon them and associate with them, so that they become friends of Satan rather than friends of the Most Merciful.

For Satan carries him through the air. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

When he speaks, he lies;

“Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches. The highest is the declaration that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that whoever possesses one of these traits has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it. It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that he said to Abū Dharr—who was among the finest believers:

He asked, “O Messenger of Allah, even at my advanced age?”

It is also established in the Sahīh that he said:

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he makes a promise, he breaks it; and when he is entrusted with something, he betrays that trust.”

In Sahīh Muslim, the wording includes:

“and make evident those who were hypocrites. They were told, ‘Come, fight in Allah’s cause, or help defend.’ They said, ‘Had we known there would be fighting, we would have followed you.’ They were closer that day to disbelief

than to faith.”

Since the “friends of Allah” are the believers who are mindful of Him, a servant’s friendship with Allah Most High is proportionate to his faith and piety. Whoever is more perfect in faith and piety is more perfect in friendship with Allah.

People therefore differ in their degrees of friendship with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, according to their differing degrees of faith and piety. Likewise, they differ in their degrees of enmity towards Allah according to their differing degrees of disbelief and hypocrisy. Allah Most High says:

“Whenever a surah is revealed, some of them ask, ‘Which of you has this increased in faith?’ As for those who believe, it increases them in faith, and they rejoice.”

He, Glorified and Most High, has thus made clear that a single person may have a share of friendship with Allah in proportion to his faith, and may also have a share of enmity towards Allah in proportion to his disbelief and hypocrisy. He Most High says:

## Page 5521

The friends of Allah fall into “two ranks”: the foremost, who are brought near to Him, and the people of the right, who follow a moderate course. Allah mentions them in several places in His Mighty Book: at the beginning and end of Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah, and in Sūrat al-Insān, Sūrat al-Mutaffifīn, and Sūrat Fātir.

He, Glorified and Most High, mentions the greater resurrection at the beginning of Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah and the lesser resurrection at its end. At its beginning, He says:

“When the Event occurs,

in Gardens of Bliss:

This is the division of humanity when the greater resurrection takes place, at which Allah gathers the first and the last, as He, Glorified be He, has described in numerous places in His Book.

Then, at the end of the surah, He Most High says:

“Then why not”—meaning, “Why do you not”—“when the soul reaches the throat,
while you are looking on,
and We are nearer to him than you, though you do not see—
then why not, if you are not subject to judgment,
bring it back, if you are truthful?”

## Page 5523

for the people of the right, while those brought near to Allah drink it pure.” This is indeed as they said. For the Most High says, “drink of it” (yashrabu bihā), not “drink from it” (yashrabu minhā), because He has given the word “drink” the additional sense of having one’s thirst quenched by it. A person may drink without having his thirst quenched. Thus, saying “they drink from it” does not indicate that their thirst is quenched, whereas “they drink of it” means that their thirst is quenched by it. Those brought near to Allah have their thirst quenched by it and therefore have no need of anything inferior to it alongside it. For this reason, they drink it pure, unlike the people of the right, for whom it is mixed with something else. This accords with what the Most High says in Sūrat al-Insān:

“Whose mixture is camphor—a spring from which the servants of Allah drink, making it flow abundantly.”

The servants of Allah are those brought near to Him who are mentioned in that surah. This is because recompense corresponds to deeds, whether good or evil. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever relieves a believer of one of the hardships of this world, Allah will relieve him of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection. Whoever makes things easy for someone in difficulty, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and the Hereafter. Whoever conceals a Muslim’s faults, Allah will conceal his faults in this world and the Hereafter. Allah continues to help His servant so long as the servant helps his brother. Whoever follows a path seeking knowledge, Allah will thereby make easy for him a path to Paradise. Whenever people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it together, tranquillity descends upon them, mercy envelops them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them among those who are with Him. Whoever is held back by his deeds will not be advanced by his lineage.”

Muslim narrated this in his Sahīh. And he said:

The close friends of Allah Most High are of two kinds: those brought near to Him and the people of the right, as explained earlier. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described the deeds of both groups in the hadith concerning Allah’s close friends:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity to a close friend of Mine has openly declared war against Me. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks.’”

The righteous—the people of the right—are those who draw near to Him through obligatory duties. They do what Allah has made obligatory upon them and refrain from what He has forbidden them. They do not oblige themselves to perform recommended acts or to forgo what is superfluous among permissible things. As for the foremost, those brought near to Him, they draw near to Him through voluntary acts after fulfilling the obligatory duties, and thus they perform

---

## Page 5525

obligatory duties and recommended acts, and refrain from forbidden and disliked acts. When they drew near to Him through all the acts dear to them that they were capable of performing, the Lord loved them with a complete love, as He, Most High, says:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him.”

This means love in its fullest sense, just as He, Most High, says:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your wrath, nor those who have gone astray.”

That is, He bestowed upon them the full and complete blessing mentioned in His words:

“Whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be with those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!”

For those brought near to Him, even permissible activities became acts of obedience through which they drew near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. All their deeds thus became acts of worship devoted to Allah. They therefore drank an unmixed draught, just as their deeds had been purely for Him. Those who followed a middle course, however, performed some deeds for themselves, for which they are neither punished nor rewarded. They therefore did not drink an unmixed draught; rather, some of the drink of those brought near was mixed into theirs, in proportion to the mixture they had made in this world.

A parallel to this is the division of the prophets, peace be upon them, into servants who are messengers and prophets who are kings. Allah, Glorified is He, gave Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the choice between being a servant and messenger or a prophet and king. He chose to be a servant and messenger. Examples of prophets who were kings include David, Solomon, and others like them, blessings and peace be upon them both. Allah Most High says in the account of Solomon, who said:

“My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as no one after me will have. Indeed, You are the Bestower.”

“So We subjected the wind to him, blowing

---

## Page 5526

gently at his command wherever he directed it. And the devils—every builder and diver—and others bound together in shackles. This is Our gift: give or withhold as you please, without being called to account.”

That is: give to whomever you wish and withhold from whomever you wish; you will not be called to account. A prophet who is a king performs what Allah has enjoined upon him, refrains from what Allah has forbidden him, and exercises his authority and disposes of wealth as he wishes and chooses, without incurring sin. A servant who is a messenger, however, gives to no one except by his Lord’s command. He does not give or withhold merely as he wishes. Rather, it is reported that he said:

“By Allah, I neither give to anyone nor withhold from anyone. I am only a distributor; I allocate as I have been commanded.”

This is why Allah ascribes the funds governed by Islamic law to Himself and the Messenger, as in His words, Most High:

“Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger.”

And His words, Most High:

“Whatever Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and the Messenger.”

And His words, Most High:

“Know that whatever spoils you acquire, one-fifth belongs to Allah and the Messenger.”

For this reason, the best-supported scholarly view is that these funds should be spent on purposes beloved to Allah and His Messenger, according to the ruler’s considered judgment. This is the position of Mālik and others among the early generations, and it is also reported as one position held by Ahmad. Another view is that the fifth should be divided into five shares, as held by al-Shāfiʿī and, according to his well-known position, Ahmad. Yet another view is that it should be divided into three shares, as held by Abū Hanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him.
