## Page 5656

The shaykh and imam, the learned and erudite scholar, the godly sage into whose heart the light of the Quran had been cast, Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him and grant him contentment—said:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds—abundant, good and blessed praise, as our Lord loves and is pleased with. I bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner, and that there is no deity besides Him. I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, whom He chose, selected and guided. May Allah bestow blessings upon him and his family, and abundant peace, until the Day of Judgment.

A Noble Principle Concerning Miracles and Miraculous Favors

Although the term “miracle” encompasses every occurrence that departs from the ordinary course of things, both in its linguistic sense and in the usage of the early imams, such as Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others—who also call such occurrences “signs”—many later scholars distinguish terminologically between the two, reserving the term “miracle”

---

## Page 5657

for a prophet, and “miraculous favor” for a friend of Allah. Both fall under the category of occurrences that depart from the ordinary course of things.

We say: The attributes of perfection fall under three headings: knowledge, power, and self-sufficiency. Alternatively, one may say: knowledge and power. Power is either the ability to act—that is, to bring about effects—or the ability to refrain from acting—that is, self-sufficiency. The first classification is better. These three attributes belong in their perfection to Allah alone: His knowledge encompasses all things, He has power over all things, and He has no need of any of creation.

The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to disclaim any claim to these three attributes, in Allah’s words:

“Say, ‘I do not tell you that I possess Allah’s treasures, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I follow only what is revealed to me.’”

Noah, peace be upon him, said likewise. Noah was the first of the messengers of firm resolve and the first messenger Allah Most High sent to the people of the earth; Muhammad is the last of the messengers and the last of those of firm resolve. Both disclaim these things.

This is because people sometimes demand that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, know the unseen, as in Allah’s words:

“They say, ‘When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?’”

And:

“They ask you about the Hour: when will it come to pass? Say, ‘Knowledge of it rests only with my Lord.’”

At other times, they demand that he bring about effects, as in His words:

“They say, ‘We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us,”

“or you have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, and cause rivers to flow abundantly through it,”

“or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you have claimed, or bring Allah and the angels before us face to face.’”

---

## Page 5658

up to His words:

“Say, ‘Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?’”

At other times, they fault him for having human needs, as in His words:

“They say, ‘What sort of messenger is this, who eats food and walks through the marketplaces? Why has no angel been sent down to him to be a warner alongside him? Or why has no treasure been bestowed upon him, or a garden provided for him to eat from?’”

Allah therefore commanded him to declare that he does not know the unseen, does not possess Allah’s treasures, and is not an angel with no need of food or wealth. He merely follows what is revealed to him. Following what is revealed to him is religion itself: obeying and worshipping Allah in knowledge and action, inwardly and outwardly.

He receives of those three only as much as Allah Most High grants him: he knows what Allah teaches him, can do what Allah enables him to do, and can dispense with whatever Allah frees him from needing, in matters that depart from the regular course of things or from what most people ordinarily experience.

Extraordinary occurrences belonging to the category of knowledge sometimes take the form of Allah enabling a servant to hear what others cannot hear. At other times, the servant sees what others cannot see, whether awake or asleep. At still other times, he knows what others do not know, through revelation and inspiration, or through the imparting of immediate knowledge or accurate discernment.

These experiences are termed unveiling, witnessing, disclosures, and communications: hearing involves communications, seeing involves witnessing, and knowledge involves disclosure. All of this is called “unveiling” and “disclosure,” meaning that the matter has been unveiled to him.

---

## Page 5659

And whatever belongs to the category of “power” involves bringing about effects. This may come through resolve, sincerity, and an answered supplication. It may also be an act of Allah in which the servant has no influence whatsoever, such as the destruction of his enemy without any action on his part, as in His saying:

“Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine has openly declared war on Me. I shall surely avenge My friends as an enraged lion takes vengeance.”

Other examples include making people yield to him and love him, and similar things. The same applies to what belongs to the category of “knowledge and unveiling”: certain aspects of his condition may be disclosed to someone else. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning glad tidings:

“They are righteous dreams that a righteous man sees or that someone else sees concerning him.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“You are Allah’s witnesses on earth.”

Both “unveiling and the production of effects” may occur within the person himself, or they may not. Rather, Allah may disclose his condition to others and act on his behalf in ways he does not anticipate. As Yūsuf ibn Asbāt said, “No servant is ever sincere with Allah without Allah acting on his behalf.” Ahmad ibn Hanbal also said, “If sincerity were placed upon a wound, it would heal.”

Yet when unveiling or the production of effects occurs in someone else for a person’s sake, that person is also its cause, even if it is in the other person that the ordinary course of things is transcended. The miracles of the prophets, their signs, and the proofs of their prophethood fall within this.

---

## Page 5660

Our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was granted every kind of “miracle and extraordinary occurrence.” As for knowledge, reports of the unseen, hearing, and sight, examples include his accounts of the earlier prophets and their peoples, his conversations with those prophets and his experiences with them, and his accounts of people other than prophets, whether friends of Allah or others. These agree with what the People of the Book possess and have inherited through mass transmission or otherwise, without his having learned it from them.

Likewise, his reports concerning divine lordship, the angels, Paradise, and Hell agree with those of the prophets before him, without his having learned from them. Their agreement with what was transmitted from the prophets can sometimes be established through the widely available scriptures in their possession and other accounts transmitted on a mass scale, and sometimes through knowledge held by select scholars among them. In matters such as these, the testimony of the People of the Book may be sought. This is among the wise purposes of allowing them to remain upon payment of the jizya. This is not the place to discuss that in detail.

His reports of matters beyond ordinary perception, both past and present, thus belong to the category of “extraordinary knowledge.” The same applies to his reports of future events, such as the dominion of his community, the fall of the Persian and Roman empires, fighting against the Turks, and thousands upon thousands of other reports he gave.

Some of these are recorded in works on “the proofs of prophethood,” “the Messenger’s biography,” and “his virtues,” as well as works of “Quranic commentary,” “hadith,” and “military campaigns.” Examples include Dalā’il al-Nubuwwa (The Proofs of Prophethood) by Abū Nuʿaym and by al-Bayhaqī, Ibn Ishāq’s biography of the Prophet, hadith works containing chains of transmission such as the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, compiled collections such as Sahīh al-Bukhārī, and other works, including material that

---

## Page 5661

is also mentioned in “works of speculative theology and disputation,” such as Aʿlām al-Nubuwwa (The Signs of Prophethood) by al-Qādī ʿAbd al-Jabbār and by al-Māwardī, al-Radd ʿalā al-Nasārā (The Refutation of the Christians) by al-Qurtubī, and very many other works.

The same applies to what others foretold about him, as found in the books of the earlier prophets. In our time, these comprise twenty-two prophetic writings in the possession of the Jews and Christians, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the books of Isaiah, Habakkuk, Daniel, and Jeremiah. Likewise, there are the predictions of people other than prophets, including rabbis and monks; reports from the jinn and disembodied voices; and predictions by soothsayers such as Satīh, Shiqq, and others. There are also dreams and their interpretations, such as Chosroes’ dream and the chief Magian priest’s interpretation of it. Similarly, the earlier prophets’ accounts of what had passed and gone by are among the signs of their prophethood.

As for “power and the production of effects,” these concern either the upper world or what lies beneath it. What lies beneath it is either simple or composite. The simple comprises either the atmosphere or the earth; the composite comprises animals, plants, or minerals. Animals, in turn, are either rational or non-rational.

Examples concerning the upper world include the splitting of the moon and the return of the sun for Joshua son of Nun. Another is its return when ʿAlī missed the prayer while the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sleeping with his head in his lap—if the hadith is authentic. Some, such as al-Tahāwī and al-Qādī ʿIyād, judged it authentic. Others, such as Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī, classified it as a report stopping at a Companion, and this is the more correct view. His ascension to the heavens is another example.

---

## Page 5662

As for “the atmosphere,” examples include his repeatedly praying for rain and for the skies to clear, as in the hadith of the Bedouin recorded in the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere; the increased frequency of shooting stars at the time of his emergence; and his night journey from the Sacred Mosque to al-Aqsā Mosque.

As for “earth and water,” examples include the mountain shaking beneath him; the multiplication of water at the springs of Tabūk and al-Hudaybiyya; water flowing from between his fingers on several occasions; and the woman’s waterskin.

As for “composite things,” examples include his multiplying food on numerous occasions, as in Jābir’s account of the Trench, the report of Abū Talha, incidents during his journeys, Abū Hurayra’s provision bag, and Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s date palms. There are also the reports of Jābir and Ibn al-Zubayr concerning date palms uprooting themselves for him and returning to their places, and his supplying water to more than one tract of land, as at the spring of Abū Qatāda. This is a vast subject. The purpose here is not to enumerate the particular kinds of his miracles, but merely to give examples.

Likewise, examples belonging to the category of “power” include the staff of Moses, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; the parting of the sea; the lice, frogs, and blood; the she-camel of Sālih; and Jesus’ healing of those born blind and of lepers, and his raising of the dead. Similarly, an example belonging to the category of knowledge is his telling them what they ate

---

## Page 5663

and what they stored in their homes. In short, the intention here is not to discuss the prophetic miracles individually, but merely to give examples of them.

As for miracles granted to people other than prophets that belong to the category of “unveiling and knowledge,” examples include what ʿUmar said in the incident involving Sāriya; Abū Bakr’s declaration that his wife was carrying a girl; ʿUmar’s foretelling that a just man would arise among his descendants; and the account of Moses’ companion and his knowledge of the boy’s circumstances.

Examples belonging to the category of “power” include the accounts of the man who possessed knowledge of the Scripture, the People of the Cave, Mary, Khālid ibn al-Walīd, Safīna—the freedman of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī. There are many other instances that would take a long time to explain: enumerating them would be like counting raindrops. The purpose is merely to give examples that most people have heard of.

As for power not connected with his own action, examples include Allah’s granting victory to those who support him and His destroying those who revile him.

---

## Page 5664

Section

An extraordinary occurrence, whether an unveiling or an exercise of power, is among the righteous deeds prescribed by religion and divine law—either obligatory or recommended—if it achieves a benefit sought by religion. If it achieves something permissible, it is among Allah’s worldly blessings, which call for gratitude. But if it involves something forbidden or discouraged, it becomes grounds for punishment or abhorrence, as in the account of the man who was given the signs but cast them off: Balʿām ibn Bāʿūrāʾ.

Nevertheless, the person concerned may be excused because of his independent judgment, his reliance on another’s judgment, deficient intellect or knowledge, an overpowering spiritual state, incapacity, or necessity. His case would then resemble that of Barh the worshipper.

The “prohibition” may concern either the means by which the extraordinary occurrence is brought about or its intended purpose. An example of the former is addressing Allah with a forbidden supplication, thereby transgressing against Him. Allah Most High says:

“Call upon your Lord humbly and privately. Indeed, He does not love those who transgress.”

The same applies to forbidden deeds that produce an unveiling or an exercise of power.

The second case includes supplicating against someone for something he does not deserve, or praying that an oppressor be aided and helping him through one’s spiritual resolve—as do the enemy’s protectors and those possessors of spiritual states who assist oppressors. If the person concerned is one of the “sane madmen” or of those overcome to such a degree

---

## Page 5665

that they may be excused, or among those whose deficiencies incur no blame, they are like Barh. Elsewhere I have explained in what matters they may or may not be excused. If, however, they possess knowledge and ability, they are like Balʿām. Whoever brings about an extraordinary occurrence through a forbidden means or for a forbidden purpose is either excused and pardoned, like Barh, or deliberately lying, like Balʿām.

Thus, extraordinary occurrences fall into “three categories”: those commended by religion, those condemned by religion, and those that are permissible, neither commended nor condemned by religion. If a permissible occurrence brings benefit, it is a blessing; if it brings no benefit, it is like other permissible things that serve no useful purpose, such as play and idle amusement.

Abū ʿAlī al-Jūzajānī said:

“Seek steadfastness, not miraculous gifts. Your soul is naturally disposed to seeking miraculous gifts, whereas your Lord requires steadfastness of you.”

Shaykh al-Suhrawardī said in his ʿAwārif:

“What he has mentioned is a great and weighty principle in this matter, and a secret whose true nature many spiritual wayfarers and seekers have overlooked. Those who strive diligently and devote themselves to worship have heard about the righteous predecessors of earlier generations and the miraculous gifts and extraordinary occurrences they were granted. Their souls therefore continually yearn for such things, and they long to be granted something of the same. One of them may remain brokenhearted, doubting the soundness of his deeds because nothing of this kind has been unveiled to him. If they understood the secret behind this, the matter would be easier for them. It should therefore be understood that Allah

---

## Page 5666

opens a door to such things for some of those who strive sincerely. The wisdom in this is that witnessing extraordinary occurrences and manifestations of divine power should broaden their experience, strengthening their resolve to renounce this world and free themselves from the promptings of desire.

He may, however, unveil true certainty to some of His servants and lift the veil from their hearts. Whoever is granted this unveiling of true certainty has no need to witness extraordinary occurrences, since their purpose was to bring about certainty, and certainty has already been attained. If something of this kind were unveiled to someone granted true certainty, his certainty would increase. Yet wisdom does not require that divine power be disclosed through extraordinary occurrences in this case, since he already has what he needs. Wisdom does require such a disclosure for the other person because of his need. This second person would be more fully prepared and qualified than the first.

The sincere seeker’s course is therefore to demand steadfastness of himself, for steadfastness is the whole of miraculous grace. Then, if something extraordinary occurs along his path, it is as though it had not occurred: he pays it no heed, and it does not diminish him. He is diminished only by failing to fulfil the obligations of steadfastness. Understand this, for it is a major principle for seekers, ascetic scholars, and Sufi shaykhs.”

---

## Page 5667

Section

The words of Allah Most High are of “two kinds”: words governing creation and words concerning religion.

His words governing creation are those in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sought refuge when he said:

“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah, beyond which neither the righteous nor the wicked can pass.”

He, glorified is He, said:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

And He Most High said:

“And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.”

The entire universe falls under these words, as do all extraordinary occurrences involving disclosure and the exercise of power.

“The second kind” consists of His words concerning religion: the Quran and the divine law with which Allah sent His Messenger. These comprise His commands, prohibitions, and statements. The servant’s share in them consists in knowing them, acting upon them, and enjoining what Allah has commanded, just as the servant’s share in the first kind, in general and in particular, consists in knowing created things and affecting them—that is, in accordance with those words.

The first kind thus pertains to divine decree and creation, while the second pertains to divine law and religion. Disclosure in the first sphere consists in knowing events in creation; disclosure in the second consists in knowing the commands of divine law. Power in the first sphere consists in bringing about effects in created things; power in the second consists in bringing about effects in religious matters. And just as

---

## Page 5668

the first kind of power is divided into effects upon oneself—such as walking on water, flying through the air, and sitting on fire—and effects upon others, such as causing illness, restoring health, bringing about destruction, enriching, and impoverishing, so too the second kind is divided into effects upon oneself, through obeying Allah and His Messenger and adhering inwardly and outwardly to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and effects upon others, through enjoining obedience to Allah and His Messenger. One is then obeyed in a manner sanctioned by divine law, so that people accept one’s commands to obey Allah and His Messenger through the words concerning religion, just as, in the first case, they accepted what one wished to bring about in them through the words governing creation.

With this established, know that the absence of extraordinary knowledge and power does not harm a Muslim’s religion. If nothing of the unseen is disclosed to him and nothing in creation is subjected to his control, this does not diminish his rank with Allah. Indeed, their absence may be more beneficial to his religion, provided that possessing them is neither obligatory nor recommended in his particular case. By contrast, the absence of religion and of acting upon it leaves a person deficient and blameworthy, either making him deserving of punishment or depriving him of reward. This is because, through knowing religion, teaching it, and enjoining it, the servant attains the pleasure, blessings, and reward of Allah alone. Knowledge of creation and the ability to affect it, however, bring none of this unless they fall within religion. Rather, he may be obliged to give thanks for them, and he may incur sin through them.

Once this is understood, there are three categories:

It pertains either to knowledge and power, or to religion

---

## Page 5669

alone, or to creation alone.

The first is exemplified by what Allah said to His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And say, ‘My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority.’”

For supporting authority combines proof and standing with Allah. It consists of His words concerning religion, decree, and creation—with Allah, through His words governing creation. The miracles of the prophets, peace be upon them, combine both aspects: they are proof from Allah of prophethood, and they belong to His decree. The greatest example is the Quran brought by Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is Allah’s law and His words concerning religion, and it is Muhammad’s proof of his prophethood, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Its very coming transcends the ordinary course of events. Thus it is the call itself, the proof, and the miracle.

The second category includes someone who knows the reports and commands brought by the Messenger, acts upon them, and enjoins them upon people; who also knows when rain will fall, prices will change, a sick person will recover, an absent person will arrive, and an encounter with the enemy will occur; and who has an influence upon human beings or other things, bringing about health, illness, destruction, birth, appointment to office, or removal from office. Such influence falls broadly into attracting a benefit, such as wealth or leadership; averting harm, such as an enemy or illness; or doing neither, such as riding a lion without any benefit, or extinguishing a fire, and the like.

As for the third category, it concerns someone who combines both, by being granted disclosure of the unseen

---

## Page 5670

and influence over creation sufficient to support insight and influence in religious matters—that is, knowledge of religion, acting upon it, and enjoining it. He is also granted knowledge of religion and the ability to act upon it that enable him to employ disclosure of the unseen and influence over creation, so that extraordinary events in creation serve religious commands. Alternatively, the ordinary course of things may be transcended for him in religious matters, so that he attains religious knowledge, acts upon it, enjoins it, and secures people’s obedience in it to a degree that others have not attained in the ordinary course of things. These are the greatest miraculous gifts and prophetic miracles. Such is the state of our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, of Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and ʿUmar, and of all Muslims.

This third category is what is entailed by:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

For the first is worship, and the second is seeking help. Such is the state of our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the elect of his community who adhere inwardly and outwardly to his law and way. Their miraculous gifts, like his miracles, were manifested only to establish a proof or meet a need. As for proof, its purpose is to make Allah’s religion manifest, so that the disbeliever believes, the hypocrite becomes sincere, and those who believe increase in faith. Their benefit was thus to bring about adherence to Allah’s religion in knowledge and practice, just as this is the purpose of jihad.

As for need, this includes obtaining a benefit they require, such as food and drink when needed, or warding off harm from them, such as defeating the enemy with the pebbles he threw at them. Thus he was told:

“It was not you who threw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw.”

Both of these ultimately serve the interests of religion, as do eating, drinking, fighting the enemy, and giving charity to

---

## Page 5671

Muslims; for this is part of religion and righteous deeds.

As for “the first category,” which concerns religion alone, it includes those who have no need of the second and derive no benefit from it. Such is the case with many of the Companions, the Successors, and the righteous Muslims, their scholars, and their devoted worshippers—although they must have some need for, or benefit from, certain extraordinary events. Some of them may neither employ the means relating to created affairs nor act upon them. The absence of an extraordinary event in creation in a person’s case is therefore due either to the absence of its cause or to the absence of any benefit in it.

Its absence because it would bring no benefit is not a deficiency. Its absence because its cause is lacking, however, may or may not be a deficiency. If this results from his failure to perform an obligation or refrain from something forbidden, then the absence of the extraordinary event is a deficiency, and this is a cause of harm. If it results from his neglect of recommended acts, it is a deficiency relative to the rank of those who are foremost and brought near to Allah, but not relative to the rank of those of the right who follow a moderate course.

If neither is the case, and he has simply not pursued a means relating to created affairs whose absence does not diminish his reward, then this is no deficiency. An example is someone whose child falls ill or whose wealth is lost, yet he does not supplicate for his child’s recovery or the return of his wealth; or someone whom an oppressor wrongs, yet he does not direct his spiritual resolve against him to prevail over him.

As for “the second category,” namely, the person endowed with disclosure of the unseen and influence over creation, it has already been explained that this may sometimes enhance his religious standing, sometimes diminish it, and sometimes count neither for nor against him. This is the predominant state of those devoted to seeking help, just as the first is the predominant state of those devoted to worship.

---

## Page 5672

And this second category is comparable to kingship and sovereignty: their holder may be a caliph and prophet, and thus the best person on earth; he may be a tyrant, among the worst of people; or he may be a just king, among those of middling rank. For knowledge of created affairs and the ability to influence them through one’s spiritual state and heart are comparable to knowledge of their conditions and influence over them through kingship and its means. The power of spiritual state and heart is like the power of kingship and physical force, except that the means of the former are inward and spiritual, while those of the latter are outward and bodily.

This makes it clear to you that the first category, provided it is sound, is superior to this category and better in the sight of Allah, His Messenger, and His righteous, believing servants of sound understanding.

This is so for several reasons:

First, knowledge of religion—both what it requires and what it reports—can be attained only through the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Knowledge of created affairs, however, can be acquired through many means. What is exclusive to the Messengers and their heirs is superior to what they share with the rest of humanity. Only they and their followers can attain this knowledge, and only they and their followers possess it.

Second, only righteous believers put religion into practice: they are the people of Paradise, Allah’s beloved, His chosen ones, those dear to Him, and His allies. And only they enjoin it.

---

## Page 5673

As for “influence over created affairs,” an unbeliever, hypocrite, or evildoer may exert it upon himself or others—as occurs through corrupt spiritual states, the evil eye, and sorcery, and as with kings, tyrants placed in power, and oppressive rulers. Knowledge exclusive to the righteous is superior to knowledge shared by those who bring about good and those who spread corruption.

Third, knowledge of religion and acting upon it benefit a person in the Hereafter and do him no harm. Unveiling and influence, however, may bring him no benefit in the Hereafter; indeed, they may harm him, as Allah Most High says:

“If they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Allah would have been better, if only they knew.”

Fourth, unveiling and influence either serve a useful purpose or they do not. If they serve no useful purpose—as when someone discovers people’s sins, rides wild beasts without any need, meets with jinn to no useful end, or walks on water when he could cross by a bridge—then they bring no benefit in this world or the Hereafter. They amount to idle amusement and play. Only someone who has not attained such things regards them as momentous.

Such things fall within the sphere of power and authority over created affairs. This is like someone who marvels at a king, at kings obeying an individual, or at the spiritual influence someone displays among people, even though it serves no useful purpose. He admires it for the power behind it, not for its benefit—such as wealth, leadership, or averting harm from an enemy or illness. Such benefits are generally attained far more often without extraordinary feats than through them. Only a little of them is attained through extraordinary feats, and they endure only through other means.

---

## Page 5674

As for the other benefit, extraordinary feats likewise cannot secure it unless accompanied by religion. Religion alone, however, secures the Hereafter without any extraordinary feat. Indeed, extraordinary feats pertaining to religion and created affairs are more far-reaching than attaining the Hereafter, as in the case of our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Likewise, the wealth and leadership that religious people attain through extraordinary feats are attained only in conjunction with religion. Otherwise, extraordinary feats alone have only a limited effect in this world.

If it is said:

“Even if extraordinary feats alone bring no religious or worldly benefit in themselves, they indicate that people will obey the person who performs them. This brings leadership and authority, which then serve as a means of securing religious and worldly benefits and averting religious and worldly harms.”

I reply:

We have been discussing only the benefit inherent in religion or an extraordinary feat, independently of people’s actions.

If, however, we discuss what people do as a result of these things, then we say, first:

True religion is more effective in securing people’s obedience and attaining leadership than extraordinary feats alone, as experience demonstrates. There is no comparison between the obedience shown to someone because of his religion and that shown to someone because of his influence. Obedience to the former is more widespread and greater, and those who obey him are the best of humanity in intellect and religion. Obedience to the latter, however, neither endures nor becomes widespread. Only ignorant people engage in it, such as the followers of Musaylima the Liar, Tulayha al-Asadī, and others like them, and desert and mountain dwellers and their like who possess neither reason nor religion.

---

## Page 5675

Secondly, we say:

Even if someone who performs extraordinary feats were to attain greater leadership and wealth than a religious person, he would, at most, become one king among others. Indeed, if he does not combine his kingship with religion, he is like Pharaoh, the leaders of the Ismāʿīliyya, and others of their kind. We have already explained that the worldly leadership kings attain through statecraft, courage, and generosity is greater than leadership attained through extraordinary feats alone, for the latter generally lasts only a short time.

Fifth: Religion benefits its adherent in this world and the Hereafter and protects him against harm in both, without his needing any accompanying unveiling of hidden matters or extraordinary influence. As for unveiling or extraordinary influence, unless accompanied by religion, they bring ruin upon their possessor in this world and the Hereafter. His ruin in the Hereafter results from his lack of religion, which consists in fulfilling obligations and abstaining from prohibitions. As for this world, extraordinary feats are perilous pursuits that people attain only by exposing their hearts, bodies, families, and wealth to danger. If someone follows the path of hunger and excessive ascetic discipline, he endangers his heart, his bodily constitution, and his religion. He may lose his reason, fall physically ill, and lose his religion.

If he follows the path of ecstatic derangement and mental confusion through renouncing desires, seeking contact with jinn spirits and a state in which souls lose awareness of their bodies—as do those among the Ahmadiyya who cultivate such derangement—he has deprived himself of his reason, squandered his wealth and livelihood, and brought the utmost misery upon himself. He has also exposed himself to Allah’s punishment in the Hereafter because of the obligations he has neglected and the prohibited acts he has committed. Likewise, if he seeks to subjugate the jinn through names and words used in oaths and adjurations, he has exposed himself to their punishment

---

## Page 5676

and their attacks. Indeed, even if the extraordinary feat consists only in directing someone to his stolen or lost property, healing the sick, or warding off an enemy—whether a ruler or armed attackers—if someone does these things for people without making his work an act of religious devotion through which he draws nearer to Allah, he is merely like a steward who safeguards people’s property, a physician or pharmacist who treats their illnesses, or a ruler’s auxiliaries who fight on his behalf. His work is exactly the same kind as theirs.

It is well known that someone who follows this path without religious guidance will show favoritism to certain people and fail to deal justly among them. He may even assist oppressors through it, as Balaam did, along with groups from this community and others. This earns him people’s enmity, which is among the most common causes of worldly harm. A person may not expose himself to this unless Allah and His Messenger command it, for whatever Allah and His Messenger command, even if it entails harm, brings benefit that outweighs its harm. The ultimate outcome favors righteousness.

Sixth: Religion comprises knowledge and practice which, when sound, necessarily give rise to extraordinary occurrences if its adherent needs them.

Allah Most High says:

“Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect.”

He Most High also says:

“If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion for distinguishing right from wrong.”

He Most High also says:

“Had they done what they were instructed to do, it would have been better for them and made them more steadfast. Then We would have granted them a great reward from Us and guided them to a straight path.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, Allah’s allies will have no fear, nor will they grieve—those who have believed

---

## Page 5677

and have feared Allah. For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beware of the believer’s discernment, for he sees by the light of Allah.” Then he recited the words of the Most High: “Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated it from Abū Saʿīd and graded it sound.

Allah Most High said, as reported from Him by His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever shows enmity to an ally of Mine has openly challenged Me to war. Nothing by which My servant draws near to Me compares with his fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely grant him refuge. I have never hesitated over anything I am going to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet he must undergo it.”

This states that Allah wages war against whoever wages war against His ally. It also states that the one He loves gains knowledge through Him by hearing and seeing, and acts through Him by grasping and walking. It further states that He grants him the benefits he asks of Him and wards off the harms from which he seeks refuge in Him. This is a vast subject.

Extraordinary occurrences, however, may accompany religious devotion, but they may also occur when it is absent, corrupt, or deficient.

## Page 5678

Seventh: Religious devotion consists in fulfilling the obligations of servanthood: doing what is incumbent upon you and what you have been commanded to do. Extraordinary occurrences, by contrast, belong to the prerogatives of divine lordship when the servant has not been commanded to bring them about. Even when they result from the servant’s efforts, it is Allah who creates them through the causes He establishes. The servant should concern himself with his duties and what he has been commanded to do.

As for concerning himself with what Allah does, when he has not been commanded to concern himself with it, this may be superfluous. Such occurrences may be valued for the benefits they offer, comparable to the benefits of authority and wealth that can support religion: multiplying food and drink, for example, and securing people’s obedience when they witness them. They may also ward off harm from religion, much as jihad repels and overcomes the enemy.

But does religion fundamentally require such occurrences because belief in prophethood cannot be complete without an extraordinary sign? Or are they unnecessary for the select few, though needed by the general public? We shall discuss this.

The most beneficial extraordinary occurrence is one that is itself religious in nature, as was the case with our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said:

“Every prophet was given signs of a kind that led people to believe. What I have been given, however, is revelation that Allah has revealed to me, so I hope to have the greatest number of followers on the Day of Resurrection.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both narrated it in their Sahīh collections. His sign was itself his call and his proof, unlike those of the other prophets. Thus we find that many among us who deviate toward a Jesus-oriented approach flee from the Quran and verbal teaching to spiritual states, just as those among us who deviate toward a Moses-oriented approach flee from faith and spiritual states to

---

## Page 5679

verbal teaching. Our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combines verbal teaching with spiritual states, and the Quran with faith.

Next in rank is the extraordinary occurrence that supports and assists religion, for extraordinary occurrences belong to the sphere of “You alone we ask for help,” while religion belongs to the sphere of “You alone we worship.” An extraordinary occurrence that does not assist religion is either a worldly enjoyment or something that distances its possessor from Allah Most High.

It is thus clear that beneficial extraordinary occurrences are subordinate to religion and arise in its service, just as beneficial leadership is subordinate to religion, and likewise beneficial wealth. Such were authority and wealth in the hands of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Whoever makes these things his goal, subordinating religion to them and making it a means of attaining them, rather than seeking them for religion’s sake in the first place, resembles someone who uses religion to secure worldly gain. His condition is unlike that of someone who practices religion out of fear of punishment or hope for Paradise, for this is commanded, and such a person follows a path to salvation and a sound religious way.

What is astonishing is that many who claim that their aspirations have risen above practicing religion out of fear of the Fire or a desire for Paradise make the object of their religious devotion the slightest extraordinary worldly feat. They may even exert tremendous effort to attain it. This is a mistake. Some, however, seek through this to make their hearts steadfast and reassured, and to gain certainty that their path and spiritual journey are sound. Such a person seeks a sign as an indication and proof of the soundness of his religion, just as

---

## Page 5680

nations ask the prophets for signs as evidence of their truthfulness. This makes them more excusable in doing so. Accordingly, since the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—had no need of signs for their religious knowledge and practice, owing to what they had witnessed of the Messenger and the knowledge they had acquired, anyone further removed from them, even if his path is sound, needs what they possessed for his religious knowledge and practice. Thus, extraordinary occurrences appear among individuals in times and places where prophetic guidance has waned, which do not appear to them or to others when prophethood and its call are manifest.

Section

There are various means of knowing created things and having them unveiled: sense perception, reason, unveiling, and transmitted reports, as well as immediate and inferential knowledge, and other means. Such knowledge is also divided into certain, probable, and other categories. Allah Most High willing, we shall discuss which of these means may be followed in rulings of Islamic law and which may not. I mean the rulings of Islamic law concerning knowledge of created things obtained through unveiling, whether awake or asleep, as I have written in the discussion of jihad.

As for knowledge of religion and its unveiling, religion comprises two kinds of matters: matters concerning reports and belief, and matters

---

## Page 5681

concerning commands and practice. The first includes knowledge of Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day. It also includes accounts of the prophets and their nations, their ranks in virtue, and the states, attributes, and deeds of the angels. It further includes descriptions of Paradise and Hell, the rewards and punishments attached to deeds, and the circumstances, virtues, and ranks of Allah’s friends and the Companions, among other matters.

This category is sometimes called “the fundamentals of religion” or “the greater creed,” while rational disputation concerning it is called “speculative theology.” It is also called “creeds and beliefs,” “theoretical questions,” “questions concerning reports,” and “the science of unveiling.”

(The second category comprises practical matters involving commands and prohibitions concerning the actions of the limbs and the heart: obligations, prohibitions, recommended acts, disliked acts, and permissible acts. Knowledge and belief may themselves be commanded or forbidden. Thus, insofar as something constitutes knowledge or belief, or a true or false report, it belongs to the first category; insofar as it is commanded or forbidden, it belongs to the second.

An example is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Insofar as this testimony is true and corresponds to what it affirms, it belongs to the first category. Insofar as it is an obligatory duty, and through it the person bearing witness becomes a believer deserving reward, whereas without it he becomes a disbeliever whose blood may lawfully be shed and whose property may lawfully be seized, it belongs to the second category.

---

## Page 5682

Muslims may agree on some means of attaining knowledge in both categories, as they agree that the Quran serves as evidence in both, broadly speaking. They may disagree over other means—for example, whether practical rulings concerning good and evil, obligation and prohibition can be known through reason as well as revelation, or only through revelation. They also disagree over whether revelation originates these rulings or merely discloses them, just as it discloses realities that exist in themselves.

The same applies to using the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus as evidence concerning the major questions in the first category, such as the divine attributes, divine decree, and other matters. This is accepted by the adherents of the Sunnah and the community across their various groups. Yet many proponents of religious innovation reject this, arguing on the basis of their own doctrines that revelation cannot establish these matters and that they are instead established through reason (1).

Indeed, many of the Qadariyyah and the Mu‘tazilah claim that the Quran cannot validly be used as evidence for Allah’s wisdom and justice, or for His being the Creator of all things and having power over all things. The Jahmiyyah among them, together with their followers among some of the Ash‘ariyyah and others, claim that it cannot validly be used as evidence for Allah’s knowledge and power, worship of Him, or His being established over the Throne.

Some extremists among the proponents of religious innovation claim that the Quran and hadith cannot validly be used as evidence for any matters requiring certainty whatsoever, basing this on their allegation that verbal indications do not yield certainty. Many proponents of religious innovation also claim that hadiths received with acceptance cannot be used as evidence concerning the divine attributes, divine decree, and similar matters in which certainty and conviction are required.
