## Page 5683

Some extremists among the speculative theologians claim that consensus cannot be used as evidence for anything. Others among them say that it cannot validly be used as evidence in matters requiring certain knowledge, because it yields only probability. There are various other claims of this kind, which this is not the place to discuss. Humanity has differed greatly over the paths to knowledge and probable belief, and the means of reaching them through evidence or inward or outward observation, whether general or particular.

Likewise, many adherents of hadith and the Sunnah may deny that anyone can attain knowledge through any path other than the one familiar to them, even denying most rational evidence without any proof for doing so. Similarly, some speculative theologians deny the spiritual unveilings experienced by Allah’s close servants, while some of our own associates go to extremes concerning them. The best course lies between the extremes.

Thus, the paths of reason, transmission, unveiling, reports, and reflection—the methods employed by the adherents of hadith, speculative theology, and Sufism—have been disputed, with people affirming or denying them. Some reject whatever they do not know; others go to extremes concerning what they do know, elevating it beyond its proper worth and rejecting everything else.

Speculative theologians and philosophizers exalt rational methods, many of which are unsound and contradictory. They are the most contradictory and divided of Allah’s creatures, each group refuting what the other claims to be certain.

---

## Page 5684

And a group of those who claim adherence to the Sunnah and hadith argue in these matters on the basis of fabricated hadiths and invented accounts known to be false. They may even invoke weak reports against strong ones. Many Sufis and faqīrs base their views on dreams, subjective spiritual experiences, and imaginings that they believe to be unveilings, though these are imaginings that do not correspond to reality and false illusions.

“They follow nothing but conjecture, and conjecture avails nothing against the truth.”

We therefore say:

As for the sources of Islamic rulings discussed in the principles of jurisprudence, there is, by the consensus of Muslims, “the Book.” None of the imams has disputed this, unlike certain misguided people who have disputed its use as evidence in some matters of belief.

The second is “the mass-transmitted Sunnah” that does not contradict the apparent meaning of the Quran but rather explains it: for example, the number of prayers and their units, the minimum thresholds for zakat and its prescribed dues, the manner of performing Hajj and ʿumrah, and other rulings known only through the Sunnah’s explanation.

As for the mass-transmitted Sunnah that does not explain the Quran’s apparent meaning, or is said to contradict it—such as the Sunnah specifying the threshold for the punishment of theft, the stoning of the adulterer, and other such rulings—the position of all the early generations is that it must likewise be acted upon, except for the Khārijites. For among their tenets—or those of some of them—is opposition to the Sunnah. Their first representative said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to his face: “This division was not intended to seek Allah’s countenance.” It is reported that they follow him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, only in what he conveyed from Allah, namely,

---

## Page 5685

the Quran and the Sunnah that explains it. But when the Messenger’s teaching differs from the Quran’s apparent meaning, they act only upon its apparent meaning. Thus they became renegades, passing out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to their first representative:

“You would indeed have failed and lost if I did not act justly.”

If someone allows that the Messenger might betray his trust and act unjustly concerning the wealth Allah entrusted to him, while believing that he is Allah’s trusted messenger of His revelation, then he has followed an unjust liar. He has allowed that someone truthful and trustworthy concerning the tidings from heaven entrusted to him by Allah might betray his trust and act unjustly concerning the wealth entrusted to him. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Does the One in heaven trust me, while you do not trust me?”

Or words to that effect. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was saying that faithfully discharging the trust of revelation is a greater responsibility. The revelation that Allah has commanded people to obey is the revelation concerning his judgments and his distribution of wealth. These people may reject many teachings of the Sunnah by impugning reason rather than rejecting the transmitted material, just as many adherents of innovation reject teachings of the Sunnah known among scholars to be mass-transmitted, such as intercession, the Cistern, the Bridge, divine decree, and other matters.

The third source:

“The mass-transmitted teachings of the Sunnah” from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, either accepted by the scholars acquainted with them or transmitted by trustworthy narrators. These, too, are among the teachings that scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, and Sufism, and most scholars generally, agree must be followed. Some speculative theologians, however, have rejected them. Many of them have denied that knowledge can be obtained through any of them, and it only entails knowledge; thus they did not

---

## Page 5686

distinguish between what had been accepted and what had not. Many jurists who rely on independent reasoning also reject numerous reports by stipulating conditions and raising counterarguments with which they dismiss and set them aside. Some, for example, reject a report because, they claim, it contradicts the apparent meaning of the Quran, established principles, or analogies drawn from those principles; because the practice of the later scholars of Medina runs contrary to it; or for other reasons discussed in the well-known debates found in works of jurisprudence, hadith, and legal theory.

The fourth source:

Consensus. Its authority is generally acknowledged among Muslims—jurists, Sufis, hadith scholars, speculative theologians, and others. Some adherents of innovation among the Mu‘tazilah and the Shia, however, have rejected it. Yet the consensus that can be known with certainty is that of the Companions; ascertaining consensus after their time has generally proved impossible. Hence scholars have differed over claims of consensus arising after the Companions. They have also differed over particular questions concerning it, such as the Successors’ agreement on one of two positions held by the Companions, a consensus from which some participants dissented before their generation had passed away, tacit consensus, and other matters.

The fifth source:

“Analogical reasoning based on textual evidence and consensus.”

This, too, constitutes authoritative evidence according to the great majority of jurists. Many jurists who rely on independent reasoning, however, have used it excessively: they have employed it before searching for textual evidence, rejected texts on its basis, and even employed invalid forms of it. Among speculative theologians, hadith scholars, and practitioners of analogical reasoning are those who reject it altogether. This is a major question, and the correct position lies between excessive and insufficient use.

---

## Page 5687

The sixth source:

“Presumption of continuity”

This means retaining the original state where revelation is not known to have established or negated something. It is unanimously accepted as grounds for withholding belief. Whether it constitutes grounds for believing that something does not exist, however, is disputed.

A similar approach is to infer the absence of a religious ruling from the absence of scriptural evidence. For example, one might argue: If the sacrificial offering or the witr prayer were obligatory, revelation would have provided evidence of that obligation, since their obligatory status cannot be known without revelation. There is no such evidence; therefore, there is no obligation.

The first approach retains the absence of obligation and prohibition known through reason until something is established that changes it. The other infers the absence of a ruling from the absence of scriptural evidence establishing it, since the existence of such a ruling necessarily entails the existence of scriptural evidence for it.

Similarly, the absence of any transmitted report serves as evidence that something never occurred when people would have had every incentive and reason to transmit it, when the Sharia requires its transmission, or when the religious commitment and customary practice of its adherents indicate that they would transmit it. Such reasoning establishes the absence of any addition to the Quran or to the publicly known Sharia, and the absence of any explicit text appointing ‘Alī, al-‘Abbās, or anyone else to the imamate.

Specialists versed in the prophetic traditions, transmitted reports, and the life of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs know that certain things of this kind did not occur, whereas others do not know this. This is because they know transmitted accounts that rule them out, and because they know that the necessary concomitants of their transmission are absent. For the existence of either of two opposites excludes the other, and the absence of a necessary consequence is evidence for the absence of that which entails it.

(The seventh source—

“Unrestricted considerations of benefit”

This is when a jurist exercising independent reasoning considers that this

---

## Page 5688

act brings a preponderant benefit, and nothing in the Sharia rules it out. This approach is the subject of a well-known disagreement. Jurists call it “unrestricted considerations of benefit.” Some call it reasoned opinion, while others regard juristic preference as closely related to it. Also close to it are the Sufis’ spiritual perception, ecstasy, and inspirations. These essentially consist in their finding that certain words and deeds benefit their hearts and their religion, and tasting the fruits they yield. This, too, is a benefit.

Some people, however, restrict unrestricted considerations of benefit to preserving lives, property, honour, intellect, and religion. This is not correct. Rather, unrestricted considerations of benefit concern both securing benefits and averting harms. What they mention about averting harm to these five things constitutes only one of these two categories.

Benefits may be secured in both worldly and religious affairs. In worldly affairs, examples include transactions and activities said to benefit people without being prohibited by the Sharia. In religious affairs, examples include many forms of knowledge, spiritual states, acts of worship, and ascetic practices said to benefit a person without being prohibited by the Sharia. Whoever confines considerations of benefit to punishments that avert harm to those matters, solely to preserve the body, has therefore taken too narrow a view.

This is a matter of great importance that deserves careful attention, for it has given rise to considerable confusion in religion. Many rulers, scholars, and devoted worshippers have perceived benefits and pursued them on the basis of this principle, although these may include things prohibited by the Sharia whose prohibition they did not know.

---

## Page 5689

and one may sometimes put forward, concerning unrestricted considerations of benefit, statements contrary to the revealed texts. Many of them, meanwhile, have neglected benefits that the Sharia requires them to consider, on the grounds that the Sharia has made no provision for them. They have thus missed obligatory and recommended acts, or fallen into prohibited and disliked acts, although the Sharia may have addressed the matter without their knowing it.

The first person’s argument is that this is a benefit, and the Sharia does not neglect benefits; rather, the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish that they must be taken into consideration. The second person’s argument is that the Sharia has provided no basis for this matter, either through an explicit text or through analogy.

Appealing to unrestricted considerations of benefit often leads to instituting as religion what Allah has not authorized. In some respects, this resembles juristic preference, rational judgments of goodness, reasoned opinion, and similar approaches. For istihsān (juristic preference) means seeking what is good or better, on the same linguistic pattern as istikhrāj (extraction). It means regarding something as good, just as finding something objectionable means regarding it as bad. Goodness is benefit; thus, juristic preference and reasoning on the basis of benefit are closely related. Rational judgments of goodness rest on the view that reason can discern what is good. Nevertheless, there are distinctions between these approaches.

The comprehensive principle is that the Sharia never neglects any benefit whatsoever. Rather, Allah Most High has perfected our religion for us and completed His favour upon us. There is nothing that brings us closer to Paradise without the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, having told us about it. He left us upon a clear path whose night is as bright as its day; none deviates from it after him except one who is doomed to perish. But as for what reason considers beneficial, even if

---

## Page 5690

the Sharia has made no provision for it, one of two things must be the case: either the Sharia has indicated it in a way unknown to the person examining the matter, or it is not beneficial, even though he believes it to be so.

For a benefit is an advantage that is actually realized or outweighs the harm. People often imagine that something is beneficial in religious and worldly affairs, when whatever benefit it contains is outweighed by its harm. As Allah Most High says concerning wine and gambling:

“Say: ‘In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.’”

Many of the beliefs and practices people have introduced—the innovations of speculative theologians, Sufis, proponents of reasoned opinion, and rulers—were regarded by them as beneficial or conducive to welfare, useful, true, and correct, although they were not. Indeed, many of those outside Islam—Jews, Christians, polytheists, Sabians, and Magians—believe that their beliefs, dealings, and acts of worship serve their interests in religious and worldly affairs and benefit them:

“Those whose efforts are lost in this worldly life, while they think they are doing good.”

Their evil deeds have been made appealing to them, so they regard them as good. If a person regards something evil as good, his juristic preference or reasoning on the basis of benefit may fall into this category. This differs from the case of those who denied them, despite being inwardly certain of their truth, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. Denying the truth and stubbornly opposing it is one thing; being ignorant of it and blind to it is another. Both types are found among the unbelievers, and both are likewise found among those Muslims who follow their desires. For just as people, in matters of issuing fatwas and transmitting hadith,

---

## Page 5691

sometimes err and at other times deliberately lie, so too do they in religious matters. Likewise, in their actions, they may do what they know to be unjust, or they may believe that something is not unjust when it is. For man is as Allah Most High says:

“Yet man undertook it; indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant.”

Thus, at times he is ignorant and at times he acts unjustly: the former concerns his faculty of knowledge, and the latter his faculty of action.

Know that this matter concerns both those devoted to knowledge and discourse and those devoted to will and action. One says, “This is permissible” or “This is good,” based on his own judgment; another does it without believing it forbidden, or in the belief that it is good for him. For example, he may find benefit in innovated listening practices: listening to whistling, clapping, reed pipes known as the shabbāba and saffāra, stringed instruments, and the like. He does this for the pleasure he finds in it, and he may also do it because he finds that it benefits his religion by heightening his spiritual states, as happens with the Quran. Another says, “This is permissible,” because of the benefit and advantage he perceives in it.

The same applies to innovated doctrines. One says, “This is true, because rational inference demonstrates it.” Another says, “It is permissible—and obligatory—to believe these doctrines and incorporate them into the religion if that is the case.” The same applies to the policies of those in authority, including governors, judges, and others.

Know that no rational person can deny that he can sometimes distinguish, through his reason, between truth and falsehood, truthfulness and lying, and between the beneficial and the harmful

---

## Page 5692

and between what promotes welfare and what causes harm. Nor can a believer deny that his faith affirms that the revealed Law brings truth and veracity in matters of belief, and benefit and welfare in actions, which include beliefs.

Thus, people have not disputed that, when goodness and badness mean benefit and harm, what is agreeable or disagreeable to man, or pleasure and pain, these qualities in actions can be known through reason. The same applies when something’s goodness is understood in terms of its existence, or when the perfection of an existing thing is described as goodness. Examples include the words of Allah Most High:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names.”

And His words:

“Who perfected everything He created.”

Just as we know that a living being is more perfect in its existence than a dead one, that a knowledgeable person is more perfect than an ignorant one, and that a truthful person is more perfect than a liar, this too can be known through reason. They differed only over whether reason takes benefit and harm into account, and whether “the basis for judging goodness” is the same for the Creator and the created.

The first two aspects, however, are established in themselves, and some instances of each can be known through reason. The first concerns truth as that which is sought; the second concerns truth as that which exists. The first relates to the heart’s love and hatred, its willing and aversion, and its discourse involving commands and prohibitions. The second relates to its acceptance and rejection of claims as true, its affirmation and negation, and its declarative discourse involving negation and affirmation.

The terms “truth” and “falsehood” encompass both categories. “Truth” may mean that which exists and is established, and “falsehood” that which is nonexistent and absent. “Truth” may also denote what ought to be intended, sought, and done—namely, what is beneficial. “Falsehood,” by contrast, denotes what ought neither to be intended, nor sought, nor done

---

## Page 5693

—namely, what is not beneficial. Benefit consists in attaining blessing, pleasure, and happiness, which means attaining pleasure and warding off pain: attaining what is sought and escaping what is feared, attaining bliss and escaping torment, and attaining good and escaping evil.

What exists and what is beneficial may be enduring and lasting, or may come to an end, especially when it lasts only a short time. Thus, “falsehood” is often applied to benefit that does not last and existence that does not endure. As it is said, “Death is truth, and life is vanity.” In its essential sense, the term applies to that whose benefits are neither unalloyed nor preponderant, as discussed earlier concerning what should be renounced—namely, what is not beneficial.

Benefit in the unqualified sense is that which is unalloyed or preponderant. But a benefit that entails forfeiting a greater one, or is followed by harm no less than itself, is, on balance, vain. Harm is more deserving of the designation “falsehood” than benefit is. As for something thought to contain benefit when it does not, or something that affords a corrupt pleasure, it contains no benefit whatsoever.

These, then, are the things that it is prescribed to renounce and abandon; they are vain. Accordingly, whatever Allah and His Messenger have forbidden is vain: it cannot contain any benefit that is unalloyed or preponderant. Hence the deeds of the disbelievers and hypocrites are nullified, as He says:

“Do not invalidate your charities with reminders of your generosity and hurtful conduct, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His likeness is that of a smooth stone covered with dust”—to the end of the verse.

He states that the charity of one who shows off and one who reminds others of his generosity is nullified, leaving him no benefit. Likewise are His words, Most High:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and do not invalidate your deeds.”

The same applies to the nullification of deeds in

---

## Page 5694

such verses as:

“Whoever rejects faith—his deeds have become worthless.”

Hence jurists describe contracts and acts of worship as either valid or invalid. An invalid act is one that fails to achieve its purpose or produce its intended effect, and thus yields none of the benefit sought from it. This includes His words:

“As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert which a thirsty person mistakes for water”—to the end of the verse.

And His words:

“The example of what they spend in this worldly life is that of a wind containing bitter frost which strikes the crops of people who have wronged themselves and destroys them.”

And His words:

“And We will turn to whatever deeds they did and make them scattered dust.”

For the same reason, beliefs and statements are described as false: they neither correspond to reality nor are true, just as those deeds are not beneficial.

Beliefs and statements may also be described as false when they do not correspond to reality, if they contain no benefit, as in the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit.”

Thus, truth, insofar as it concerns the human being, comes down to whatever benefits him in knowledge, speech, action, and state. Allah Most High says:

“He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity”—up to His words—“Thus does Allah illustrate truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as waste, while what benefits people remains in the earth. Thus does Allah set forth examples.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Those who disbelieve and turn others away from the path of Allah—He has rendered their deeds worthless.”

“But those who believe, do righteous deeds, and believe in what has been sent down to Muhammad”—up to His words—“Thus does Allah set forth their likenesses for mankind.”

---

## Page 5695

That being so, and given that every deed not intended to seek Allah’s Face is vain and fruitless, bringing its doer no benefit when he needs it, every deed not intended to seek Allah’s Face is vain. For such a deed either brings no benefit whatsoever, or brings benefit in this world or in the Hereafter. The first case is clear. The question of its benefit in the Hereafter, after death, is likewise clear: the revealed texts conveyed by the messengers establish that, after death, no deed benefits a person except what he intended for Allah’s Face.

In this world, however, a person may experience pleasure and joy, and he may be recompensed for his deeds here. Yet if those pleasures are followed by greater harm and cause him to miss what is more beneficial and lasting, they too are vain. Thus, every deed not intended to seek Allah’s Face is vain, even if it affords some pleasure.

As for created things, they were once nonexistent and absent. Thus, the truest words ever spoken by a poet are those of Labīd:

“Indeed, all things apart from Allah are vain.”

As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The truest words ever spoken by a poet are Labīd’s: ‘Indeed, all things apart from Allah are vain.’”

These words encompass both truth in existence and truth in purpose. Every existing thing is vain without Allah, and every intended end is vain unless Allah is sought. In these two senses, His words:

“Everything will perish except His Face”

have been interpreted as “except what is intended for His Face,” and “nothing exists except through Him.” This is according to one interpretation. As for the other interpretation, which is transmitted from a group of the early generations and was adopted by Imam Ahmad—may He have mercy on him—

---

## Page 5696

in his Refutation of the Jahmiyyah and the Heretics. Ahmad said:

“As for His words, ‘Everything will perish except His Face’: Allah revealed, ‘Everyone upon it will perish.’ The angels then said, ‘The inhabitants of the earth have perished,’ and hoped that they themselves would remain. Allah Most High then revealed that the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth would die, saying: ‘Everything’ among living beings ‘will perish’—meaning that it will die—‘except His Face,’ for He is ever-living and does not die. When this was stated, they became certain that they would die.”

He mentioned this when refuting the Jahmiyyah’s claim that Paradise and Hell will cease to exist.

What we have discussed makes clear that what is good is true, truthful, beneficial, conducive to welfare, wise, and correct; whereas what is bad is false, untruthful, harmful, corrupting, foolish, and mistaken.

As for the points of uncertainty, dispute, and disagreement among people, they come down to a single issue: all of Allah’s acts are good and beautiful. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

“Who perfected everything He created.”

And He Most High says:

“The handiwork of Allah, who perfected all things.”

And He Most High says:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Indeed, Allah is beautiful and loves beauty.”

He is a just Judge. Allah Most High says:

“Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, as do the angels and those endowed with

---

## Page 5697

knowledge—He upholds justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, Allah does not wrong anyone even by an atom’s weight; and if there is a good deed, He multiplies it.”

And He Most High says:

“And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.”

The entire Muslim community agrees upon all this in general, without detailed explanation. Once it is explained in detail, however, they disagree.

The issue concerns these corrupt deeds and pains—evil that actually exists and affects living creatures. Such evil must be either a deed or a pain experienced by a living creature. The evil of such a reprehensible deed or pain lies in the harm it causes.

Regarding these deeds and this suffering, the Mu‘tazilah and their followers among the Shia claim that these deeds are not His creation, nor did He bring them into being. They also maintain that He may not inflict pain except as recompense for a previous deed or with compensation through some subsequent benefit. Many of the affirmationists and the determinists who follow them, however, say: Rather, He created all of it; He does whatever He wills and decrees whatever He wishes. With respect to Him, there is no distinction between creating harms and benefits, or good and evil.

The latter say that it is utterly inconceivable for Him to act unjustly or foolishly. Rather, if it were supposed that He did anything whatsoever, His doing it would be wise, just, and good, since nothing is reprehensible except what He has forbidden, and no one has forbidden Him anything. They place granting creatures bliss and tormenting them on the same footing, as they do punishing one who does good and raising the ranks of disbelievers and hypocrites.

Both groups agree that He neither benefits from His servants’ acts of obedience nor suffers harm from their disobedience.

---

## Page 5698

But the former say: Doing good to others is intrinsically good, even if the benefactor gains nothing from it.

The latter say: Whatever is good when done by us is good when done by Him, and whatever is reprehensible when done by us is reprehensible when done by Him. The latter, along with the vast majority of people, deny this. The former say: When He commands something, He has willed it of us. Good and evil are understood only in terms of what benefits or harms—as when one of us commands someone else to do something: he must necessarily want him to do it and help him do so. He has endowed the disbelievers with the utmost capacity and is no longer able to make them believe voluntarily. Their disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience occur without His will or choice.

Others say: A command does not entail any will whatsoever. I have explained elsewhere the middle position between these two views. The same applies to His commanding: the former say that He commands only what serves His servants’ welfare, while the latter say that His commands are not contingent upon such welfare. There are several premises that clarify these difficulties.

One is that what is good when done by Him need not be good when done by us, and what is reprehensible when done by Him need not be reprehensible when done by us. For the Mu‘tazilah have likened Allah to His creation. In our case, an act is good because it brings benefit and reprehensible because it brings harm; it is also good because we have been commanded to do it and reprehensible because we have been forbidden to do it. Both considerations are categorically inapplicable to Allah Most High, even if

---

## Page 5699

the act is good in another respect, as one of the shaykhs said:

An act I deem reprehensible when done by another—
Yet when You do it, I find it fair.

The second premise is that good and evil may be qualities of our actions, and some of these qualities may be discerned by reason, even if they are explained in terms of what benefits or harms, perfects or diminishes. The Lawgiver’s rulings concerning what He commands and forbids sometimes reveal and confirm the qualities of acts, while at other times they make evident in an act qualities it did not previously possess. An act may be good in itself, good because it is commanded, or good on both grounds.

Whoever denies that acts have intrinsic qualities, holding that an act is good only because it is commanded and that rulings consist solely in the relation of the divine address to the act, has denied the benefits and harms, right and wrong, taught by the revealed laws, as well as the fitting correspondence between the rulings of the Sharia and their underlying reasons. In particular, he has denied understanding of religion, which consists in knowing the wisdom, purposes, and merits of the Sharia.

The third premise is that Allah created all things and has power over all things. Whoever holds that any action lies outside His power and will has deviated concerning His names and signs. This premise stands contrary to the position of the Qadariyyah.

The fourth premise is that when Allah commands His servant to do something, He has willed it of him

---

## Page 5700

by His legislative, religious will, even if He has not willed it of him by His universal, decretive will. To affirm without qualification that His commands entail His will is therefore mistaken, as is denying this without qualification. The correct approach is to distinguish between the two, as revelation does:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens.”

“Allah does not intend to place you in difficulty.”

He also says:

“Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted.”

And He says:

“Those are the ones whose hearts Allah did not will to purify.”

And He says:

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does what He wills.”

There are many similar passages.

The fifth premise:

His love and pleasure necessarily entail His religious will and religious command. Likewise, His hatred, anger, and displeasure necessarily entail the absence of His religious will. Love, pleasure, anger, and displeasure are therefore not merely will. This is the position of the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah.

Whoever holds that these things mean will—as do many of the Qadariyyah and many of those who affirm divine decree—is committed to one of two positions:

Either he holds that, since disbelief, wickedness, and sins are things Allah detests from the standpoint of religion, He also detests their coming into existence, and that they occur apart from His will and volition. This is the position of the Qadariyyah. Or he says that, since Allah wills and decrees them, He therefore loves them and is pleased with them, as one group among those who affirm divine decree maintains.

Both positions have their serious difficulties. Allah Most High loves the God-fearing and loves those who act justly; He is pleased with the believers, and He loves what He commands, whether as an obligation or as a recommendation. Yet this is not

---

## Page 5701

true of the disbelievers, the wicked, and the wrongdoers. He does not approve of disbelief for His servants, nor does He love anyone who is arrogant and boastful. Nevertheless, whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen.

The best defence offered by those who affirm divine decree and hold that love means will is that He loves these things just as He wills them in a universal, decretive sense; likewise, He loves them and is pleased with them in that sense. This is, however, open to objections discussed elsewhere.

If it is said, “This division of will is unknown in our case. Rather, when one of us commands something, he either wills it or does not will it. A distinction between will and love, however, is recognizable in our case,” the answer is: “This is indeed as it must be, for there is nothing like Allah Most High. His commanding us is not like one of us commanding his slave and servants.”

When one of us commands his slave, he does so either because he needs the slave or the action commanded, or because he needs only to issue the command. The first is exemplified by a ruler commanding his troops to do what safeguards his dominion and enables them to benefit him. For guiding people and directing them through commands and prohibitions is a form of kindness towards them, yet a benefactor among human beings himself stands in need of the good he does. Allah Most High says:

“If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against yourselves.”

And He says:

“Whoever does good, it is for his own benefit; and whoever does evil, it is to his own detriment.”

Allah Most High has not commanded His servants because He needs their service, nor does He need to command them. Rather, He has commanded them only out of kindness and as a blessing He has bestowed

---

## Page 5702

upon them. Thus, He commanded them to do what benefits them and forbade them what harms them. Sending messengers and revealing scriptures are among His greatest blessings upon His creation, as He says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds.”

And He Most High says:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a favour upon the believers by raising among them a messenger from among themselves.”

And He says:

“O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, a healing for what is in the hearts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.”

“Say, ‘In Allah’s bounty and mercy—in these let them rejoice.’”

Whoever Allah blesses with obedience, in addition to giving him the command, has received His blessing in full, as He says:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you.”

These are the believers. But whoever He does not bless with obedience, instead leaving him without His aid until he disbelieves and disobeys, has fallen into misery because he exchanged Allah’s blessing for disbelief, as He says:

“Have you not seen those who exchanged Allah’s blessing for disbelief and brought their people into the abode of ruin?”

Since the commands and prohibitions of the revealed law are a universal blessing and mercy, the fact that some people—the disbelievers—do not benefit from them does not detract from this. Likewise, sending down rain and causing sustenance to grow is a universal blessing, even if some people are harmed by it for another wise purpose. Similarly, His willing whatever He wills of created things—their individual beings and their actions—does not entail that He loves everything among them.

When He gives a servant a command, this provides guidance and direction. If the servant carries out what he is commanded, he becomes beloved to Allah; otherwise, he is not beloved to Him, even though Allah wills his existence, His willing him into existence being for another purpose. Bringing into existence is therefore distinct from prescribing religious law.

(If it is said, “Love and approval entail compatibility and affinity between the one who loves

---

## Page 5703

and the one who is loved, and bring the lover joy, pleasure, and delight upon perceiving his beloved. Likewise, hatred arises only from an incompatibility between the one who hates and the object of his hatred; perceiving what he hates therefore causes him hurt, hatred, and the like. Compatibility and incompatibility imply need, since a living being does not love what he does not need; and how could he hate what does not harm him? Allah, however, is self-sufficient, and need cannot be attributed to Him. Were need possible for Him, this would entail His having come into existence and being contingent, whereas He has no need of any of creation. He Most High has said—that is, in the divine hadith:

‘O My servants, you can never harm Me, nor can you ever benefit Me.’

For this reason, love and approval have been interpreted as will, since He brings about benefit and harm.”

The answer has two aspects.

The first is to show that the same objection applies to the opposing view. We say:

Will exists only because of an affinity between the one who wills and what he wills, and its compatibility with him likewise implies need. Otherwise, a living being neither benefits from nor wills what he does not need. Similarly, when he wills to punish and harm someone, this can only arise from aversion and hatred. Otherwise, a living being does not dislike or repel something that causes him no pain whatsoever.

Likewise, the very act of benefiting or harming another is, in a living being, at variance with need; for one of us does good to another only to obtain some benefit or avert some harm, and harms another only to obtain some benefit or avert some harm. Thus, if someone affirms one attribute and denies another, yet what he affirms entails the same objection as what he denies, affirming the one and denying the other is no more justified than the reverse. Were someone to reverse the argument and deny the will that he has affirmed

---

## Page 5704

and affirm the love that he has denied, on the grounds he mentioned, there would be no difference between the two positions. In that case, one must either deny all of these—which is impossible, since it is self-evidently known that Allah benefits creation and shows them kindness, and that this necessarily entails will—or affirm them all, as the scriptural texts do. Thus, if someone imagines that an unacceptable consequence follows from this, one of two things must be true: either that consequence does not follow, or, if it does, it is not unacceptable.

The second answer is that what is known with certainty is that Allah is eternal, necessarily existent, and perfect, and that He cannot have come into existence, be contingent, or have any imperfection. What remains open to examination, however, is whether these matters affirmed by the scriptural texts necessarily entail His having come into existence, being contingent, or having any imperfection. Allah is self-sufficient and necessarily existent in His own right. It is already established that the subsistence of attributes in Him does not entail His having come into existence, being contingent, or having any need.

To claim that He must depend upon His inseparable attributes is equivalent to saying that He depends upon His own essence. Yet it is known that He is self-sufficient in Himself, necessarily existent in His own right, and existent through Himself. Thus, if the notion that He needs Himself means that His essence subsists only through His own essence, this is true: Allah has no need of the worlds or of His creation, and He is self-sufficient in Himself. As for saying without qualification that He has no need of Himself, this is false, for He needs Himself. Either expression, when used without qualification, may suggest a false meaning. There is no creator but Allah Most High.

Thus, if He, glorified be He, is All-Knowing and loves knowledge, All-Pardoning and loves pardon, Beautiful and loves

---

## Page 5705

beauty, Clean and loves cleanliness, Good and loves what is good, loving those who do good, the God-fearing, and the just, possessing every beloved attribute, the Most Beautiful Names, and the loftiest attributes, loving Himself and praising Himself—while creation cannot adequately praise Him, for He is as He has praised Himself—then, just as a believing servant loves himself and loves, for Allah’s sake, those who love Allah and whom Allah loves, Allah, glorified be He, is all the more entitled to love Himself and to love His believing servants for His own sake, and to hate the disbelievers. He is pleased with the former and rejoices in them, and He rejoices in the repentance of a servant who turns to Him from among the latter. He detests and hates the disbelievers, and He loves to be praised and extolled, as when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke to al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ. When al-Aswad said, “I have praised my Lord with words of praise,” he replied, “Your Lord loves praise.”

He, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“No one loves praise more than Allah, and no one loves an excuse more than Allah; for this reason He sent the messengers. No one is more patient than Allah in bearing offense: they ascribe to Him a child and a partner, yet He grants them well-being and provides for them.”

Thus, He rejoices in what He loves, is offended by what He hates, and patiently bears what offends Him. His love, pleasure, joy, wrath, and patience in bearing what offends Him are all aspects of His perfection, and all belong to His attributes and actions. He is the One who created all creatures and their actions. They can never harm Him, nor can they ever benefit Him.

When He rejoices in and is pleased with what some of them do, He, glorified be He, is the One who created their actions, just as, when He rejoices in and is pleased with what He creates, He is Himself the Creator. As for all those who offend Allah and His Messenger, He is the One who enabled them and, in His wisdom, patiently bore their offenses

---

## Page 5706

and thus He had no need of anyone else, nothing lay outside His will, and no one did anything He did not will. This is the view of the Qadariyyah in general, and it represents the utmost perfection and might. As for contingency, it would follow if His existence depended on another’s joy. As for temporal origination, the argument rests on attributes subsisting in Him, from which His temporal origination is inferred. It has been explained elsewhere that the Jahmiyyah’s approach to denying the attributes rests entirely on invalid reasoning by analogy; a detailed explanation is given elsewhere.

Whoever reflects on the texts of the Quran and Sunnah will find them supremely precise and sound. They declare Allah free of every imperfection and affirm every perfection for Him. He, exalted is He, has no perfection awaiting attainment such that He would be deficient before attaining it. Rather, it is part of His perfection that He performs an act after not having performed it. Since He is perfect in His essence, attributes, and actions, His perfection does not depend on another, nor does He need anyone besides Himself. Rather, He is the Self-Sufficient, and we are the needy. Allah, exalted is He, says:

“Allah has certainly heard the words of those who said, ‘Allah is poor, while we are rich.’ We shall record what they said and their killing of the prophets without right.”

In His love, pleasure, abhorrence, wrath, joy, anger, patience, pardon, and compassion, He, glorified be He, possesses a perfection that creatures cannot comprehend—a perfection surpassing every perfection, for every perfection is derived from His. His is the beautiful praise that His servants cannot adequately recount; He is only as He has praised Himself. His is the self-sufficiency by which He needs none besides Himself:

“There is no one in the heavens and earth but will come to the Most Merciful as a servant.”

“He has fully accounted for them and counted them precisely.”

“And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.”

---

## Page 5707

Thus, this great principle—the question of His creation and command, and the attributes and actions connected with it, including His love, pleasure, joy in what He loves, abhorrence, and patience with what offends Him—relates to questions of divine decree; the revealed law and the path being asked about; the divine attributes; and reward and punishment, promise and warning. These four principles are universal and comprehensive, and concern Him and His creation.

In their breadth, comprehensiveness, and ability to dispel doubts, they resemble the questions of attributes of essence and action; essence, reality, and limit; and the related questions concerning the attributes, the inherence of temporally originated events, and the denial of corporeality, with all the distinctions and careful analysis these entail.

For those who deny His attributes and those who deviate concerning His names and signs have rejected much of the truth brought by the messengers, on the basis of their beliefs concerning the negation of body and accident, the denial that temporally originated events can inhere in Him, and the denial of need. These things may rightly be denied in one respect, yet rightly affirmed in another. They thus fell into denying the indubitable truth brought by the messengers and revealed in the Scriptures—the truth with which created beings are innately endowed and to which both revelation and reason bear witness. And Allah knows best.

## Page 5708

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

A group of Sufis discussed the “Seal of the Saints” and magnified his importance. These included al-Hakīm al-Tirmidhī—this was one of his errors, for his statements are generally sound, unlike Ibn Arabī, whose statements contain much confusion, particularly concerning union—as well as Ibn Arabī and others.

Several individuals, including Ibn Arabī, each claimed to be that Seal. A claimant might qualify this by saying that he was the seal of Muhammadan sainthood, or perfect sainthood, or something similar, so as not to entail that Allah would create no saint after him. Sometimes they went to extremes concerning him, as Ibn Arabī did in his Fusūs, making him a source of inward support for the Seal of the Prophets. This followed from their false exaggeration, whereby they may place sainthood above prophethood, agreeing with extremists among the philosophers who may place the perfect philosopher above a prophet.

Likewise, the ignorant among the Qadariyyah, Ahmadiyyah, and Yūnusiyyah may give their shaykh precedence

---

## Page 5709

over the Prophet or any other prophet, and they may even attribute a degree of divinity to their shaykh.

Likewise, some of the Sa‘diyyah place a saint above a prophet. Some of them have said, “Al-Shāfi‘ī is followed as an authority, but Abū Bakr and ‘Umar are not.” The same applies to the extremists among the Rāfidah, who may claim that the imam inwardly sustained the Prophet, just as they may regard him as a god.

As for exaggerating the status of a saint who is not a prophet until he is placed above a prophet—whether he is called a saint, an imam, or a philosopher—and their expectation of the awaited one, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan or Ismā‘īl ibn Ja‘far, which parallels the Sufis’ attachment to the Ghawth and the Seal of the Saints: the falsity of all this is evident from the known texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the consensus of the ummah. Allah has divided those whom He has blessed into four groups: the prophets, the utterly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. The highest rank anyone below a prophet can attain is that of the utterly truthful, just as the best of this ummah after its Prophet was a man of consummate truthfulness.

This was also the highest rank attained by Mary, as stated in His words:

“The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. His mother was a woman of truth.”

I used this as evidence for the consensus reported by a number of scholars—including al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and others of our school, Abū al-Ma‘ālī, and, I believe, al-Bāqillānī—that she was not a prophetess. They cited this consensus to establish the miraculous gifts of the saints through what took place at her hands. Some people had claimed that she was a prophetess, so I cited this verse, and the person I was addressing was delighted with this argument. For Allah mentioned this to explain the utmost extent of her excellence and to counter the Christians’ exaggeration concerning her, just as

---

## Page 5710

one might say to someone who claimed that a man was a king, a wealthy man, or the like: “He is no more than a village chief or the owner of an orchard,” thus stating the utmost extent of his authority and wealth. Had the Messiah possessed a rank above messengership, or his mother a rank above that of consummate truthfulness, it would have been mentioned. Such exaggeration originated among the Christians. Extremists among the Sufis and the Shia, together with the philosophizing Sabians who have joined them, resemble them in some respects; hence they can all be refuted on the same basis.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning Abū Bakr and ʿUmar: “These two are the foremost of the mature men among the people of Paradise, from the earliest to the latest generations, except for the prophets and messengers.”

The explanation of this issue belongs elsewhere: everyone other than the prophets is beneath them.

The discussion here concerns only what they say about the Seal of

---

## Page 5711

the Friends of Allah. We say:

This is an invalid designation, with no basis in the Quran, the Sunnah, or any statement transmitted from someone generally accepted by the Muslim community. Broadly speaking, however, it is understood that the last God-fearing believer remaining in the world will be the last of Allah’s friends.

Second, we say:

The last of Allah’s friends, or their seal—whether an actual person or merely a hypothetical figure—need not be superior to other friends of Allah, let alone the best of them. This notion arose solely from an analogy with the Seal of the Prophets. Seeing that the Seal of the Prophets was their foremost, they imagined an analogy based merely on the shared word “seal.” They therefore said: “The Seal of the Friends of Allah is the best of them.” This reasoning is mistaken, for the superiority of the Seal of the Prophets over the other prophets does not follow merely from his being their seal. Rather, other evidence establishes it.

We further say:

On the contrary, the earliest of Allah’s friends in this community, the first among them, is the best of them. The best of this community is the Seal of the Prophets, and the best of Allah’s friends is the first of them to follow the Seal of the Prophets. This is because a friend of Allah receives his knowledge and guidance from the Prophet and follows him. The closer he is to the Prophet, the better he is; the farther away, the reverse. This differs from the Seal of the Prophets, who receives his knowledge and guidance from Allah alone. His coming later in time therefore entails no inferiority in rank. Indeed, Allah may bring together in him qualities that He distributed among the other prophets.

What we have stated—that the earliest of Allah’s friends are the best of them—is established by the Quran, the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains, and the consensus of the early generations.

Related to this is the belief held by certain groups that some people of later generations may surpass the eminent Companions. This view is found among those associated with scholarship, worship, jihad, leadership, and kingship. Even among students of jurisprudence, some have said: “Abū Hanīfah had a greater understanding of jurisprudence than ʿAlī.” Others have said: “Al-Shāfiʿī may be followed as a legal authority, but Abū Bakr and ʿUmar may not.”

They sometimes cling to specious arguments based on reason or spiritual experience, arguing that later practitioners of every discipline master it more thoroughly than their predecessors. They benefit from their predecessors’ attainments in addition to the knowledge peculiar to themselves, as is found among practitioners of arithmetic, natural philosophers, astrologers, and others.

---

## Page 5712

And Ibn Masʿūd’s statement: “Whoever among you wishes to follow an example should follow those who have died. They were the Companions of Muhammad, the purest of this community in heart

## Page 5713

and deepest in knowledge, and least given to affectation. They were people whom Allah chose to accompany His Prophet and establish His religion. So recognize their due rights and hold fast to their guidance, for they followed the straight path.”

There are also the statements of Jundub and others—many such statements are recorded elsewhere. Indeed, this contradicts explicit Quranic texts, such as His words:

“And the first forerunners,” and the rest of the verse.

And His words:

“Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal,” and the rest of the verse.

And His words:

“And those who came after them,” and the rest of the verse, as well as other passages.

However, this issue is not the purpose of the present discussion. Rather, its purpose is to discuss the seal of the saints. A similar notion is held by a group including Ibn Hūd, Ibn Sab‘īn, al-Niffarī, and al-Tilimsānī: that what comes later must be superior to what came earlier. They believe that the world progresses from its beginning toward its culmination, like a child growing older or a plant growing stronger after its initial weakness. On this basis, they maintain that the Messiah is superior to Moses. They take this so far as to posit a human being coming after Muhammad who is more perfect than he is, as the Ismā‘īlīs, Qarmatians, and Bātinīs maintain.

There is no evidence whatsoever for this claim—that whoever comes later within a given kind is the best of that kind. It neither holds universally nor is its converse valid. Rather, it is established through the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, “is the best of creation”—meaning after the Prophet. Likewise, al-Rabī‘ ibn Khuthaym said:

“I do not rank anyone above our Prophet

---

## Page 5714

nor do I rank anyone above Abraham after our Prophet. All the prophets who followed his religion, such as Moses, Jesus, and others, rank below him.” Likewise, all the other prophets of the Children of Israel rank below Moses. Muslims, Jews, and Christians agree that Moses is superior to the other prophets of the Children of Israel, apart from their disagreement concerning the Messiah.

The Quran attests in two verses to the distinction of the messengers of firm resolve. Allah says:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary.”

And He says:

“He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus.”

These five are the messengers of firm resolve. As established in the authentic hadiths concerning intercession, they refer the request to intercede for those gathered on the Day of Resurrection from one to another after Adam. They must therefore be regarded as superior to their descendants. This includes instances of an earlier person being superior to a later one, and of a later person being superior to an earlier one.

The fundamental error in this matter is to make chronological precedence or succession the basis for ranking prophets, saints, scholars, or rulers. This is a false principle. Sometimes superiority belongs to an earlier member of a given category, and sometimes to a later one. Thus, among those versed in grammar, medicine, and arithmetic, there are instances in which earlier figures—such as Ptolemy, Sībawayh, and Hippocrates—are superior, while in other instances the reverse is true.

---

## Page 5715

As for their assumption that later practitioners of every discipline are more proficient than their predecessors because they have perfected it, this is refuted, first, by the fact that it does not hold universally. No work on Arabic comparable to Sībawayh’s book has been composed since; nor has anything more complete than Ptolemy’s book—or, indeed, the writings of Hippocrates—been composed after them.

Furthermore, we say that this may be conceded in disciplines acquired through reasoning by analogy, considered judgment, and ingenuity. But as for virtues connected with following the prophets, the closer a person is to the prophets, provided his natural disposition is sound, the more fully he receives from them. The excellence he possesses consists of religious virtues learned from the prophets. Thus, whoever opposes this belongs to the innovators who depart from the ways of the prophets, believing that they possess a share of knowledge and spiritual states beyond the prophets’ sphere. The greater a person’s appreciation of prophethood and its stature, the more firmly grounded he is in this matter.

As for spiritual experiences and saintly miracles, some are false; those that are genuine were undoubtedly more complete and excellent among the early generations. A departure from the ordinary course of events sometimes occurs because a servant needs it, while someone superior to him may experience no such departure. For such an occurrence has both a cause and an intended end: a person of spiritual perfection may have risen beyond that cause, or may have no need of the end intended by it. Moreover, the later generations have no saintly miracle without the early generations having had something of the same kind that was more complete.

---

## Page 5716

As for his words:

“They will have the reward of fifty of you, because you find helpers in doing good, whereas they find none.”

This is correct: if someone from the later generations performs a deed like one performed by someone from the earlier generations, he will have the reward of fifty. Yet it is inconceivable that anyone from the later generations could do what some of the foremost early believers, such as Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, did. No prophet like Muhammad will ever again be sent, with whom someone could act as they acted with Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

As for his words:

“My community is like rain: one does not know whether its beginning or its end is better.”

Although there is some weakness in this report, its meaning is that some among the later generations resemble those of the earlier generations and come close to them. Indeed, the resemblance and closeness are so great that an observer cannot tell which is better, even though one is, in reality, better than the other.

This gives the later generations glad tidings that some among them will approach the early believers in excellence, as stated in the other hadith:

“The best of my community are its first and its last, and between them is a middle mass—or crookedness. I wish I could see my brothers.” They asked, “Are we not your brothers?” He replied, “You are my Companions.”

This affirms the superiority of the Companions, for they possess the distinctive merit of companionship, which is more complete than brotherhood alone.

Likewise, his words:

“Which people are most astonishing in faith?”

Through to his words:

“People who come after me and believe in the pages that are hung up.”

This indicates that their faith is more astonishing than the faith of others; it does not indicate that they are superior. For the hadith states that they

---

## Page 5717

mentioned the angels and the prophets, and it is well known that the prophets are superior to those who believe in the pages that are hung up.

Similarly, the fact that the poor enter Paradise before the rich does not mean that, once they have entered, they will rank higher than all the rich. They enter first only because they are spared the reckoning.

This subject of comparing degrees of merit—whether between different categories of beings, deeds, and attributes, or between individuals within the same category—is a vast subject in which many people err. May Allah guide us to the straight path.

## Page 5722

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section

Judge Abū Ya‘lā said in ‘Uyūn al-Masā’il:

Issue

“Those who affirm prophethood have attained knowledge of Allah Most High through the establishment of prophethood, without examining rational proofs or reasoning from them. This is contrary to the Ash‘arīs, who maintain that such knowledge cannot be attained until one examines rational proofs and reasons from them.”

He also said:

“We do not deny the validity of rational inquiry, nor do we deny that knowledge can be attained through it. Our disagreement concerns only whether knowledge can be attained without it.”

He argued that once prophethood is established by the occurrence of a miracle, we know that there is a Sender who sent the prophet, since there can be no prophet without a Sender. Once the existence of a Sender is established, this dispenses with the need to examine rational proofs and reason from them to establish His existence.

## Page 5723

Al-Bayhaqī also stated in his Book of Creed what al-Khattābī mentioned in al-Ghunya ‘an al-Kalām wa-Ahlihi:

“Some who have investigated the existence of the Maker and the world’s beginning in time have followed a method of reasoning based on the premises of prophethood and the miracles of messengership. The evidence for these is obtained through sensory perception by those who witness them, and through widely transmitted reports by those who do not. Once prophethood is established, it becomes a basis for the obligation to accept what the Prophet calls people to. This was how most of those who responded to the Messenger came to believe.”

He mentioned the account of Ja‘far and his companions with the Negus, the account of the Bedouin who asked, “Who created the heaven?”, and other accounts.

I say:

Many speculative theologians maintain that knowledge of the Lord’s existence must come first, together with knowledge of His attributes by which it is known that He is the One who manifests the miracle. Otherwise, it would be impossible to infer from the miracle that the messenger is truthful, let alone that the Lord exists. As for the method mentioned by the earlier scholars, it is sound if precisely formulated. The Quran presents it in the account of Pharaoh, who denied the Lord.

Allah Most High says:

“Go, both of you, to Pharaoh and say, ‘We are messengers of the Lord of all worlds.’”

“Send the Children of Israel with us.”

“He said, ‘Did we not raise you among us as a child?’”

—up to His words—

“Pharaoh said, ‘And what is the Lord of all worlds?’”

“He said, ‘The Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, if you would be certain.’”

“He said to those around him, ‘Do you not hear?’”

“He said, ‘Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.’”

“He said, ‘Indeed, this messenger of yours who has been sent to you is truly mad.’”

“He said, ‘The Lord of the east and the west and everything between them, if you would use reason.’”

“He said, ‘If you take any god other than me

---

## Page 5724

, I will surely have you imprisoned.’”

“He said, ‘Even if I bring you something clear?’”

“He said, ‘Then bring it, if you are truthful.’”

“So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a serpent, plain to see.”

“And he drew out his hand, and it was white for all to see.”

Here Moses presented Pharaoh with clear proof, making it evidence that he was truthful in claiming to be the Messenger of the Lord of all worlds, and that he worshipped a god other than Pharaoh.

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“If they do not respond to you, then know that it was sent down with Allah’s knowledge and that there is no god but Him.”

He thus made clear that the miracle demonstrates both His oneness and messengership. This is because a miracle—an act that departs from the customary course of events—in itself demonstrates the existence of the Maker, as do all other things that come into being. Indeed, it furnishes a more specific proof, for ordinary events do not have the same evidentiary force as extraordinary ones. Thus, when extraordinary events occur, the Lord is glorified, extolled, and magnified in a way that does not occur with ordinary events. Recalling His greatness brings about a humility within souls that ordinary events do not evoke, for these are fresh signs and are therefore given their due.

Their manifestation points to the messenger; and once it becomes clear that they call for acknowledging him as Allah’s Messenger, both lordship and messengership are thereby established. This is especially so according to those who hold that a miracle’s indication of the messenger’s truthfulness is self-evident. This is the position of a group of Mu‘tazilite speculative theologians, such as al-Jāhiz, and groups from other schools, such as those Ash‘arīs and Hanbalīs who say that the distinction between a miracle, sorcery, and a saintly wonder is known directly, without inference.

## Page 5726

And he was asked:

Which deserves greater priority: treating what Allah dislikes in your heart—such as envy, resentment, malice, arrogance, showing off, seeking acclaim, dwelling on one’s own deeds, hardness of heart, and other impurities and corruptions peculiar to the heart—or occupying oneself with outward deeds, such as prayer, fasting, and various acts of devotion, both voluntary and vowed, while these things remain in one’s heart? Give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.

He replied—may Allah have mercy on him:

Praise be to Allah. Some of these matters are obligatory upon a person, and what is more obligatory has greater merit and excellence. As Allah Most High said, according to what His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, narrated from Him:

“My servant draws near to Me through nothing comparable to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him.”

Then He said:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary deeds until I love him.”

Outward deeds cannot be righteous and acceptable except through the workings of the heart, for the heart is a king and the limbs are its soldiers. When the king becomes corrupt, his soldiers become corrupt. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, in the body there is a morsel of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound; and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt.”

Likewise, the deeds of the heart must affect the deeds of the body. If what takes precedence is what is more obligatory, whether it is termed

---

## Page 5727

inward or outward, what is termed inward may be more obligatory, such as abandoning envy and arrogance, for this is more obligatory upon a person than voluntary fasting. Conversely, something termed outward may be more meritorious, such as night prayer, which is better than merely dismissing certain passing thoughts from the heart, such as wishing for blessings like those enjoyed by others, and the like.

Inward and outward deeds each support the other. Prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing and engenders humble devotion and other tremendous effects. It and charity are the best of deeds. And Allah knows best.
