## Page 5728

He was asked:

Did the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say, “Increase me in bewilderment concerning You”?

Some of those who know Allah have said, “Knowledge of Allah begins in bewilderment and ends in bewilderment.” When asked, “What causes bewilderment?” the answer was, “Two things: the many changes in a person’s states, and the gravity of wrongdoing coupled with fear of falling into despair.”

Al-Wāsitī said, “An affliction descends upon the hearts of those who know Allah, leaving them between despair and hope. It neither gives them hope of attainment, so that they might rest, nor makes them despair of the quest, so that they might rest.”

One of them said, “When shall I reach the path of the hopeful, while I remain in the bewilderment of the bewildered?”

Muhammad ibn al-Fadl, a knower of Allah, said, “Whenever one passes from one state to another, astonishment and bewilderment confront him.” He also said, “Those who know Allah best are the most bewildered concerning Him.”

Al-Junayd said, “The intellect of the wise culminates in bewilderment.” Dhū al-Nūn said, “The ultimate end of those who know Allah is bewilderment.”

One of them recited:

“I am bewildered concerning You; take my hand,
O Guide of those bewildered concerning You.”

Please give us a clear and thorough explanation of this matter.

---

## Page 5729

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The statement mentioned, “Increase me in bewilderment concerning You,” is among the reports falsely attributed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. No scholar of hadith has transmitted it; only an ignorant person or a heretic would relate it. This statement implies that he was bewildered and that he asked for greater bewilderment. Both notions are false.

Allah guided him through what He revealed to him, taught him what he did not know, and commanded him to ask for increased knowledge, saying:

“My Lord, increase me in knowledge.”

This implies that he possessed knowledge and was commanded to seek more of it. Likewise, he and the believers were commanded to seek guidance by saying:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Indeed, you guide to a straight path.”

How could someone who guides others be bewildered?

Allah condemned bewilderment in the Quran, saying:

“Say, ‘Shall we invoke besides Allah what can neither benefit nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like someone whom the devils have lured away in the land, bewildered, while he has companions calling him to guidance, “Come to us”?’ Say, ‘Indeed, Allah’s guidance is the true guidance.’”

In short, bewilderment belongs to the same category as ignorance and misguidance. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the most perfect of all creation in knowledge of Allah and His commands, the most fully guided himself and the most accomplished in guiding others, and the furthest of all creation from ignorance and misguidance. Allah Most High said:

“By the star when it sets! Your companion has neither strayed nor erred, nor does he speak from his own desire.”

And Allah Most High said:

---

## Page 5730

“This is a Book which We have revealed to you so that you may bring people out of darkness into light, by their Lord’s permission, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.”

Allah Most High also said:

“And He sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their differences”—up to His words—“Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they had differed. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

Allah has thus guided the believers through him. Allah Most High also said:

“Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will grant you a double share of His mercy, give you a light by which to walk, and forgive you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Allah has therefore guaranteed those who believe in him a light by which to walk. As Allah Most High said:

“Is one who was dead, whom We brought to life and gave a light by which to walk among people, like one who is in darkness from which he cannot emerge?”

Allah Most High also said:

“And thus We have revealed to you an inspiration by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. Indeed, you guide to a straight path.”

There are many such passages in the Quran and hadith.

No person of knowledge and faith has praised bewilderment. Rather, it has been praised by a group of heretics, such as Ibn ‘Arabī, the author of al-Fusūs, and other heretics like him. They themselves are bewildered, so they praised bewilderment and deemed it superior to uprightness. They claimed that they were the most perfect of creation, that the Seal of the Saints among them would surpass the Seal of the Prophets in knowledge of Allah, and that the prophets acquired knowledge of Allah from them; and they were, in

---

## Page 5731

this, like someone who says, “The roof fell upon them from beneath them”—of whom it is said, “Neither reason nor Quran!” For the prophets lived earlier, so how could those who came earlier acquire knowledge from those who came later? Moreover, according to Muslims, Jews, and Christians, these men are not superior to the prophets. Thus, these people have departed from both reason and religion—the religion of Muslims, Jews, and Christians. We have refuted them at length elsewhere. Their statements concerning “the unity of being, indwelling, and union” are among the worst statements made by heretics.

As for other shaykhs who speak of bewilderment, if one of them is describing his own bewilderment, this does not imply praise of bewilderment. Rather, the bewildered person is commanded to seek guidance. Thus, it is related that Imam Ahmad taught a man to supplicate:

“O Guide of the bewildered, guide me to the path of the truthful, and make me one of Your righteous servants.”

As for the person who said, “Knowledge begins in bewilderment and ends in bewilderment,” he may intend a sound meaning: namely, that the seeker travelling the spiritual path is bewildered before attaining knowledge and guidance. Everyone seeking knowledge and guidance experiences a degree of bewilderment before attaining what he seeks.

His statement, “It ends in bewilderment,” may mean that a person continues to seek guidance and knowledge, remaining bewildered with regard to what he has not yet attained. This does not praise bewilderment. Rather, it means that a person inevitably experiences some degree of bewilderment for which he needs knowledge and guidance.

---

## Page 5732

His statement, “Bewilderment arises from two things: the first is the great variation in spiritual states, and the other is the severity of evil and the fear of despair,” describes a particular spiritual journey. Not every seeker experiences this. Some seekers, however, undergo such differing states that they no longer know what to accept or reject, what to do or leave undone. Anyone in this condition must continually supplicate Allah, glorified and exalted be He, humbly beseech Him, and seek guidance through the Quran and Sunnah.

The same applies to the severity of evil and the fear of despair. Some seekers are tried with acts of disobedience that make them fear falling into despair of Allah’s mercy, because of their intense fear and the many transgressions they perceive in themselves. Such a person should recognize the vastness of Allah’s mercy, His acceptance of His servants’ repentance, and His joy at it.

As for another’s statement:

“A visitation descends upon the hearts of those who know Allah, leaving them between despair and hope. It neither gives them hope of attainment, allowing them to rest, nor makes them despair of the quest, allowing them to rest.”

The response is that this, too, is a passing state experienced by some seekers. It is not something inevitable for everyone who follows the path to Allah, nor is it a praiseworthy ultimate goal. Rather, it is something that happens to some seekers, as it is related that al-Shiblī used to recite verses expressing this meaning:

---

## Page 5733

“One day a cloud from You spread its shade over us;
Its lightning shone for us, but its rain was slow to fall.
Neither does its cloud disperse, so that the hopeful might despair,
Nor does its rain arrive to quench those thirsting for it.”

The speaker of such words is more in need of Allah’s pardon and forgiveness for them than of being praised or taken as an example for them. There are many such instances, which we have discussed elsewhere when addressing the utterances that arise among some people: reproaching divine Lordship, invoking the bewildered madman to make a case against Him, offering excuses for the lover, and similar matters. Those who affirm what these utterances entail have sided with disbelief and heresy. Rather, one must acknowledge Allah’s grace, generosity, and kindness, and one’s own shortcomings and sins. As stated in the authentic hadith:

“The best supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; none has the right to be worshipped but You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I abide by Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge before You Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ Whoever says this in the morning with certainty in it and dies that day will enter Paradise; and whoever says it in the evening with certainty in it and dies that night will enter Paradise.”

And in an authentic divine hadith:

“Allah Most High says: ‘O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you, then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.’”

And in an authentic hadith:

---

## Page 5734

“Allah says: ‘Whoever draws near to Me a handspan, I draw near to him an arm’s length. Whoever draws near to Me an arm’s length, I draw near to him a fathom. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.’”

And in an authentic hadith:

“I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me.”

It is established that every blessing from Allah Most High is grace, and every punishment from Him is justice. His wisdom, mercy, and justice have been demonstrated in ways that astound the mind. This matter touches upon major foundational questions concerning divine decree, command, promise, threat, and the divine names and attributes, which have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is to discuss what has been related from these shaykhs. The statement, “You neither give them hope of attainment, so that they might find rest, nor make them despair of seeking, so that they might find rest,” describes a passing state experienced by someone whose aspirations have become attached to a particular object, leaving him wavering between despair and hope. This is a blameworthy state, for the servant should not stipulate a particular thing for Allah to grant him. Rather, his aspiration should be to do what is commanded, refrain from what is forbidden, and patiently bear what is decreed.

Once he is helped to accomplish these three things, there will follow desired blessings that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

Even if his aspiration becomes attached to something and he asks Allah for it, Allah grants him one of three things: He either answers his supplication promptly, stores up an equivalent good for him, or averts an equivalent evil from him.

The term “attainment” is ambiguous, for every wayfarer has a goal

---

## Page 5735

that he reaches.

When someone is said to have attained to Allah, to affirmation of His oneness, to knowledge of Him, or the like, this encompasses diverse forms and widely differing degrees that none but Allah Most High can enumerate. To despair of attaining the knowledge of Allah and affirmation of His oneness that He loves and approves is a major sin. Rather, one must hope for this and aspire to it.

Yet whoever hopes for something seeks it, and whoever fears something flees from it. If a person strives, seeks the help of Allah Most High, and persists in seeking forgiveness and exerting himself, Allah will surely bestow upon him from His bounty what he never imagined. If he finds that his heart does not open and that he does not experience the sweetness of faith or the light of guidance, let him repent and seek forgiveness frequently, and persist in striving to the best of his ability. For Allah says:

“And those who strive for Us—We will surely guide them to Our ways.”

He must fulfill his obligations both outwardly and inwardly and adhere to the straight path, seeking Allah’s help and disclaiming any power or strength except through Him. In short, no one has the right to despair; rather, he must hope for Allah’s mercy, just as he has no right not to despair; rather, he must fear His punishment.

Allah Most High says:

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of nearness to their Lord, each striving to be closest. They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is to be feared.”

Some have said:

“Whoever worships Allah through love alone is a heretic, and whoever worships Him through fear alone is

---

## Page 5736

a Harūrī; whoever worships Him through hope alone is a Murji’ī; and whoever worships Him through love, hope, and fear is a believer who affirms His oneness.”

As for the words:

“When shall I reach the path of those who hope, while I remain lost in the bewilderment of the perplexed?”

This is a description of a blameworthy state in which the speaker finds himself, just as someone might describe the deficiency of his faith, the weakness of his knowledge, and the doubts that mar his certainty. Such a state is not something to seek; rather, it is something from which one seeks refuge in Allah.

As for Muhammad ibn al-Fadl’s statement:

“Whenever one who knows Allah passes from one state to another, astonishment and bewilderment confront him.”

This may mean that whenever he advances to a station of knowledge and certainty, he begins to yearn for a station of knowledge he has not yet reached. He is thus bewildered concerning what he has not attained, not what he has attained.

His statement:

“Those who know Allah best are the most bewildered concerning Him”

means that they are the most eager to increase in knowledge and understanding. Their extensive knowledge and understanding make them aware of matters they do not yet know. They remain bewildered concerning these matters, seeking to know and understand them. Undoubtedly, the one who knew Allah best of all creation said:

“I cannot encompass all praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

And created beings have been given only a little knowledge. As for the report that al-Junayd said, “The reasoning of rational people ends in bewilderment”—

---

## Page 5737

I do not know this to be a saying of al-Junayd. Whether he actually said it is open to question; indeed, it seems more likely that it is not characteristic of his known statements. If he did say this, he meant not knowing what he had not yet attained. He did not mean that the prophets and Allah’s righteous servants had attained no certainty, knowledge, or guidance. Al-Junayd is far above intending such a meaning, and such a statement is to be rejected, whoever says it.

But if what is meant is that, however much knowledge, certainty, and guidance those who know Allah attain, there remain matters they have not reached, then this is correct. This is illustrated by the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad and Abū Hātim in his Sahīh:

“O Allah, I ask You by every name belonging to You, by which You have named Yourself, which You have revealed in Your Book, which You have taught to any of Your creation, or which You have kept exclusively with Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen, to make the Quran the springtime of my heart, the light of my breast, the dispeller of my sorrow, and the remover of my worry and distress.”

He said:

“Whoever says this, Allah will remove his worry and distress and replace them with joy.”

He thus stated that Allah has names which He has kept exclusively with Himself in the knowledge of the unseen. Neither an angel nor a human being knows these names. If someone means that the minds of rational people have not attained knowledge of such matters, this is correct. But if he means that rational people possess neither knowledge nor certainty, but only bewilderment and doubt, this is categorically false.

As for what is related from Dhū al-Nūn on this subject—although Dhū al-Nūn did make statements for which he was censured, and al-Hārith ibn Miskīn disciplined him, and he was summoned by

---

## Page 5738

al-Mutawakkil to Baghdad, was accused of heresy, and was counted by people among the philosophers—I do not know whether he said this or not. Al-Junayd, by contrast, was predominantly characterized by uprightness and adherence to the Prophet’s example, although everyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected except those of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. No one other than the Messenger is protected from error. Nevertheless, teachers whose paths are known to be sound are understood not to intend meanings whose falsehood is self-evident according to reason and religion.

This is all that this sheet could accommodate. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 5739

He was asked:

About a man who loves a scholar: when they meet and then part, the man experiences something akin to fainting because of their separation. Yet when the scholar is occupied and pays him no attention, he does not experience this state. Does this arise from the man who feels this love, or from the scholar’s influence?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Its cause lies in both of them. It is like water: when a thirsty person drinks it, he experiences pleasure and refreshment, caused both by his thirst and by the coolness of the water. Likewise, when fire catches in cotton, the effect is due both to the fire and to the cotton.

When a scholar gives a student his attention, the student experiences pleasure, delight, and joy because of the scholar’s attentiveness and interest. Such is the state of one who loves in relation to the beloved. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 5740

He was asked:

What is the wisdom behind the fact that those engaged in remembrance, contemplation, spiritual discipline, striving against the self, and similar practices are granted unveilings, miraculous gifts, and other spiritual states that are not granted to those engaged in acquiring knowledge, studying it, and investigating it—despite their limited knowledge and the ignorance of some of them?

Indeed, if someone spends the night in focused devotion, engaged in remembrance with an attentive heart, he is bound to experience a vision or have something opened to him. Yet if he spends a night repeatedly reviewing a chapter of jurisprudence, he experiences nothing of the kind. Many devoted worshippers even find sweetness and delight in remembrance that they do not find when reciting the Quran, although the Sunnah affirms the superiority of the scholar over the worshipper—especially when the worshipper needs the very knowledge whose pursuit occupies the scholar instead of devotional practice.

One hadith states:

“The angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge out of pleasure with what he does. The scholars are the heirs of the prophets, and the superiority of the scholar over the worshipper is like the superiority of the moon over all the stars.”

Another hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“On the Day of Resurrection, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to the worshippers and those who strove in His cause: ‘Enter Paradise.’ The scholars will say: ‘It was through our knowledge that they worshipped and strove.’ Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say

---

## Page 5741

to them: ‘In My sight, you are like My angels. Intercede.’ Their intercession will be accepted, and then they will enter Paradise.” There are also other hadiths and reports to this effect.

Moreover, many devoted worshippers prefer worship to seeking knowledge, despite being ignorant of matters that invalidate much of their worship, such as the things that invalidate ablution, prayer, or fasting. Some may even relate a story along these lines: Rābi‘a al-‘Adawiyya—may Allah have mercy on her—once came to pray in Jerusalem through the night until dawn. Beside her was a house in which a jurist spent the night repeatedly reviewing the chapter on menstruation. When morning came, Rābi‘a said to him, “You there! Those who have attained their goal have reached their Lord, while you are preoccupied with women’s menstruation!” Or they relate something similar. What, then, prevents those engaged in acquiring knowledge from experiencing what those engaged in worship experience, despite the superiority of knowledge over worship?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. There is no doubt that those granted both knowledge and faith are higher in rank than those granted faith alone, as the Quran and Sunnah indicate. The knowledge commended in the Quran and Sunnah is the knowledge handed down by the prophets. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The scholars are the heirs of the prophets. The prophets did not leave behind dirhams or dinars; rather, they left behind knowledge. Whoever acquires it has acquired an abundant share.”

This knowledge falls into three categories:

---

## Page 5742

“Knowledge of Allah, His names and attributes” and related matters. On such subjects Allah revealed Surah al-Ikhlās (Sincerity), the Throne Verse, and similar passages.

“The second category”: knowledge of what Allah has revealed concerning past events, future events, and present realities. On such subjects Allah revealed the verses containing narratives, promises and warnings, descriptions of Paradise and Hell, and the like.

“The third category”: knowledge of what Allah has commanded concerning the heart and the bodily faculties: faith in Allah, encompassing the heart’s knowledge and states, and the words and deeds expressed through the bodily faculties. This knowledge includes knowledge of the foundations of faith and the pillars of Islam, as well as knowledge of outward words and deeds. It also includes the knowledge found in the jurists’ books concerning the rulings governing outward actions. That is but one part of a part of a part of religious knowledge, just as the unveilings experienced by people of spiritual purity are but one part of a part of a part of knowledge concerning the created world.

People fall into error in these matters because they understand what the terms used in the Quran and Sunnah denote, yet do not know the realities of things as they exist. Many a man memorizes the wording in which knowledge is expressed—the foremost instance being the memorization of the Quran’s wording—yet lacks the understanding, or even the faith, that would give him any advantage over someone who has been given

---

## Page 5743

the Quran but not the memorization of the wording in which knowledge is expressed. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“The believer who recites the Quran is like a citron: its taste is pleasant and its fragrance is pleasant. The believer who does not recite the Quran is like a date: its taste is pleasant, but it has no fragrance. The hypocrite who recites the Quran is like sweet basil: its fragrance is pleasant, but its taste is bitter. The hypocrite who does not recite the Quran is like a colocynth: its taste is bitter, and it has no fragrance.”

A man may have memorized the Quran’s wording and surahs without being a believer; indeed, he may be a hypocrite. A believer who has not memorized its wording and surahs is therefore better than him, even if others benefit from that hypocrite just as they benefit from sweet basil. As for someone who has been granted both knowledge and faith, he is a knowledgeable believer and is therefore superior to a believer who does not match him in knowledge, although they share in faith. This is a principle that must be understood.

There is “another principle” here: not every deed that produces unveilings or an ability to exercise influence over the created world is superior to a deed that produces neither. Unless such unveilings and influence serve as a means of supporting Allah’s religion, they are merely part of the enjoyment of this worldly life. Such things may be attained by unbelievers among the polytheists and the People of the Book, even when they are not attained by the people of faith, who are the people of Paradise, whereas those others are the people of the Fire.

---

## Page 5744

Thus, the merits of deeds and their relative ranks are not determined by such things; they are determined only by the evidence of the Quran and Sunnah. Many deeds may therefore bring a person worldly authority and wealth, yet the noblest people in Allah’s sight are those most mindful of Him. Whoever worships Allah without knowledge does more harm than good, even if he attains unveilings and an ability to exercise influence over the created world, and even if many ordinary people follow his example. We have discussed this subject at length in its appropriate places. This, then, is “a second principle.”

“A third principle” is that the superiority of one deed over another may be unqualified, as with the superiority of a fundamental of religion over a subsidiary matter, or it may be qualified. One of two deeds may be better for Zayd, while the other is better for Amr; or the two may be equal for a particular person. At a particular time, a deed of lesser merit may be preferable to one of greater merit. Likewise, a deed of lesser merit, for someone able to perform it and benefit from it, may be better than a deed of greater merit for someone who is not.

For example, reciting the Quran is superior to remembrance alone, as established by the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Muslim community. No weight is to be given to the disagreement of ignorant worshippers on this matter. Yet reciting the Quran is forbidden during bowing and prostration, whereas remembrance is prescribed. Likewise, remembrance and supplication during circumambulation of the Kaaba, at Arafat, and in similar circumstances are better than reciting the Quran. The same applies to prescribed remembrances, such as those said upon hearing the call to prayer, entering the mosque or one’s home, leaving either of them, and upon hearing

---

## Page 5745

roosters crowing and donkeys braying, and on similar occasions. In these circumstances, such remembrances are better than reciting the Quran.

Moreover, most spiritual seekers do not understand the Quran when they recite it. They have not yet tasted the sweetness of faith through which the Quran increases their faith. When they devote themselves to remembrance, it grants them a measure of faith whose sweetness and delight they experience. Remembrance is therefore more beneficial to them at that point than recitation they do not understand, when they do not yet possess the faith that would grow through reciting the Quran. But once a person has been granted faith, the Quran increases his faith in a way that remembrance alone cannot. This, then, is “a third principle.”

“A fourth principle” is that a person may perform a deed of greater merit without fulfilling its conditions or being sincere in it. By neglecting its conditions, he falls below someone who performs a deed of lesser merit in full.

These principles and others like them make clear the answer to this questioner, although this sheet cannot accommodate a detailed explanation. And Allah knows best.

---

## Page 5746

The shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About some people who persisted for a time in “spiritual discipline,” then believed that they had refined their essence and said: “We no longer care what we do. Commands and prohibitions are merely formal observances for ordinary people; if they too refined their essence, these would cease to apply to them. Prophethood ultimately amounts to wisdom and the promotion of welfare, and its purpose is to keep ordinary people in check. We are not ordinary people, such that we should be subject to the restraints of religious obligation, for we have refined our essence and understood wisdom.”

Does this statement constitute disbelief on the part of the one who says it? Or is he to be deemed an innovator without being declared a disbeliever? Can such a statement come from someone whose heart holds submission to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace?

He answered:

There is no doubt among people of knowledge and faith that this statement constitutes one of the gravest and most extreme forms of disbelief. It is worse than the position of the Jews and Christians, for the Jew and the Christian believe in part of the Scripture and disbelieve in part. They are indeed the true disbelievers, as has been stated. They acknowledge that Allah issues commands and prohibitions, promises reward and threatens punishment, and that all this applies to them until death. This is if they adhere to Judaism and Christianity in their altered, abrogated forms. But if they are among the hypocrites of their own religious community—as is generally the case with their scholastic theologians

---

## Page 5747

and philosophers—then they are worse than the hypocrites of this ummah, since they openly profess disbelief while concealing hypocrisy. Thus, they are worse than those who outwardly profess faith while concealing hypocrisy.

The point is that those who adhere to an abrogated religion containing alterations are better than these people who claim that commands and prohibitions no longer apply to them at all. In this state, they stand outside all scriptures, religious laws and faiths; they acknowledge no command or prohibition from Allah as binding upon them under any circumstances.

Indeed, they are worse than polytheists who hold fast to remnants of earlier religions, such as the Arab polytheists who retained remnants of the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him. Those people had some measure of truth to which they adhered, even though they were also polytheists. These people, however, acknowledge no truth as binding upon them, imagining that they have been left without restraint, subject to neither commands nor prohibitions.

Whoever maintains that he, or some other group, is no longer subject to any command or prohibition, such that nothing is obligatory or forbidden for them—such people are the most disbelieving people on earth. They are of the same kind as Pharaoh and his ilk. Yet even they must adhere to something by which to live, for humankind cannot live without some form of command and prohibition. Thus, they abandon obedience to and worship of the Most Merciful for obedience to and worship of Satan.

It was Pharaoh who said to Moses:

“And what is the Lord of the worlds?”

Yet he had gods whom he worshipped, as his people said to him:

“and abandon you and your gods.”

---

## Page 5748

But many of these people do not go so far as to deny all obligations and prohibitions and cast off the bonds of servitude altogether. Rather, they claim that certain duties no longer apply to them, or that certain forbidden things are lawful for them. Some claim that the five daily prayers are no longer obligatory for them because they have attained their goal. Others may claim exemption from prayer while in a state of witnessing and presence. They may also claim exemption from congregational prayers, considering their own spiritual focus and presence sufficient. Some claim that Hajj is no longer obligatory for them, despite their ability to perform it, because the Kaaba circumambulates them, or because of some other satanic state. Others consider it lawful to break the fast in Ramadan without a valid religious excuse, claiming that they have no need to fast.

Some consider wine lawful, claiming that it is forbidden only to ordinary people, who quarrel and fight when they drink it, but not to the discerning elite. They claim that it is forbidden to ordinary people who have no righteous deeds, whereas those with pure souls and righteous deeds are permitted to drink it, unlike ordinary people.

This “specious argument” had already occurred to some of the early Muslims, and the Companions agreed that they should be put to death if they did not repent of it. Qudāmah ibn Madʿūn and a group of others drank wine, interpreting the words of the Most High as permitting it:

“There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have consumed, provided they are mindful of Allah, believe, and do righteous deeds.”

When this was reported to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, he, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, and the rest of the Companions agreed that if they acknowledged its prohibition, they were to be flogged; but if they persisted in declaring it lawful, they were to be put to death. And ʿUmar said

---

## Page 5749

to Qudāmah: “You have missed the mark! Had you truly been mindful of Allah, believed, and done righteous deeds, you would not have drunk wine.”

This verse was revealed because, when Allah, glorified is He, prohibited wine—which occurred after the Battle of Uhud—some of the Companions asked, “What, then, of our companions who died while still drinking wine?” Allah therefore revealed this verse, explaining that whoever consumed something when it was not yet prohibited incurred no blame, provided he was among the believers who were mindful of Allah and acted righteously.

Likewise, when He changed the direction of prayer and commanded them to face the Kaaba after they had been commanded to face Jerusalem, Allah Most High said:

“Allah would never let your faith go to waste.”

That is, your prayers facing Jerusalem. He thus explained that whoever acts in obedience to Allah will be rewarded by Allah for doing so, even if He prohibits that act at another time. Whoever regards as lawful something He has not prohibited incurs no blame, provided he is among the believers who are mindful of Allah, even if Allah prohibits it at another time.

Once He had prohibited wine, however, regarding it as lawful became comparable to praying towards the Rock after that had been prohibited, observing the Sabbath as an act of worship, regarding fornication as lawful, and other matters concerning which the Shariah has established rulings different from those that previously applied. No one is entitled to hold fast to any provision of an abrogated law. Whoever does so is like someone clinging to abrogated provisions of earlier religious laws.

For this reason, the Companions agreed that they would put to death anyone who declared wine lawful. Those who had done so then regretted it, realized that they had been mistaken, and despaired of repentance. Then he wrote

---

## Page 5750

—ʿUmar—to Qudāmah, saying:

“Hā Mīm.”

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.”

“The Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, Severe in punishment.”

“I do not know which of your two sins is greater: your first declaring what is forbidden lawful, or your subsequently despairing of Allah’s mercy?”

This matter, upon which the Companions agreed, is also agreed upon by the imams of Islam; they do not dispute it. Whoever denies obligations whose obligatory nature is manifest and established by mass transmission—such as the five daily prayers, fasting the month of Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the Ancient House—or denies the prohibition of things whose forbidden nature is manifest and established by mass transmission—such as acts of sexual immorality, injustice, wine, gambling, fornication, and the like—or denies the permissibility of things whose lawful nature is manifest and established by mass transmission—such as bread, meat, and marriage—is an unbeliever and apostate. He is called upon to repent; if he repents, he is spared, and otherwise he is put to death. If he conceals such beliefs, he is a clandestine unbeliever and hypocrite who, according to most scholars, is not called upon to repent. Rather, once this is exposed, he is put to death without being called upon to repent.

Among these are those who deem certain acts of sexual immorality lawful, such as forming bonds of brotherhood with women outside the prohibited degrees of marriage and being alone with them, claiming that these women receive blessings through what they do with them, even though it is forbidden by the Shariah.

The same applies to those who deem such conduct lawful with beardless youths and claim that taking pleasure in looking at them and having physical contact with them is a path for some spiritual wayfarers, whereby they ascend from love of the created being to love of the Creator. They encourage acts that lead to the gravest sexual abomination, and may even deem that abomination itself lawful, as do those who say that sodomy is permissible by right of slave ownership. All of these are unbelievers by the consensus of the Muslims, and they are comparable to

---

## Page 5751

those who deem it lawful to kill Muslims unjustly, take their women captive, seize their wealth as spoils, and commit other forbidden acts whose prohibition is manifest and established by mass transmission.

Some people, however, may be excusably ignorant of certain rulings. No one is therefore judged an unbeliever until the proof has been established against him through the message reaching him. As Allah Most High says:

“So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers.”

And He Most High says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

Thus, if a man embraces Islam without knowing that prayer is obligatory upon him, or without knowing that wine is forbidden, he does not become an unbeliever for failing to believe that the former is obligatory and the latter forbidden. Indeed, he is not punished until the proof brought by the Prophet reaches him.

Scholars have even differed concerning someone who embraces Islam in dār al-harb (the abode of war), does not know that prayer is obligatory, and then learns of its obligation: must he make up the prayers he missed while ignorant? There are two positions within the school of Imam Ahmad and elsewhere:

The first is that he is not required to make them up. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah.

The second is that he must make them up. This is the well-known position among the followers of al-Shāfi'ī.

Indeed, the disagreement among scholars extends to anyone who omits an obligation before the proof reaches him: for example, someone who neglects prayer when water is unavailable, believing that prayer is not valid with dry ablution; or someone who eats until he can distinguish a white thread from a black thread, believing that this is what the verse means, as happened

---

## Page 5752

to some of the Companions—or someone who touches his penis or eats camel meat without performing ablution, then learns that ablution is obligatory in such cases. In these and similar cases, must he make up the missed acts of worship? There are two positions within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

The underlying question is whether a revealed ruling becomes binding upon a legally accountable person before he has had the opportunity to hear it. There are “three views” within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. One holds that it becomes binding in all cases; another holds that it does not become binding in any case; and a third distinguishes between an address that abrogates an earlier ruling and one that introduces a ruling—as with those who face the qiblah (direction of prayer).

The correct view, supported by the scriptural evidence, is that a revealed ruling does not become binding upon anyone before he has had the opportunity to hear it. Thus, he is not required to make up the missed acts in the cases mentioned or others like them. Moreover, they agree that he bears no sin, for Allah has pardoned this community for mistakes and forgetfulness. If this is so regarding the attribution of sin, how much more so regarding declaring someone an unbeliever?

Many people may grow up in places and times in which much of the knowledge conveyed by the prophets has faded away, until no one remains to convey the Book and wisdom with which Allah sent His Messenger. Such a person consequently does not know much of what Allah sent His Messenger with, and there is no one there to convey it to him. A person in this situation does not become an unbeliever.

For this reason, the imams agree that someone who grew up in a remote desert region, far from people of knowledge and faith, and who has only recently embraced Islam, is not judged an unbeliever for denying any of these manifest rulings established by mass transmission until he learns what the Messenger brought. Hence the hadith states:

“A time will come upon people when they will know neither prayer nor zakat nor

---

## Page 5753

fasting nor Hajj, except for elderly men and women who say, ‘We knew our forefathers saying, “There is no god but Allah.”’ They know neither prayer, zakat nor Hajj. He then said, ‘Nor fasting. It will save them from the Fire.’”

This principle is also supported by what al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated in their Sahīh collections from Abū Hurayrah: the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“A man—who had never put forward a single good deed—instructed his family to burn him when he died, then scatter half of him over the land and half over the sea. For, by Allah, if Allah had power over him, He would punish him as He had never punished anyone in all creation. When the man died, they did as he had instructed. Allah then commanded the land to gather what it contained, and commanded the sea to gather what it contained. Then He said, ‘Why did you do this?’ He replied, ‘Out of fear of You, my Lord, and You know best.’ So Allah forgave him.”

Another wording states:

“A man had sinned excessively against himself. When death approached him, he instructed his sons, saying, ‘When I die, burn me, then grind me to powder and scatter me over the sea. By Allah, if my Lord has power over me, He will punish me as He has never punished anyone.’”

He said: “They did that to him. Then Allah said to the earth, ‘Give back what you have taken,’ and there he stood. He said to him, ‘What prompted you to do what you did?’ He replied, ‘Fear of You, my Lord’—or he said, ‘Dread of You.’ So he was forgiven on that account.”

Another transmission states:

“Allah said to everything that had taken any part of him, ‘Give back what you have taken of him.’”

Al-Bukhārī also related this account through Hudhayfah and 'Uqbah ibn 'Amr, from Hudhayfah, who reported that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“There was

---

## Page 5754

a man among those who lived before you who thought poorly of his own deeds. He said to his family, ‘When I die, take me and scatter me over the sea on a hot day.’ They did so, and Allah gathered him together. Then He said, ‘What prompted you to do what you did?’ He replied, ‘Nothing but fear of You.’ So he was forgiven.”

Another transmission states:

“A man was approaching death. When he had lost all hope of surviving, he instructed his family, ‘When I die, gather a large quantity of firewood for me and set it alight. Once it has consumed my flesh, reached my bones and burned them, take them and grind them to powder. Then choose a day and scatter me over the sea.’ Allah gathered him together and said to him, ‘Why did you do that?’ He replied, ‘Out of fear of You.’ So Allah forgave him.”

‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amr said, “I heard him—meaning the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace)—say that.” The man had been a grave robber.

This man thought that Allah would have no power over him if he were scattered in this way, and that He would not restore him to life once he was in that state. Both denying the power of Allah Most High and denying the resurrection of bodies, even after they have been scattered, constitute disbelief. Yet despite his belief in Allah and in His command, and his fear of Him, he was ignorant of this matter, misguided and mistaken in this assumption. Allah therefore forgave him for that.

The hadith explicitly shows that the man hoped that Allah would not restore him to life if he did that. At the very least, this means that he doubted the Resurrection. That is disbelief—if the proof conveyed by prophethood has been established against one who denies it, he is judged a disbeliever—and it plainly shows his lack of belief

---

## Page 5755

in Allah Most High. Whoever interprets his words, “If Allah has power over me,” as referring to decreeing or constraining has gone far afield and distorted the words from their proper meanings. He only ordered that he be burned and scattered so that he would not be gathered together and restored to life.

He said:

“When I die, burn me, then grind me to powder, then scatter me on the wind over the sea. For, by Allah, if my Lord has power over me, He will surely punish me as He has never punished anyone.”

His introducing this second sentence with the conjunction fa (“for”), immediately after the first, shows that it gives the reason for the first: he did this so that Allah would not have power over him once he had done so. Had he acknowledged that Allah would have the same power over him whether he did this or not, doing it would have served him no purpose. Furthermore, decreeing his fate and constraining him are both consistent with punishment, whereas he set his being scattered in opposition to the Lord’s having power over him. He said:

“For, by Allah, if Allah has power over me, He will surely punish me as He has never punished anyone in all creation.”

The condition cannot be identical to its consequence. Moreover, had that been his meaning, he would have said, “For, by Allah, if my Lord requites me—or if my Lord punishes me—He will surely inflict a punishment on me,” as is the usual manner of speaking in such cases. Furthermore, the word qadara has no basis in the language with the meaning “to constrain.”

Whoever cites His words, “And measure the links well,” and His words, “And whoever has his provision restricted,” as evidence for this has cited what does not support his claim.

For the wording in His statement, “And measure the links well,” means: make them to the proper measure, neither exceeding it nor falling short. And His statement, “And whoever has his provision restricted,” means that He has allotted him enough provision to meet his needs

---

## Page 5756

without any surplus, for if his provision fell below that, he could not survive.

As for interpreting qadara as qaddara, meaning to decree good and evil, he did not say, “If my Lord decrees punishment for me.” Rather, he said, “If my Lord decrees my fate.” Decreeing encompasses both good and evil, so it would not be sound to say, “If Allah decrees my fate,” because whatever will benefit or harm him has already been decreed and settled for him. Moreover, had he meant decreeing or constraining, he would not have thought that what he did could prevent either. There are many proofs that this distorted interpretation is false, but this is not the place to elaborate on them.

At most, this shows that he was a man who did not know all the attributes that rightfully belong to Allah, or understand in detail the implications of His being All-Powerful. Many believers may be ignorant of such matters without being disbelievers. Whoever examines the authentic hadiths will find similar reports supporting this, such as what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from ʿĀ’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—who said:

“Shall I not tell you about myself and the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace?”

We said, “Yes.”

She said: “When it was my night, on which the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was staying with me, he returned, took off his cloak, removed his sandals and placed them by his feet. Then he gently picked up his cloak, moved quietly, gently opened the door and went out, then gently closed it. three times. Then he turned away, and I turned away. He quickened his pace, and I quickened mine; he jogged, and I jogged; he ran, and I ran. I reached home before him and went inside. I had barely lain down when he said, ‘What is the matter with you, Ā’ishah, panting and out of breath?’

She said: “I replied, ‘Nothing.’

Here was Ā’ishah, the Mother of the Believers, asking the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—whether Allah knows everything that people conceal. ## Page 5758

after the proof has been established is one of the fundamentals of faith, and denying His knowledge of all things is like denying His power over all things. Nevertheless, she deserved blame for her sin. It is thus clear that this statement constitutes disbelief. However, its speaker is not to be declared a disbeliever until he has received sufficient knowledge to establish against him the proof whose disregard constitutes disbelief. Evidence demonstrating the falsity of this statement abounds in the Quran, the Sunnah, and the agreement of the early generations of this Muslim community, its imams, and its shaykhs; there is no need to set it out at length. Indeed, it is a necessarily known tenet of Islam that commands and prohibitions remain binding upon Allah’s servants until death.

As for the question, “Could such a statement come from someone whose heart holds submission to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace?” the answer is:

This cannot come from anyone who acknowledges prophethood at all. Rather, whoever says this disbelieves in all the prophets and messengers, for they all brought commands and prohibitions binding upon Allah’s servants until death. Indeed, this statement cannot come from anyone whose heart holds submission to Allah and who acknowledges Him as the God of all creation. Such acknowledgment necessarily entails being a servant of Allah, submissive to Him. Whoever permits a person to do whatever he wishes without submitting to Allah in worship has denied that Allah is his God.

---

## Page 5759

As for their claim to have attained tajawhur, whereupon they say, “We no longer care what we do,” they should be asked: “What do you mean by this?” If they mean that the soul has become pure and undefiled, no longer drawn toward ruinous desires and whims, then, were this true, it would mean that the soul had become obedient, with no impulses toward disobedience. It would readily comply with what is commanded and have no inclination toward what is forbidden. At most, this would mean that it was protected from sin and did not seek to do evil. This would not exempt it from commands and prohibitions, just as the angels remain subject to them.

If such people say, “What we do does not contradict this,” they should be told: “If what you do belongs to the category of ruinous desires, then you have contradicted your claim that your souls no longer have any such desires. If it belongs to the category of righteous deeds, then there is no objection to deeds of that kind.” Thus, their words are plainly self-contradictory if, by the soul’s tajawhur, they mean its purity and freedom from human impurities. Moreover, such perfection is impossible for human beings so long as their souls remain in their bodies.

For this reason, the shaykhs rejected such claims, as related in the well-known reports from Shaykh Abū ʿAlī al-Rūdhbārī and others. The highest-ranking people are the prophets—peace be upon them—yet Allah commanded them to repent and seek forgiveness. Even the Seal of the Messengers received this command from Allah in some of the last Quranic revelation sent down to him, when He said:

“When Allah’s help comes, and the conquest,
and you see people entering Allah’s religion in multitudes,
then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

---

## Page 5760

For this reason, the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars was that the prophets are protected from being allowed to persist in sins, and that Allah restores them through the repentance He loves—“He loves those who repent”—even if the good deeds of the righteous count as misdeeds for those brought near to Him. Whatever sins they committed were for the sake of the perfection attained in the end through repentance, not the deficiency at the outset through sin.

As for others, such protection is not assured to them. Only the ignorant among the Rāfidah and the extremist ascetics claim absolute infallibility for anyone other than the prophets. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

As for their statement, “Prophethood ultimately comes down to wisdom and welfare,” there is no doubt that Allah sends the prophets to bring about the welfare of His servants in this life and the Hereafter. There is no doubt that Allah has commanded His servants to do what benefits them and forbidden them from doing what harms them. Nor is there any doubt that wisdom consists of knowledge and acting upon it, as Mālik ibn Anas and other leading scholars explained. But what in any of this entails that some servants should be exempt from its requirements? Only someone foolish and corrupt departs from wisdom and welfare:

“Who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?”

“And Allah does not love corruption.”

As for their statement, “Its purpose is to keep ordinary people in check, and we are not ordinary people,” the first claim is heresy and hypocrisy, and the second is a lie and a fabrication. The purpose of the revealed laws is not merely to keep ordinary people in check; rather, their purpose is to bring about righteousness inwardly

---

## Page 5761

and outwardly, for both the elite and ordinary people, in this life and the Hereafter. However, keeping ordinary people in check is one of the benefits of the punishments prescribed in this world. As ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“Indeed, Allah restrains through governing authority what He does not restrain through the Quran.”

Hypocrites and the wicked are deterred by the punishments they witness and restrained from violating prohibitions. This is one of the benefits of the prescribed punishments administered by the ruler.

As for the benefits of the commands and prohibitions, they are too great for any discourse or book to enumerate. Indeed, they encompass every good that is sought and desired, while departing from them entails every evil and corruption.

These people’s claim to belong to the elite places them among the very dregs of the hypocrites among ordinary people. They fall within Allah’s description of the hypocrites in His words:

“Among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ but they are not believers.”

“They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none but themselves, though they do not realize it.”

“In their hearts is a disease, and Allah has increased their disease. They will have a painful punishment because they used to lie.”

“When they are told, ‘Do not spread corruption on earth,’ they say, ‘We are only setting things right.’”

“Indeed, it is they who spread corruption, but they do not realize it.”

“When they are told, ‘Believe as the people have believed,’ they say, ‘Shall we believe as the fools have believed?’ Indeed, it is they who are the fools, but they do not know.”

And so on, until His words:

They also fall within such words of His as:

to seek judgment from false authorities, although they were commanded to reject them. Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

unlike someone who refrains from them while acknowledging the excellence of those who perform them at that stage and esteeming their spiritual state. this verse is evidence against them, not in their favor. Al-Hasan al-Basrī said, “Allah has set no endpoint for the deeds of the believers short of death,” and he recited His words:

## Page 5764

“And we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us.”

They said this while in Hell. They explained that they had persisted in neglecting prayer and zakat, denying the Hereafter, and engaging in vain discourse with those who did so, until certainty came to them.

Clearly, while in that state, they did not believe in it during their worldly lives, nor were they among those of whom Allah said:

“And of the Hereafter they are certain.”

Rather, what is meant is that what they had been promised came to them: that is certainty. The same meaning occurs in the authentic hadith concerning the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When ʿUthmān ibn Mazʿūn died, one of the women testified that he would enter Paradise. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to her, ‘How do you know? By Allah, although I am Allah’s Messenger, I do not know what will be done with me.’”

He also said:

“As for ʿUthmān, certainty has come to him from his Lord.”

That is, what He had promised him had come to him: that is certainty. The word yaqīn (certainty) follows the morphological pattern faʿīl. Whether faʿīl here has the sense of mafʿūl, a passive participle—meaning death—as in habīb (beloved), nasīh (one sincerely advised), and dhabīh (one slaughtered), or whether it is a verbal noun used in place of a passive participle, as in His words:

“This is Allah’s creation,”

and His words:

“Allah’s command has come,”

and the expressions, “The ruler struck,” and “May Allah forgive you”—it has also been said: their expression “a mighty power,” and similar expressions, which are numerous—the meaning does not differ under either analysis.

Rather, certainty is what the servants have been promised concerning the Hereafter. His words:

“Until certainty comes to you,”

are like saying, “What you have been promised will come to you.”

But as for supposing that the meaning is: “Worship Him until you attain certainty, and thereafter no worship

is required of you”—this is disbelief by the unanimous agreement of the leading scholars of the Muslims. The leading scholars and spiritual masters of the religion have always vehemently denounced these hypocrites, even if they are ascetics and devoted worshippers, people of spiritual unveiling and influence over creation, or masters of dialectical theology and rational inquiry in the sciences. Some of these things may be found among people of disbelief and hypocrisy, including polytheists and the People of the Book. What distinguishes the people of Paradise from the people of Hell is faith and piety—the qualities of Allah’s allies. As He said:

“Indeed, Allah’s allies shall have no fear, nor shall they grieve—those who believed and were mindful of Him.”

As for their appeal to the story of Moses and al-Khadir, they invoke it in two ways:

(The first is their claim that al-Khadir was directly witnessing the all-encompassing will of the Lord and the universal divine will, which is the “cosmic reality.” For this reason, they maintain, he was free of blame for violating the commands and prohibitions of the revealed Law.

This is profound ignorance and misguidance—indeed, profound hypocrisy and disbelief. ## Page 5767

Furthermore, Moses, peace be upon him, believed in divine decree and understood it. Indeed, his followers among the Children of Israel also believed in divine decree. Would anyone with the least intelligence imagine that Moses sought to learn from al-Khidr belief in divine decree and that it removes blame, when Moses knew more about divine decree than al-Khidr did? Moreover, if this had been the underlying meaning of al-Khidr’s story, he would have explained it to Moses, saying, “I was witnessing the divine will and decree.” But that was not the case. As for the second point, some of these people imagine that certain friends of Allah may depart from the prophetic law, just as al-Khidr was permitted not to follow Moses. Many of them rank someone whom they claim to be a friend of Allah above a prophet, either absolutely or in certain respects, claiming that al-Khidr’s story provides evidence for their position. All these assertions are among the gravest forms of ignorance and misguidance—indeed, among the gravest forms of hypocrisy, heresy, and disbelief.

For it is known as a matter of necessity in Islam that the mission of Muhammad ibn Abd

Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—extends to all people: Arabs and non-Arabs, kings and ascetics, scholars and ordinary people; that it endures until the Day of Resurrection—indeed, it encompasses both jinn and humankind—and that no created being may depart from following and obeying him or from adhering to the religion he prescribes for his community and the way he has established for them: fulfilling what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden. ## Page 5770

For this reason, since distortion and alteration have crept into what the People of the Book transmit from the prophets, we believe whatever we know to have truly come from them, reject whatever we know to be false, and neither affirm nor deny whatever we cannot ascertain. As al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When the People of the Book relate something to you, neither affirm nor deny it. They might tell you something false and you believe them, or tell you something true and you disbelieve them. Rather, say: ‘We believe in what has been sent down to us and what has been sent down to you.’”

One point that exposes their error in citing the story of Moses and al-Khidr to justify contravening the revealed law is that Moses—peace be upon him—was not sent to al-Khidr, nor did Allah oblige al-Khidr to follow and obey him. Indeed, it is established in the two Sahīh collections that al-Khidr said to him:

“Moses, I possess knowledge from Allah which He has taught me and which you do not know; and you possess knowledge from Allah which He has taught you and which I do not know.”

This was because Moses’ mission was restricted to his own people. It is also established in the authentic hadith collections, through several chains of transmission, that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said, describing the distinctions Allah had granted him over the other prophets:

“A prophet would be sent exclusively to his own people, whereas I have been sent to all humankind.”

Thus, the call of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—extends to all people. No one may exempt himself from following and obeying him, nor can anyone dispense with his message, whereas al-Khidr was permitted not to follow and obey Moses

---

## Page 5771

having no need of him because of what Allah had taught him.

No one whom Islam has reached may say to Muhammad, “I possess knowledge from Allah which He has taught me and which you do not know.” Whoever permits this, or believes that any person—whether an ascetic, a devoted worshipper, or anyone else—may exempt himself from Muhammad’s call and from following him—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is a disbeliever by the consensus of the Muslims. The evidence for this in the Quran and Sunnah is too abundant to recount here.

The story of al-Khidr involves no departure from the revealed law. Thus, when al-Khidr explained to Moses his reasons for doing what he had done, Moses agreed with him, and they no longer differed. Had al-Khidr’s actions contravened the law revealed to Moses, Moses would not have agreed with him. Similar situations occur among believers: one of two people may know of a circumstance that makes an action permissible under the revealed law, while the other is unaware of that circumstance, even though he may be superior to the first.

For example, two people enter someone’s house. One knows that the owner willingly allows him to make use of his home, whether through verbal permission or otherwise, and so he does so. This is permissible under the revealed law. The other, unaware of this permission, refrains.

Making a hole in the boat was a case of this kind. Al-Khidr knew that ahead of them was a king who seized every boat by force. It was in the boat owners’ interest, and what they would have chosen had they known this, to prevent him from seizing it . . . (1) better than having it taken from them.
